docs.title: Flux
docs.text:
Flux searches for better designs and keeps only what it can prove. It makes designs with a script, a model or a coding agent, checks each one against your tests, measures the ones that pass with real tools, and decides from your objectives. It is built for hardware and software design-space exploration: RTL on an open 7 nm flow, Python and C code, cache prefetchers, or any program with settings to tune.

  • First loop

    A complete loop from an empty folder, in Python only: no model, no hardware tools.

    First loop →

  • Loop crafter

    Build the document in your browser, step by step, with the web app's own configurator.

    Loop crafter →

  • Write a loop with an agent

    Say what you want, give it your files, and let an agent write and check the loop.

    Write a loop with an agent →

docs.title: How a loop works
docs.text: A loop is a folder: a document, problem.yaml, and the scripts it names. Each pass, Flux chooses what to try, makes a design, runs your checks (a design that fails is never measured), runs the measurements cheapest first, and keeps the design that best meets your objectives. Every design, number and refusal goes on the record, so a run can stop and resume, and a result can be traced to what produced it.

docs.title: Preview app
docs.text: The preview runs the Flux web app in your browser: it needs JavaScript.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
Start with the working loop, copy a bundled example, or use flux new NAME. The document describes the experiment; the scripts beside it define how to generate, check, and measure a design. Use the Document reference for defaults and allowed values; flux help document prints the same essentials in a terminal, one part at a time (flux help document keys, test, measure, golden, software, search, trunk, layout, presets).

Keep each file where its role is: the scripts the document names beside it, papers and specs in library/, method notes in knowledge/, the gate's tests in tests/ (hidden from the agents), a Python package the commands import in lib/src/<package>/ (only lib/src is put on the Python path). flux task check notes a file no document names outside those folders: delete it, or name it.

docs.title: Define the goal and interface
docs.text:
Write statement as the goal and contract as the interface and restrictions. State the function signature or module ports, supported inputs, numerical accuracy, and any implementation restrictions. Put executable checks in flow.check: prose alone does not establish correctness.

Choose the artifact language, such as python, systemverilog, or cpp. Flux uses it for the generated file extension. Say it: without it the design is a .txt file.

statement: Find a fast implementation of count_primes(n).
contract: >-
  Export count_primes(n). Return the number of primes strictly below n for
  nonnegative integer n. Do not change the interface or the benchmark.
language: python

docs.title: Choose how designs are made
docs.text:
Approach Configuration Use it when Script design: {run: "..."} You can render each parameter into a design FluxAgent design: flux You want generated code or algorithms; this is the default Coding agent design: claude (also codex, opencode) The design needs edits across files or interactive checks Fixed candidates design: {catalog: [...]} You already have artifacts to compare Tune settings A search space, with no generator command Commands consume the chosen settings directly

A script generator writes {artifact}; its stdout is not the artifact. For example:

flow:
  design:
    run: ["{python}", "{home}/render.py", "{artifact}", "{block}"]

The search supplies {block}. Use {point} when the generator needs the entire point as a JSON file, or {params} for settings shared by your own commands. See Search and agents for the search and agent setup.

Commands accept a string or a list of arguments. A string is split into arguments, rather than executed by a shell: if you need a pipeline, put it in a script or explicitly use bash -c. Prefer argument lists when paths or values contain spaces. A command beginning with flux uses the same Flux installation as the loop.

docs.title: Build a gate, cheapest check first
docs.text:
Checks run in the order written. The first failure refuses the candidate and later checks do not run. Name them for the action they perform:

flow:
  check:
    build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"
    correctness:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      timeout_s: 120

A check named build treats every nonzero exit as a build failure. Any check exiting 3 also means the candidate did not build. Other checks use the default N failing pattern when it is present; otherwise exit 0 passes and a nonzero exit counts as one failure. Debug output on stderr is retained and is not, by itself, a failure.

For a checker with a different output format, specify the pattern deliberately:

flow:
  check:
    tests:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      count_re: 'failures=(\d+)'

count_re captures an integer failure count. fail_re counts matching failures instead. These patterns scan stdout and stderr; a match can report failure even when the process exits 0. Keep debug messages distinct from your machine-readable test summary.

For RTL, define the ports and reference function in golden.py, then use:

flow:
  check:
    lint: "fluxpreset rtl lint {artifact}"
    golden: "fluxpreset golden {artifact} --golden {home}/golden.py"

The golden model describes vectors, clocked designs, and floating-point tolerances. flux tools lists the built-in checks and their commands, and the configurator offers them as a check's Type or a measurement's Tool under Flux presets.

docs.title: Measure surviving designs
docs.text:
Measurements run stage by stage in document order. Start with a cheap screen and put the costliest measurement last. A custom stage must print the metrics it declares:

flow:
  measure:
    screen:
      run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} --quick"
      metrics: [time_ms, bytes]
      cutoff: {metric: bytes, below: 4096}
    confirm:
      run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} --full"
      metrics: [time_ms, bytes]
      timeout_s: 1800

The --quick and --full flags here are flags your benchmark must implement. It should print, for example, time_ms=2.31 bytes=2048. Metrics can appear on stdout or stderr. A nonzero exit is a failed measurement, whatever the command printed before it: its numbers are not taken, the design is refused at that stage (a refused row on the record, kept), and its task in Live is ✗. Use metrics_re for a different output format.

Every stage must declare the metrics required by its objectives. The command belongs to the application, or is one of Flux's presets (fluxpreset rtl measure ...; see Presets). Declare the tools it requires too:

flow:
  measure:
    screen:
      run: "fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage synth --clock-ps 1000"
      metrics: [fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count]
      needs: [yosys, openroad]
    confirm:
      run: "fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage place --clock-ps 1000"
      metrics: [fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count]
      needs: [yosys, openroad]
      timeout_s: 1800

needs: [tool_name] declares required executables for a custom stage. A stage is skipped when a declared tool is missing; check the reported stage before treating a screening number as a confirmed result.

docs.title: Cutoffs and estimates
docs.text:
cutoff decides whether a measured design proceeds: at is a minimum, below is a maximum, and within retains a fraction of the best result for that metric. A list requires every condition to pass:

cutoff:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, at: 1000}
  - {metric: area_um2, below: 80}

An optional estimate can screen a design before paying for the tool:

estimate: {kind: surrogate, margin: 0.05}

The surrogate uses prior measurements at that stage and needs at least three rows. An estimate outside a cutoff or objective limit by more than the margin skips that stage. Estimates are not measurements; enable this only when that screening trade-off fits your experiment. The reference also covers command and model estimators.

docs.title: Define what wins
docs.text:
Separate limits (objectives with goal) from preferences (objectives without one):

objectives:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, direction: maximize, goal: 1000}
  - {metric: area_um2, direction: minimize, goal: 80}
  - {metric: power_w, direction: minimize}

This asks for at least 1000 MHz, at most 80 µm², then minimum power among feasible designs. Goal-less preferences are compared in their written order. An absolute goal uses the deepest stage unless its stage names another. If nothing meets every limit, the report describes the closest standing design and its shortfall; it does not produce a feasible decision artifact.

Use balance: true on multiple goal-less objectives for a compromise at the frontier's knee. A relative limit such as {metric: speedup, direction: maximize, keep: 0.9, above: 1.0} keeps 90% of the best measured gain over the baseline, instead of specifying an absolute goal.

docs.title: Control time and concurrency
docs.text:
budget:
  passes: 10
  repairs_per_design: 6
  designs_at_once: 1
  tools_at_once: 1

passes bounds the whole run; repairs_per_design bounds attempts to fix a design. designs_at_once is designs at once, wherever they are made: passes, branches, a search pass's designs. A pass is one design, so passes: 6 with designs_at_once: 3 makes six designs, three at a time. tools_at_once is tool runs at once across the whole loop: checks, measurements and the agents' own probes. They are separate knobs. On a server, an administrator must allow parallel work for the app; otherwise its concurrency cap wins. In the configurator, both are Extra › Running, which also says whether the admin allows the loop parallel work and links to its Settings › Preferences › Advanced. Keep timed benchmarks isolated with tools_at_once: 1. The budget reference includes those settings.

The configurator's Graph step starts with Runs as Passes | Trunk: Trunk says the document's flow: as trunk: (passes or a trunk) and redraws the ring -- Design says its agents (claude + codex), Search a bud every 10 decided designs when an agent works it. Design's panel then gives each agent a pick of its own, with its Thinking, its effort and its Model (the agent's own list, as in Settings, or any name; empty, the agent's own), written as that agent's model:; + Add an agent adds one, the same agent again with another model too (by: [claude, {by: claude, model: opus}]). Its Per design card keeps the prototype: a failed design goes back to its agent, never repaired in a branch. Extra › Running reads Designs · Tool runs, the same under Passes and Trunk: under Trunk, Designs at once counts branches, and twice that may wait. Back to Passes, Design keeps its first agent and its model, and a notice says so. Where trunk mode cannot run the loop (a search over parameters, Plan, Design not by a coding agent) the switch is disabled and its line names what stands in the way.

Omit passes, or use 0, to run until manually stopped. Finding a feasible design or a stalled search does not end an unlimited run. Individual attempts still have their budgets and timeouts; Run, stop, resume explains stopping and resuming.

docs.title: Add context and reusable settings
docs.text:
params: {input_size: 1000000, repetitions: 9}
flow:
  knowledge:
    library: [spec.md, reference.py]
    hidden: [check.py]

params reaches scripts through the {params} JSON file. knowledge.library joins the loop's library, which agents read on demand (flux library), never pasted; knowledge.hidden keeps the gate's files from the agents. Knowledge, skills, hidden paths covers what agents read and what they may not.

Check each edited document with flux task check FOLDER, then do a bounded run with flux task run FOLDER --passes 1. Continue with Search and agents or look up the remaining fields in the Document reference.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Which loop shape fits which problem. Start with flux new NAME, or copy a bundled example from flux/applications/ in the source, including its scripts.

docs.title: Pick a starting point
docs.text: You have Start from Model? A program with settings to tune (flags, block sizes) flux new NAME, commands using knob placeholders No A script that writes a design from settings flux new NAME, a generator command and a search space No A hardware family you can spell from settings Copy applications/adder16/ No A function you want written and made fast Copy applications/primes/ Yes A hardware module you want written Copy applications/mul8/ Yes Only a description, a spec, some files flux ask Yes

docs.title: Tune a program's settings
docs.text:
statement: The fastest block size and thread count for my kernel.
flow:
  search:
    params: sweep
    space:
      block: [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
      threads: [1, 2, 4, 8]
  check: "{python} {home}/check.py {block} {threads}"
  measure:
    bench:
      run: "{home}/run.sh --block {block} --threads {threads}"
      metrics: [time_ms]
objectives: [{metric: time_ms, direction: minimize}]
budget: {tools_at_once: 1}
  • Time alone. Set budget.tools_at_once: 1, and pin the program's own threads if it has any. Measured side by side, runs disturb each other: a block size can look many times better than it is. Checks share the one pool of slots, so no check runs beside a timing either.
  • Keep the gate even when correctness seems obvious: a setting that crashes or returns the wrong answer is refused before it is timed.
  • A knob is any placeholder: {block} works in any command, and in a generator script.

docs.title: Choose a search for the space
Trade-offs and limits
docs.text:
• One limit, then the rest: a goal on the first objective, then the next decides among the designs that meet it: "the smallest that makes 1 GHz".
  • A true trade-off: two objectives without a goal and the pareto search. The report shows the front; balance: true picks its knee.
  • A hard limit on a cost: make it a check (refuse what exceeds it), a stage cutoff, or a search's floor ({metric: storage_bytes, at: 98304}).

docs.title: When a model writes the designs
docs.text:
• It gets it wrong a lot: give it the facts in flow.knowledge (a spec, reference code, a method note) and skills. flux log RECORD shows what it was told and what it said.
  • Numeric hardware (floating point, transcendentals, fixed point): use a golden model and design.prototype: true. The model proves the algorithm in Python on every input first, and the loop spells it as RTL. A prototype too costly to be worth synthesising (over 2,000) is made cheaper before anything is built.
  • A coding agent instead: flow.design: claude (or codex, opencode). It writes in its own folder; the loop runs the gate and brings a failure back to the same session. With a prototype stage, it writes the prototype, which suits hard numeric functions better than asking for RTL directly.
  • Let it run: a run goes on until you stop it, and each start resumes from the record. When nothing is left to try, it explores for a better design.
  • Steer it: a note typed in the TUI (f), or in the loop's Chat in the web app, reaches the next prompt.

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text:
• flux task run FOLDER --json answer.json: the decision, the front and the refusals as JSON.
  • flux loop summary --loop RECORD --html: the summary as an HTML page with the front, the best so far over time, and every design.
  • flux log RECORD: every model and agent turn, for when a run did not go as you expected.

docs.title: Knowledge, skills, hidden paths
docs.text: What the model and the agents can look up besides the document, and what they may not read. The fields are in the Document reference.

docs.title: Files, notes and papers
docs.text:
flow:
  knowledge:
    library: [spec.md, reference.py, notes/]
    by: claude
    insights: {by: rules}
  • The library: the loop's library/ folder, plus the files and folders library lists beside the document (a spec, reference code, a method note; a folder counts as each of its files). Each project the loop is linked into adds its library, read-only, at library/<project>@<group>/ -- while the loop's owner is a member of that project. The AI looks the library up when it needs it, with the commands in Reading the library. flux library lists the library one line each, flux library "<words>" gives the nearest files with their best passages, flux library read NAME reads one. Hidden paths never appear.
  • by says who summarises the papers: flux, FluxAgent (the default), or an agent.
  • insights: {by: rules} draws facts from the loop's results, no AI; {by: <agent>} has that agent draw conclusions, each citing its designs; unsaid or {by: off}, none. flux library insights prints them (--json for data).

  • by: off turns all reading off.

  • A project's knowledge (web app, a project's Knowledge tab): entries its people keep, each one insight under one of the project's topics, proven by designs of its loops -- added by hand, or proposed by Flux's collector for curators to accept or reject. A loop linked into the project reads its accepted entries with flux library: flux library lists each project's topics and its entries' headlines after the library, flux library "<words>" [--topic t] [--project p] gives the matching entries whole, flux library entry <id> one; --json for data. A pinned entry comes first. The entries are those of the loop's start: a change reaches the next start. See Groups › Knowledge.

  • Project entries become ideas. Each accepted entry becomes one idea in every linked loop's ideas notebook, tagged with its project ("from silicon@hw-lab" in Results › Ideas). It is scored, suggested and queued like any other idea, so the loop tries it only if it ranks. A global project's entries reach a loop only with the link's learning on. When an entry is retired, its idea is marked for deletion for a person to decide.

A model that keeps getting a design wrong usually lacks a fact, not effort: a method note with the method and the facts (not a design) helps more than more passes.

docs.title: Reading the library: flux library
docs.text:
The library -- the loop's own and every project library it reads -- is read in pieces, never a whole PDF at once:

flux library                               # every document, one line each: name · pages or lines · what it is;
                                           #   then each linked project's topics and accepted entries' headlines
flux library "QUERY" [--n 5]               # the nearest files, each with its digest or its line and its 3 best
                                           #   passages, and the project entries that match, whole
flux library digest  PAPER                 # its digest
flux library outline PAPER                 # its sections, each with its pages and lines
flux library read    PAPER --section 3.2   # one section
flux library read    PAPER --around "QUERY"  # the passages that match best, with a little context
flux library read    PAPER --lines 120-220 # or --pages 3-4 for a PDF; --from 221 goes on from a line
flux library entry   12                    # one project entry, whole
flux library insights                      # what the run has concluded so far
  • Names. A document is named by its place in library/: booth.md, papers/x.pdf, silicon@hw-lab/x.pdf for a project's (a file name or stem one document has is accepted too).
  • Outline. From its headings: Markdown #, LaTeX \section, a PDF's numbered headings (3.2 Method) and the usual unnumbered ones (Abstract, References ...). A document with none is cut by its pages (a PDF) or in chunks of 120 lines.
  • Capped. Long answers end with the exact command that continues (… continue: flux library read x.pdf --from 221). Every passage says where it is: section, page, lines.
  • Formats. Text files as they are; PDFs; Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files, HTML pages and EPUB books, converted to Markdown-like text (headings as #, list items as -, a table's cells joined by |, links and image descriptions kept).
  • Title. An HTML page's <title>, an EPUB's title, else the file's name without its suffix, is the document's title wherever the library names it: flux library's line (ks.html · "Kogge-Stone adders" · 40 lines · …), its outline, Files › Library.
  • Hidden. A path the loop or a project hides from its agents is refused.
  • Outside a loop's run, name the loop with --loop or run it in the loop's folder. In a project's chat flux library reads that project. Plain text; --json for data.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: front matter with name and description, then the instructions, and any files they use. Put skills in the loop's skills/ folder and they are used without a word in the document, by the model and every coding agent of the loop. The built-in flux-loop-commands skill (how to read the loop's results with flux loop ...) comes with them.

skills: [skills, ../shared-skills]           # these folders instead of skills/
skills: {"off": [flux-loop-commands]}        # skills/ and the built-in one, this one off
skills: "off"                                # none at all

--skill DIR on flux task run or flux ask adds a folder for one run.

A project can hold skills too: its skills/ folder, edited on its page's Skills tab. A loop linked into it gets them at skills/<name>@<group>/, read-only, after its own and in its projects' order (a name already taken is not taken twice). They are listed where the loop's own are, marked with the project, and switched off the same way (skills: {off: [name]}, or skills: "off" for none).

docs.title: Hidden from AI
docs.text:
A gate is only as good as the agent's ignorance of it. An agent that can read the tests can write a design that passes them and nothing else. knowledge.hidden names paths the loop's agents may not read:

flow:
  knowledge:
    hidden: [tests/, golden.py, "params/*.json"]

The loop's own checks, measurements and scripts read these paths as ever, and a check's failure text still reaches the agent. Paths are relative to the loop's folder. An agent's own hidden: option adds paths for that agent alone. Hiding is not a security boundary: for secrets, rely on the sandbox.

In the web app, hide a path:

  • in Files, from a file's or folder's Actions › Hide from AI;
  • in the configurator's Graph, on the Hidden bubble of the Knowledge group;
  • when adding files to New loop › Agent, with Hide from AI on the file;
  • with flux ask --hidden PATH on the command line.

Chat can read hidden files to answer you; the loop's own agents cannot.

Wherever the web app lists a hidden path (Files, the Hidden bubble, Prompt's files, the files an agent wrote for a new loop, a chat proposal), the path has a lock before its name and nothing else: no pill or word beside it. Point at the lock to read hidden from AI, or the folder or pattern that hides the path.

docs.title: Ideas cleanup
docs.text:
The loop keeps an ideas notebook: each hypothesis a model or agent proposed, with the designs that tested it. Over many passes it fills with the same idea in other words. knowledge.ideas says who cleans it up before a pass, once it has grown. Unsaid, FluxAgent does it at the default thresholds; say who else, other thresholds, or off:

flow:
  knowledge:
    insights: {by: rules}
    ideas: claude                        # an agent; or {by: flux, open: 30, new: 15}; or off
  • When: before a pass (under trunk:, in a Setup once a design is decided), once the notebook holds at least open open ideas (20 by default) and new of them (10) came, or got new evidence, since the last cleanup. Otherwise Live notes it (Setup · tidy ideas) and no model is asked.
  • What it does: merges ideas that say the same thing into one, three or more at once when they are one idea (the merged ones keep their text and evidence, counted under the kept idea; nothing is deleted). It may give a new idea a priority, and mark for deletion an idea that is no usable idea (off the problem, contradicting itself, against a stated constraint, empty or garbled), for a person to decide. A duplicate is always merged, never marked; it never marks an idea that was tried, that is queued or that is close to another idea: how a tried idea fared is the evidence score's to weigh.
  • A suggestion each pass: with nothing queued, a pass may suggest the best-scored idea not measured yet; Live's Design box says suggested idea when a design takes it. ideas: {suggest: false} turns this off (beside by, open and new). Under trunk: each turn of the agent is told the queued idea or the suggestion the same way.
  • Undo: flux loop ideas --unmerge 7 makes idea 7 its own idea again; naming a kept idea undoes every merge into it. flux loop ideas shows each idea's number and its merges. An idea is said by its number as "idea 7", never "#7", which is a design's.
  • Delete: flux loop ideas --delete 7 deletes idea 7 by hand, as the bin in Results › Ideas does; --restore 7 brings it back. Deleting is a person's call.
  • Mark for deletion: an agent marks an idea that is wrong, a duplicate or useless, with a reason. The idea stays until a person accepts the mark in Results › Ideas, which deletes it, or rejects it.

FluxAgent does it in every loop unless the document says otherwise, so ideas: flux needs no line. ideas: claude has an agent do it; ideas: off (or {by: off}) turns it off. In the web app it is the Ideas bubble of the Graph's Knowledge group, beside Lessons.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text: workbench/ beside the document is the agents' own folder: tools they build and notes they keep, shared by the loop's agents and kept across runs. knowledge.workbench says who sums it up for the next prompt when it changed (off, flux, or an agent); by default, whoever digests the papers. In the web app it is Files › Workbench; the library and its digests are Files › Library.

docs.title: Loop crafter
docs.text:
The web app's own configurator, running in this page: build a loop's problem.yaml step by step, with the document beside each step. Nothing leaves your browser; Download problem.yaml, save it in your loop's folder with the scripts it names, then run flux task check FOLDER.

The loop crafter needs JavaScript. Without it, build your own loop walks through the same file by hand.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• The form writes the document; you still supply the scripts, reference models and data its commands name. First loop has a complete example.
  • Check the loop with flux task check FOLDER, then run one pass: flux task run FOLDER --passes 1.
  • Configure explains each step's choices, and the Document reference every field. Loop names follow the naming rule.
  • Save draft keeps the form (not the files) in this browser. The agents offered here are the built-in ones; in the web app the agent menus offer the agents its server offers (their program found), and one a document names that is not offered shows (not available).

docs.title: Search and agents
docs.text:
A loop separates what to try next (flow.search) from how to make the design (flow.design). The gate and measurement stages establish the results. You can change the search or generator while keeping those checks, measurements, and objectives.

The configurator's Graph draws the loop as a ring: Search (search) chooses what to try, Design (design) makes it, Check (check) and Measure (measure) establish the facts, and Choose (choose) decides. A failed check goes back to Design. The setup boxes beside the ring run before the passes or feed every prompt. Each key under flow: (and trunk:) is its box's name in the Graph; an older document's names (orchestrate, generate, test, select, feedback, and Search's search for params) still load, meaning the same.

docs.title: Search a space of settings
docs.text:
Use a finite space when you can list meaningful choices. The generator and other commands receive those choices as placeholders:

flow:
  search:
    params: sweep
    space:
      algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
      wheel: [0, 1]
    seeds:
      - {algorithm: list_sieve, wheel: 0}
  design: {run: "{python} {home}/render.py {artifact} {algorithm} {wheel}"}

The seed is measured first; an omitted knob uses its first choice. The first seed is the home point. Order numeric choices meaningfully because local search uses that order.

search How it chooses experiments sweep Enumerate distinct combinations; a useful baseline for a small space montecarlo Sample distinct random points gradient Follow measured improvements among nearby choices anneal Make local moves and sometimes accept worse points to escape a region genetic Evolve a population through selection and mutation pareto Explore trade-offs; requires at least two objectives by: flux beside the space, no search FluxAgent proposes legal points from the space and measured history; by: claude an agent does control Compare the home point with only some of the incumbent's knobs kept (keep: [...]) phases Run several of these in order, each with its own options run Your own search script: search: {run: "...", timeout_s: 600} (contract)

A pass carries what the search proposes, and each search decides how much that is:

Search One pass carries It hears back sweep every point (batch_size for fewer) nothing: it reads no result montecarlo batch_size points, 8 unsaid nothing: it reads no result anneal one neighbour after each pass gradient a wave of moves from the incumbent: all of them, or wave after each pass genetic a generation: population points, 8 unsaid after each pass pareto up to wave points after each pass by: flux beside the space batch_size points, 4 unsaid after each pass control one point phases what the phase at work proposes as that phase does run what the script prints in one round after each pass

So --passes counts proposals, not points: a pass of a sweep over 48 points measures all 48, and one of a gradient a whole wave. budget.designs_at_once is how many of a pass's designs are made and checked at once. A search finishing its finite walk does not, by itself, stop an unlimited run. Use a pass cap for a bounded sweep.

Within a pass, its designs climb the stages cheapest first. After each stage, every design past its cutoffs goes on to the next stage, so only the cutoffs save the costly runs (between stages).

Designs checked again -- a rejected result's Measure again, a re-evaluation, a probed draft a person asked to Evaluate -- are the re-check, a pass of its own between two passes (R, numbered 1.5 after pass 1), never counted in budget.passes.

Configure a search's own options under its name:

flow:
  search:
    params:
      gradient: {steps: 16, patience: 2, reach: adjacent}
    space:
      block: [16, 32, 64, 128]
      order: [ijk, ikj, jki]

The search reference lists each search's options and defaults. For a multi-phase search, keep the space and list the phases in order, each {search: ..., <its options>} (policy: beside a phase's search sets that phase's emphasis):

flow:
  search:
    space: {block: [16, 32, 64, 128], order: [ijk, ikj, jki]}
    params:
      - {search: montecarlo, name: sample, samples: 8, seed: 0}
      - {search: gradient, name: tune, knobs: [block], steps: 8, policy: tune}

docs.title: Conditional choices and components
docs.text:
Avoid measuring a knob that has no effect on a chosen algorithm:

space:
  algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
  wheel: {values: [0, 1], when: {algorithm: [list_sieve]}}

This is the space inside flow.search. Inactive choices sit at their home values and are not repeatedly measured as different designs. A nested component groups its knobs:

space:
  prefetch:
    optional: true
    distance: [1, 2, 4]
    degree: [1, 2]

The search sees prefetch.on, prefetch.distance, and prefetch.degree. {point} provides these as nested JSON to a generator. A choice can also use from: "out/invented/*.sv" beside values to include filenames discovered when the document loads.

docs.title: Let a model or agent explore designs
docs.text:
A model or agent can write designs without a predefined knob space. Say who decides what to try next (by; unset, the rules) and the policy (policy) in flow.search; who writes the code is flow.design, set apart:

flow:
  search: {by: claude, policy: adaptive}
  design: claude

policy sets the search's emphasis: adaptive (the default), explore, improve, tune, finetune or variations. search picks an algorithm over a space (and decides alone; by beside it has no effect). Prefer search: sweep for enumerating knob combinations. gradient is coordinate descent over discrete choices, rather than derivatives; pareto explores trade-offs across the first two objectives. Without a space, these walks do not run.

In the configurator, the whole search is the Search box on the Graph: its Policy, then its Parameters fold, closed until a parameter or a search is set: the parameters to vary (each a name and its values) and, once there is one, Search by (an algorithm, or AI: FluxAgent or an agent, picked under it).

A finite budget or manual stop controls the run; reaching a goal or keeping the same incumbent does not stop an unlimited run.

docs.title: Put agents in the right steps
docs.text:
Name an installed agent directly, and use {by: ..., ...} only when adding options:

flow:
  search: {by: claude, policy: adaptive}
  plan: {by: claude, session: pass}
  design: {by: claude, timeout_s: 1800, probe: {gate: 20, stages: 3}}
  choose: {by: claude}
  knowledge: {by: claude, insights: {by: rules}}

claude, codex, and opencode are built in; a server can offer additional named agents. They can plan, generate, and advise decisions. flow.check and flow.measure remain commands: an agent cannot replace their factual results. Selection still uses the objectives; an agent's advice is checked and can fall back to the rules.

A critic is a second opinion on one box: critic: under search (the direction picked for a pass), check (a design the checks passed), measure (a stage's numbers) or choose (the pick). It is flux (FluxAgent), an agent, or {by: ..., rounds: N}. A rejection is a verdict: the direction is picked again, the design fails, the numbers are marked, or the pick is made again without it.

flow:
  check:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    critic: claude
  choose: {critic: {by: flux, rounds: 2}}

See critics for each box's rules.

An agent keeps one session per pass, unsaid: on design one until the design is admitted, its repairs and send-backs going on in it -- begun as a warm start unsaid; on a decision step such as plan or a critic one for that step's turns in the pass (session: pass), each critic its own. session: keep keeps it across passes (below). The papers' digest, the workbench and the ideas have no session: each of their turns stands alone.

docs.title: Several Design agents
docs.text:
Design may list coding agents, the way a trunk does: each pass's design is made by the next agent in turn -- pass 1 by the first, pass 2 by the second, and round again.

flow:
  design:
    by:
      - claude
      - {by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex, effort: high}
      - {by: opencode, model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5}
    timeout_s: 900
  • Each entry is an agent's name, or {by: <agent>, ...its own options}; its model is its model:, as one agent's is (design: {by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex}). The older args: [--model, <model>] still works. Design's own options (timeout_s, session, probe, ...) are every agent's; an entry's own options win for that agent.
  • Designs at once. With budget.designs_at_once, a pass that starts takes the agent whose turn it is, so the agents keep taking turns whichever design ends first. The turn follows the pass's number, also across a stop and a start.
  • A design stays with its agent. Its repairs, the turns that continue it after a time-out and its last turn are the same agent's.
  • Sessions are each agent's own. Each agent has its own warm start, and with session: keep its own kept sessions, one per design at once: an agent never resumes another's session.
  • The prototype (design.prototype) is written by the first agent of the list.
  • Refused: an empty list, the same agent with the same options twice (give it another model or options of its own, or drop it), and FluxAgent in the list (by: flux designs alone).
  • Where it shows. The Agents tab and Live's Timeline name the agent of each turn; Results tags each design with the agent that made it (and its model) once the loop has designs by two or more.
  • In the configurator, Configure › Graph › Design: Add an agent, then a tab per agent, named by the agent and its model; each tab holds that agent's settings and, past the first, its remove. One agent alone is written as before (design: claude).

docs.title: Warm starts
docs.text:
Unsaid, a design by Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode starts warm (session: seeded): before the first design the agent spends one turn reading the loop's folder, its scripts, the checks, the stages and its tools, and designs nothing. Each design's session then starts from where that one ended, with its own whole brief, so it does not read all that again. Designs never see each other's work this way: what each reads of earlier designs, results and ideas, it reads itself, as they stand when it starts.

flow:
  design: {by: claude}                        # warm starts (the default)
  design: {by: claude, session: fresh}        # every design's session starts from nothing
  design: {by: claude, seed_timeout_s: 1800}     # warm starts, that first turn at most 30 minutes

  • That first turn has up to an hour (seed_timeout_s, in seconds: 300 to 10800, that is 5 minutes to 3 hours) to study the loop: it reads the scripts, runs the help of the tools and commands they use and tries the build and check commands' help or dry runs, writing only in its own folder. It ends as soon as it has summed up what it learned, so the limit is a cap. It is its own: the agent's time limit, the turns that may time out and the last turn are the designs'. If it runs past its limit, the designs start from nothing. Changing it does not make that first session again. Refused beside session: fresh or keep, and on any other box.

  • The shared first session is made again when the problem document, the loop's files, the agent or its model change, after 24 designs, and after 12 hours.

  • With several designs at once, one is made and the others wait for it, at most 10 minutes. A design that cannot wait that long starts from nothing; only the designs that start while it is being made do, and every later one starts warm.
  • If it cannot be made or a design cannot start from it, that design starts from nothing; the Agents tab says why.
  • FluxAgent and an agent of your own (run:) always start from nothing. Trunks keep their own sessions.
  • Live's Timeline shows that first turn on the Setup row; the Agents tab marks each design that started warm.

docs.title: Sessions kept across passes
docs.text:
Off unless said. session: keep on any box an agent works, or a critic, keeps the agent's sessions from pass to pass, so it goes on in the conversation it had -- the files it read, what it worked out -- instead of reading the problem again each pass:

flow:
  design: {by: codex, session: keep}            # a new session after 8 turns
  plan: {by: claude, session: keep, turns: 4}
  search: {by: claude, session: keep, turns: forever}        # never renewed for its turns
  • turns: N (8 unsaid) starts a new session after N turns; turns: forever never renews it for its turns. A change to the problem document, the agent, its model or Flux starts a new one too.
  • One session per design at once (budget.designs_at_once).
  • An agent of your own keeps its session only when it declares a resume command (agent options); without one it starts a new session every pass, and flux task check says so.
  • The Agents tab says whether each turn resumed its session or started a new one.

Agents can check their current file against the loop's gate and stages during a turn (a probe). probe budgets those checks per turn. Direct use of certain raw tools is restricted by default; allow can give specific tools back when that suits the task. See agent options.

Probed drafts are kept, unverified. Drafts an agent probed but did not hand in are listed as unverified, named by the pass they were probed in and their try there (#p4.1, #p4.2 ...). They never count -- not in a frontier, a standing, a chart, a decision or an idea's evidence. Evaluate (Results, or flux loop evaluate p4.2) has the loop's next re-check check and measure one as a design of its own.

For FluxAgent, use search: {by: flux, policy: adaptive} and design: flux (model, its old name, is refused: the check says to write flux). Models and agents explains endpoint and agent setup.

docs.title: Two ways to run: passes or a trunk
docs.text:
A document runs its loop one of two ways, and the root key says which: flow: runs passes, trunk: runs a trunk. Both are complete ways to run a loop; pick by how the designs are made.

  • Passes (flow:): each pass makes one design -- a search picks a point, a script, FluxAgent or an agent writes it -- then checks, measures and decides it; a failed check goes back to Design for a repair, and the next pass starts from what was learned. Choose passes for a search over a space, a scripted generator, a plan, FluxAgent's drafts, or an agent you want to steer pass by pass (designs_at_once runs several passes side by side, budget.pipeline starts the next design once the current one passed Check; several Design agents take turns).
  • Trunk (trunk:): a coding agent keeps one session for the whole run and hands in one design a turn; branches check, measure and decide each one meanwhile, so neither waits for the other. Choose a trunk when a coding agent is the designer and you want it to keep going on its own, with several agents or models at once if you like.

Everything else -- checks, measurement stages, objectives, knowledge -- is written the same under either key. Say trunk: where the document says flow:, with the same contents:

trunk:
  design: {by: [claude], timeout_s: 3600}     # a list: one trunk each (one agent is fine)
  check: {...}                                 # as under flow:
  measure: {...}
budget:
  designs_at_once: 3                          # branches at once (the admin's limit applies); twice that may wait
  passes: 0                                   # designs handed in; 0 = until stopped
  • The trunk. Each Design agent keeps one session for the whole run, resumed at the next start. A turn is one design: the agent hands it in (flux hand-in) and its turn ends; the next design is a new turn that resumes the same session, told what it handed in, what ended since and its probe budget, whole again for each design. The agent keeps its memory; its own compaction keeps the conversation bounded. A turn lasts design.timeout_s at most. A turn with no design is followed by the next at once: the run ends only when stopped. An agent with no resume: command starts each design in a new session, its brief pointing at flux loop tried --by for what it handed in before.
  • The branches. Up to budget.designs_at_once branches take the designs off the queue, first in first out (the agents in turn). A branch is a pass that runs Check, Measure's stages and Choose exactly as a pass does, with no Search, no Design and no repair. Each check and stage in it is bounded by its own timeout_s.
  • The queue. At most twice the branches that run designs wait: twice budget.designs_at_once, or twice the admin's limit when it is lower (each agent at most its share). Lowering designs_at_once keeps every design already waiting: the next start says when more wait than the queue now holds, and no hand-in is taken until fewer than the new limit wait.
  • Ideas work as they do in passes. Each turn of a trunk is told the idea queued in Results › Ideas to test next, else the best-scored idea not measured yet as a suggestion (ideas: {suggest: false} turns that off). A design handed in names the idea it tests, and its check and measurements become that idea's evidence; the agent can add ideas for later. The ideas cleanup runs once the notebook has grown, as it does before a pass.
  • Notes (Overview › Note to the loop) reach the trunk agents as they reach a pass's Design agent: a note reaches each agent at every turn while it stands -- every turn's message starts with the notes, the ones the agent has not seen yet marked (new), and a new session's brief with all of them. A removed note is gone from the next turn. When the notes are long, the newest are said and the agent reads the older ones with flux loop notes. The branches read them too, and the Notes card shows a note read once the loop has taken it, whoever took it.
  • Search is off by default under trunk:: the trunk agents decide what to try. Say search: flux (FluxAgent) or an agent (search: claude) and a Search bud writes new ideas to the notebook every 10 decided designs; it never picks a direction. The Graph's Search box then reads "bud · every 10". A bud is short: an agent's turn has 5 minutes and 15 commands; FluxAgent answers in one reply, reading the record with its tools for 5 rounds at most within the same 5 minutes.
  • Repairs are the agent's own: repairs_per_design does nothing under trunk:.
  • Refused under trunk:: a space or a search (a search script too), plan, a Design not by a coding agent, both flow: and trunk:. flux task check says what runs.
  • The prototype stage (design.prototype) does not run under trunk:, and flux task check warns.
  • The start is a loop of passes' start: the baseline when the document asks it, then the re-check (Re-Evaluate's designs, the re-measures a rejection asks), then the Setup and the trunks.
  • Written otherwise: a document that says flow: with design: {session: trunk} (an older form) is refused now: say trunk: in place of flow:, the same contents.
  • Setup runs once before the trunk starts. Run setup on Live runs it again; it also runs again when the library changes.
  • Several agents. Each agent of Design's list is a trunk of its own, tagged t1, t2, ... in the list's order. An agent of the list is its name or {by: <agent>, model: <model>}; Design's own options (timeout_s, session, ...) are every agent's. The same agent may appear twice with different models: two trunks.
trunk:
  design: {by: [claude, {by: claude, model: opus}, codex], timeout_s: 3600}

docs.title: One loop, one design
docs.text: A loop answers one problem with one design. Several blocks of one IP are one design: say them in the statement and the contract, and bundle them under one top module, as the bundled nlu does. Several problems are several loops; a chart can draw them side by side.

docs.title: Models and agents
docs.text:
Flux talks to two kinds of AI, configured apart:

  • FluxAgent (flux in a document, a chat or --author; model, its old name, is the same): Flux's own model, on any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, for the loop's own calls (proposing points, writing designs with design: flux, reviewing, digesting papers).
  • Coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or one a server adds. Each runs on its own endpoint, model and login, never on FluxAgent.

A loop whose designs come from a script, with no flux or agent in its flow, needs neither. flux selftest says which model and endpoint a run would use, and whether a coding agent is on PATH; flux agent test NAME says whether one is ready.

docs.title: FluxAgent
docs.text:
By default Flux asks a local Ollama (OLLAMA_BASE_URL, the model in FLUX_LLM_MODEL). A remote OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LocalAI, vLLM, llama.cpp's server, a hosted service) uses:

export FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL=https://your-model-server.example/v1
export FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL=your-model-name
export FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY=your-key          # only if the endpoint checks keys
flux selftest
Variable What it does FLUX_LLM_MODEL The local model's name OLLAMA_BASE_URL The local server's root FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL An endpoint of your own; setting it switches to it FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL The model's name on that endpoint FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY, FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY_FILE Its key, or a file whose first line is the key FLUX_LLM_REMOTE 1 forces the remote endpoint, 0 the local one FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S Seconds one request may take; raise it for slow servers and long turns FLUX_LLM_STREAM 0 turns streaming off, for proxies that break it

--model NAME on flux task run and flux ask overrides the model for one run. If a service refuses the structured output Flux asks for, turn off Structured answers in Admin › Runtime › Agents › FluxAgent; with no server, FLUX_THINK='{"model": {"structured": false}}'.

docs.title: Settings that last
docs.text:
Every flux command reads ~/.config/flux/flux.env (or the file FLUX_CONFIG names): NAME=value lines, used only where the shell did not set the variable. Keep the key in its own file (mode 600) rather than in flux.env:

FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL=https://your-model-server.example/v1
FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL=your-model-name
FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY_FILE=~/.config/flux/server.key

Keep keys in the environment or the web app's settings, never in a loop's document.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Ollama on this machine:

ollama pull qwen3:4b                  # any tag; then
export FLUX_LLM_MODEL=qwen3:4b
flux task run my-loop --passes 1     # a loop folder of your own

A large model on a CPU takes minutes per turn; use a GPU, or a smaller model for small problems. For an Ollama on another machine, set OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://HOST:11434.

A server of your own (LocalAI, vLLM, llama.cpp's server): set FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL, FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL and, if it checks keys, FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY, as above. Raise FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S (for example to 1800) for long turns with tools.

OpenRouter: FLUX_LLM_REMOTE=1, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL set to an OpenRouter model id. With FLUX_LLM_REMOTE=1 and no FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL, Flux asks OpenRouter.

OpenCode on a server of your own: in OpenCode's configuration (~/.config/opencode/opencode.json), read the key as "apiKey": "{env:FLUX_AGENT_API_KEY}" and set FLUX_OPENCODE_API_KEY (in flux.env, or OpenCode's card in the web app). Tell OpenCode the model's real limits, and keep a thinking model's reasoning short, or it can end turn after turn on an empty reply:

"models": {"MODEL": {"limit": {"context": 58112, "output": 16384},
                     "options": {"reasoningEffort": "low"}}}

and "timeout": 1800000 in the provider's options.

docs.title: Coding agents
docs.text:
An agent must be installed and logged in where Flux runs (in the web app, Account › Agents). An agent's Instructions (Admin › Runtime › Agents; your own under Account › Agents) go to it on every turn. Flux's Nix development shell carries Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, and Flux finds them on PATH; nothing else to install. To run another copy, a newer one say, set FLUX_<NAME>_BIN to its program: it wins while it names a runnable file, and Flux falls back to the PATH's when it does not (an editor extension's binary that an update moved). An agent added under a name of its own (Admin › Runtime › Agents, a custom of kind Claude Code) runs its kind's program unless it has one: its own Program, else FLUX_<NAME>_BIN, else what the built-in agent of its kind runs (FLUX_CLAUDE_BIN, else claude on PATH). Check one with:

flux agent test claude          # its program and login
flux agent test claude --live   # also one short question
Variable What it does FLUX_<NAME>_BIN The agent's program, e.g. FLUX_CLAUDE_BIN, FLUX_CODEX_BIN, FLUX_OPENCODE_BIN FLUX_<NAME>_ARGS Extra arguments, added before the prompt FLUX_<NAME>_BASE_URL, FLUX_<NAME>_MODEL, FLUX_<NAME>_API_KEY The agent's own endpoint, model and key FLUX_<NAME>_OAUTH_TOKEN A login token, for agents that take one FLUX_<NAME>_TIMEOUT_S Seconds per turn (default 1800); a document's timeout_s wins

FluxAgent's settings (FLUX_REMOTE_*, FLUX_LLM_*, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) are not an agent's. Without settings of its own, an agent runs on its own configuration file and login. In the web app, each agent's card says "not configured" when it has neither.

FLUX_<NAME>_MODEL without an endpoint picks one of the agent's own models: every turn gets --model (OpenCode's as provider/model). flux agent models claude lists what an agent offers on your own login. A document's own model: beside the agent ({by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex}) wins over every setting; the older args: [--model, …] still works.

The loop runs the checks and measurements; an agent can check its file against them as it works, within a budget. See Agent options for probe, allow, timeout_s and the rest.

docs.title: Which model for which problem
docs.text:
The loop does not make a weak model strong: it keeps what passes and refuses what does not. A mid-size model can write a correct Python loop or a small adder on its first draft, but hard numeric hardware (a floating-point function within 1 ULP) needs more than RTL from a plain prompt. What helps:

  • a prototype stage (design.prototype: true with a golden model): the algorithm proven in Python on every input, then spelled as RTL by the loop;
  • a method note in flow.knowledge: the method and the facts, not a design;
  • a stronger model, or a coding agent, writing the prototype.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
• No answer: a run that needs a model asks its endpoint first and stops before the first pass when it does not answer, refuses the key, or lacks the model. flux task check shows the same line.
  • Start with the log: flux log RECORD shows every model and agent turn: the prompt, the reply, the tool calls, and the error.
  • Timeouts: raise FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S for the model, timeout_s for an agent.
  • Context: an agent that outgrows its endpoint's context window continues in a fresh session; raise the window if you can.

docs.title: Document
docs.text:
Everything a loop's document, problem.yaml, can say, and the contract every command it names must follow: arguments, placeholders, what to print, exit codes.

Use Configure for why you would choose each setting, flux task check FOLDER to validate a document, and flux task migrate FOLDER --write to upgrade an older one.

docs.title: The document at a glance
docs.text:
Only statement is required. A complete document; the numbered marks say where each part is described:

statement: Count the primes below n, as fast as possible.  # (1)!
contract: >-  # (2)!
  A Python module defining count_primes(n) that returns
  exactly how many primes are below n.
language: python

flow:  # (3)!
  search:
    params: sweep
    space: {method: [trial_division, sieve, slice_sieve]}
  design:
    run: "{python} {home}/render.py {artifact} {method}"
  check:  # (4)!
    build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"
    correctness:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      timeout_s: 60
  measure:  # (5)!
    quick:
      run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} 50000"
      metrics: [time_ms]
      cutoff: {metric: time_ms, below: 20}
    full:
      run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} 1000000"
      metrics: [time_ms]

objectives:  # (6)!
  - {metric: time_ms, direction: minimize, goal: 20}

budget: {passes: 5, tools_at_once: 1}  # (7)!
params: {n_max: 1000000}  # (8)!
  1. What to make. The only required field.
  2. Rules every design must follow: names, ports, what is forbidden.
  3. Who does each box of the loop: here a search over three methods, and a script that writes each design (flow settings).
  4. The checks, in order; the first that fails refuses the design (check settings).
  5. The measurements, cheapest first. cutoff decides which designs go on to the next stage (measurement settings).
  6. What decides. A goal makes an objective a limit: here at most 20 ms (objectives).
  7. How much to spend (budget).
  8. Your own settings, handed to every command as the {params} file.

docs.title: Files and loading
docs.text:
• The folder is the loop. Its name is the loop's id: letters, digits, _, - and, after the first character, .; flux new keeps it to 60. There is no id key; saying one is refused.
  • The document is problem.yaml (or problem.yml, problem.json). Alternates beside it are NAME.problem.yaml; each keeps its own results.
  • Beside it: your scripts, library/ (papers and notes the model reads), workbench/ (the agents' own tools and notes, kept across runs), skills/ (read unless skills: says otherwise), and out/ (the results, written by Flux).
  • Parsing: a YAML or JSON error reports its line and column; a document that is not a mapping is refused. Unknown keys are refused with a "did you mean" hint.
  • Older documents are never upgraded silently: flux task migrate FOLDER shows what changes and --write saves it. A document of a form older than Nov 12, 2026 is refused, naming the commit that still brings it up.
  • Normal form: equivalent spellings (plan: flux and plan: {by: flux}) load to the same document and share one record.

docs.title: Document fields
docs.text:
Field Values / default Purpose statement Required non-empty string What to build or optimize contract String; empty Interface and rules every design must follow (names, ports, what is forbidden) language String; inferred, else text The design's file type (table below) flow Map; defaults below Who does each step: search, generation, checks, measurements, and the supporting boxes trunk Map; unset The loop run as a trunk instead of passes, in place of flow with the same contents: Design's by may list agents objectives List; empty Limits and ordered preferences (objectives) budget Map; defaults below Run length, repairs, concurrency, prototypes (budget) params Map; empty Your own settings, handed to any command as the {params} JSON file skills off, a folder or list of folders, or {from, off}; skills/ Skills (a folder with SKILL.md) the model and agents can load (skills) baseline true, false, or a map; absent A reference measured before pass 1 (baseline)

language sets the design file's extension, matched without case:

Language Extension Language Extension systemverilog .sv cpp, c++ .cpp verilog .v c .c vhdl .vhd cuda .cu python .py opencl .cl text .txt rust .rs yaml .yaml markdown .md json .json shell, bash .sh chisel, scala .scala anything else . + the name, lower case, no spaces

When language is absent it is inferred only from a check or stage that starts with a built-in tool's full command (in practice the Verilator lint line, which gives systemverilog); otherwise it is text. Say it explicitly.

docs.title: Flow settings
docs.text:
flow says who does each box of the loop's drawing. A box takes a word, an agent's name, or {by: <word or agent>, ...settings, ...agent options}:

flow:
  design: claude                                # an agent, no options
  choose: {by: claude, session: pass}           # an agent with options
  plan: flux                                    # FluxAgent
  notes: off                                    # a word

flux is FluxAgent, Flux's own model working a box (its endpoint and model are set in Models and agents). model, its old name, is refused: write flux (the check says so, and suggests it). claude, codex and opencode are built in; a server can add agents of its own (named by FLUX_AGENTS). The old form {agent: X} is refused: write {by: X}.

Box Values (first is the default) Purpose flow.search.by unset (the rules, no AI), flux, tools, agent Who decides what to try next (given is the rules, under that name) flow.search.policy adaptive (default), explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations Sets the search's emphasis flow.search.params unset, sweep, montecarlo, anneal, gradient, genetic, pareto, {gradient: {...}}, module:Class, a list of phases How the points of space are picked (search settings) flow.search.run A command, with timeout_s (600) Your own search script proposes the points (search command) flow.search.scope {list: ..., brief: ..., check: ..., timeout_s: 120} The scopes of one whole design a pass may work on (scope) flow.plan off, flux, agent Write the pass's plan, checked before use flow.design flux, agent, a list of agents, {run: ...}, {catalog: [paths]} Write each design flow.check A command, or an ordered map of named checks; never an agent Decide correctness (checks) flow.measure An ordered map of named stages; never an agent Put numbers on passing designs (measurements) flow.choose unset (the objectives choose), agent Make the decision; an agent only breaks ties flow.notes unset (your notes are read), off Take your notes from the loop's Chat into the next prompt flow.knowledge A map (knowledge): library, by (who digests, or off), insights, ... What the model and agents can look up

Each box is named as the configurator's Graph draws it: search is Search, plan Plan, design Design, check Check, measure Measure, choose Choose, notes Notes, knowledge Knowledge. A document written before these names (orchestrate, generate, test, select, feedback, and Search's search for params) still loads, meaning the same; one box said both ways is refused. Server › Old data offers to rewrite such a document with the new names, comments kept.

  • search: {by, policy, params, space}. by unset is the rules (they pick the work, no AI); flux (FluxAgent picks); tools (FluxAgent with tools: standings, history, decisions, knowledge); or an agent. policy sets the search's emphasis -- adaptive (default), explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations. params is the algorithm that picks the points of space (sweep, montecarlo, anneal, gradient, genetic, pareto, phases) and decides alone. A space with by: flux or an agent and no search: that one proposes the points. A search word under policy:, or a policy name under params:, is refused naming the right key. The bare word is shorthand: search: explore is {policy: explore}, search: sweep {params: sweep}, search: claude {by: claude}.
  • search.scope, for a loop of one whole design (no knobs): each pass works on one scope of it. list is a command printing the scopes, one a line, its name first; brief, given {scope}, prints what the design agent is told of it; check, given {scope} and {artifact}, checks the scope on a design that passed the gate (N failing of M, or its exit). Each pass the orchestrator picks its direction and a scope in one decision, seeing which scopes the latest passes took and how their checks ended. While the scope's check fails, the design goes back to the same agent with the failures, until it is clean or the pass's tries_per_pass are spent; every design that passes the gate is kept and measured as usual. For a spec kept in the loop's folder: list: fluxpreset ndf list --spec {home}/spec, brief: fluxpreset ndf clauses {scope} --spec {home}/spec (it names the units that depend on it), and fluxpreset ndf scope {scope} --spec {home}/spec lists the unit and its dependents for a check of your own.
  • design takes exactly one form. {run: ...} is your script (generator contract); {catalog: [a.py, b.py]} reads the listed files (relative to the folder) in turn; flux (FluxAgent) and agents write the design. by may list coding agents -- {by: [claude, {by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex}]} -- each pass's design by the next in turn (several Design agents); an entry's own options are that agent's. session is seeded (the default: one session per design until it is admitted, each a warm start), fresh (the same, each started from nothing; pass says it too) or keep here.
  • session: seeded (Design only, the default for Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode): one turn first reads the loop's files and tools and designs nothing; each design's session starts from where it ended, never from another design's work. Made again when the document, the loop's files or the agent change, after 24 designs and after 12 hours; a design that cannot start from it starts from nothing. session: fresh turns it off. seeded and fresh are refused on any other box. seed_timeout_s (3600 unsaid, 300 to 10800) is that first turn's own time limit, whatever the agent's timeout_s; it ends sooner once it has learned the loop, a change keeps the first session, and it is refused without the warm start: {by: claude, seed_timeout_s: 1800}. A generator command has no timeout_s of its own: it uses the largest check timeout.
  • session: keep (with turns: K, 8 unsaid, or turns: forever) on any box an agent works, or a critic: the agent's conversation is kept across passes, one session per design at once, a new one after K turns or when the document, the agent, its model or Flux changes; forever never renews it for its turns. Off unless said; refused on the papers' digester. {by: codex, session: keep, turns: 4}, {by: claude, session: keep, turns: forever}.
  • check and measure are never an agent's. by: on them is refused: they establish facts.
  • choose: {by: claude} adds an agent that breaks ties among designs the objectives cannot separate; the objectives' choice stands otherwise.
  • plan is checked before use; a plan that fails the check falls back to the document's order.
  • Thinking. One switch, think: true or false, beside whoever works a box. Where FluxAgent works it -- search, plan, design, the critic of check, measure or choose, and knowledge with its workbench and ideas -- {by: flux, think: true} lets it reason before it answers (slower, often better; its thinking shows in the task's live view); think: false, it answers straight. Beside an agent -- any box, critic or Knowledge section an agent works, an agent added under a name of its own too -- {by: claude, think: false} runs it at its effort for not thinking, true at its effort for thinking (both the admin's, below); refused for an agent of your own run. An agent's effort (agent options) is the finer level and wins over its think. Unsaid, the server's thinking by default decides: untouched, FluxAgent answers straight and each agent works at its own effort (no flag), as before. The configurator shows Thinking under the agent wherever one is chosen -- a box, a critic, a Knowledge section -- default, on, off, its help line saying the admin's default, with its effort beside it (FluxAgent's levels or the agent's kind's); a box nothing thinks on shows none, nor does an agent with a command of its own. Search with tools says it as {by: tools, think: true}. FluxAgent proposing the points of a search over parameters (Search's AI search) has its own, written beside it: search: {by: flux, think: true, effort: high, space: {...}}.
  • Effort (FluxAgent). Beside by: flux wherever think goes, effort: low | medium | high | max sets how hard FluxAgent works -- whether it thinks, how long it works and how long its answer may be -- at once; max also checks its own answer. It comes before the box's think. Unsaid, the admin's choice holds (thinking by default). The configurator shows effort beside FluxAgent's Thinking.
flow:
  search: {by: flux, think: true}             # FluxAgent reasons over what to try next
  plan: {by: flux, effort: max}                # works hardest and checks its own plan
  design: {by: codex, think: false}           # the design agent at its effort for not thinking
  choose: {by: claude, effort: high}          # the finer level, as it is
  check: {check: "true", critic: {by: flux, think: true}}         # the critic reasons before it judges
  knowledge: {by: flux, effort: high, ideas: {by: flux, think: false}}   # papers, and the ideas cleanup

docs.title: Critics
docs.text:
A critic is a second opinion on one box, said as critic: inside it. Only four boxes take one:

Box What the critic judges A rejection rounds search The direction picked for a pass, before any design work is spent on it The direction is picked again with the objection yes check A design the checks passed The design fails; the objection is its note on the record no measure A stage's numbers The result is marked rejected and never chosen; it is not measured again no choose The pick The decision is made again without it; the critic says whether it rejects the design or the pick yes 
flow:
  search: {by: claude, critic: flux}
  check:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    critic: claude
  choose: {critic: {by: claude, rounds: 2, timeout_s: 600}}

A critic is flux (FluxAgent), an agent, your own agent ({by: {run: [...]}}), or {by: ..., rounds: N, ...agent options}. rounds (1 to 5, default 1) is how many times the box answers an objection, on search and choose only. A rejected design or pick stays rejected in later passes; a rejected direction is about its own pass. A box without critic: has none.

A search critic needs someone who picks: by: flux, by: tools or an agent. With the rules, a search over a space, or under trunk:, nobody picks a direction, so there is nothing to judge and the loader warns. An idea queued by hand is not judged. When the rounds run out the last pick goes ahead, and a critic that fails or runs out of time has no opinion: it never stops the loop.

A critic runs wherever its box runs: in every pass, in pass 0 (the baseline), in an R pass (Measure again, a hand rejection that asks for a measurement), in Re-Evaluate and in the re-evaluation of an invalidation. Numbers it already judged are not judged again.

The select critic says in its verdict what it rejects, with rejects:

  • design: the design itself. It is final, like a rejection by hand: it never lapses, and only Restore in Results counts it again.
  • pick (also when the critic says nothing, as every verdict before): only this pick. It lapses once the numbers it judged change (the design measured again, measured on a new stage, or measured under other inputs), and the design can be chosen again.

The metrics a critic names in wrong are cleared: struck through in Results, their values kept. Results names each rejection's critic and links its critique in Live. The older flow.critique is refused as a key of an older document (the message names the Flux that still reads it); budget.critique_rounds is not a budget key: it is ignored with a warning.

docs.title: Check settings
docs.text:
flow.check is one command (a check named test) or an ordered map. Checks run in the order written; the first that reports failures refuses the design and the rest do not run.

test:
  build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"                  # a bare command
  correctness:                                                # or a map
    run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    timeout_s: 60
Field Default Purpose run Required Command string or argument list count_re (\d+) failing One capture group holding the number of failures fail_re Absent One match per failure; used instead of the default count pattern timeout_s 120 Seconds before the check is stopped; a check stopped there refuses the design ("timed out after 120s") and the loop goes on needs The loop's needs, else unlimited A resource hint: the cores and GB of memory it uses at most, and the labels of the machine it runs on

Check names are a letter, then letters, digits, _ and -. A check named build uses no default pattern: any non-zero exit means the design did not build. count_re or fail_re at the level of flow.check (not inside a check) is refused. How a check's output becomes a verdict is in the check contract.

docs.title: Measurement settings
docs.text:
flow.measure is an ordered map of stages, cheapest first. A stage is a command or a map:

Field Default Purpose run Required Command string or argument list (as a check's; command: is refused, as everywhere a document runs a command); {metrics} in it is the stage's metrics, comma-separated (fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} ...) metrics Required unless metrics_re The names printed as name=value -- a number, or a dictionary (below) metrics_re Derived from metrics Map of metric name to a regex with one capture group needs Inferred for fluxpreset prog count/size; else empty Programs required on PATH; a missing one skips the stage ("NOT RUN"). As a map, also a resource hint: {tools: [yosys], cores: 8, memory: 48} timeout_s 600 Seconds before the stage is stopped, with every process it started (a helper it left in the background too) cutoff None A gate before the next stage, or a list of gates that must all pass estimate Off Predict first, and skip designs the estimate already rules out

A stage's command that exits non-zero is a failed measurement, whatever it printed: its numbers are not taken and the design is refused at that stage. The refusal is a row on the record, kept (it is read back for that design until the document changes or Re-Evaluate measures it again), and the stage's task in Live ends failed (✗). An exit 0 with none of the stage's metrics printed is refused on the record too ("no metric matched in the output").

A stage names its metrics only. A metric printed as a dictionary, name={"a": 1, "b": 2} (or inside a JSON object of metrics), is read as one: each finite value becomes name.a, name.b, a test each, and name is their mean: nothing declares it a dictionary. The dictionary may say its own aggregate with the key _a -- name={"a": 1, "b": 2, "_a": "sum"} -- which is no test; any value but mean, median, min, max or sum refuses the measurement. Missing, null and non-finite values stay unmeasured, never zero. An objective ranks the dictionary by name (its _a, else its mean), by another aggregate it says -- {metric: name, aggregate: sum, direction: minimize, unit: us}: mean, median, min, max or sum; said, it wins over _a -- or by one test, {metric: name.a}. An objective says no type:; an old type: is refused (an old type: dict alone ranked by aggregate: mean). A dictionary no objective names is an extra measurement: recorded, shown folded under its name in Results and Settings › Preferences (its mean, its entries a click away), never ranked. Metric names are unique per stage; evaluator: stages are gone and refused.

Cutoffs gate the next stage: {metric: M, at: N} keeps designs at least N, {metric: M, below: N} at most N, {metric: M, within: F} within the fraction F (0 < F <= 1) of this run's best on that stage. Exactly one rule per condition. M is any number the design has at that stage: measured there or carried from an earlier stage (below).

Estimates: {kind: surrogate|command|model, margin: 0.05}; run (the command) only with kind: command (estimate contract). A design whose estimate misses a cutoff or a limit by more than the margin is skipped and never measured.

Stages measure different things. One stage may time a design and the next measure its area; a stage need not repeat what an earlier one measured. A design's numbers at a stage are, for each metric, the deepest measurement at or before it: a later stage replaces an earlier one's number for the same metric, and a metric only an earlier stage measured is carried forward. Results, flux loop results, show and the report say where a carried number came from ("fmax_mhz=500 (from timing)").

A design's checks and stages share a folder. Within a pass, the loop's own checks and stages of one design run with FLUX_REUSE_DIR set to a folder of that design's, kept across its steps: a tool that keeps its intermediate files there under a key of its inputs (the presets do) continues instead of starting again. The folder goes with the pass; nothing is shared with another design (Compiling).

flow:
  measure:
    timing: {run: "{python} {home}/sta.py {artifact}", metrics: [fmax_mhz], cutoff: {metric: fmax_mhz, at: 250}}
    area:   {run: "{python} {home}/area.py {artifact}", metrics: [area_um2]}
objectives:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, goal: ">= 300"}   # judged on area, with timing's number carried
  - {metric: area_um2, direction: minimize}

Every objective must be measured by at least one stage. A limit pinned with stage: must name a stage that has its metric (measured there or before), and a cutoff may name only a metric its stage has; otherwise the run says the question cannot be answered as posed. task check and the run's first step note an objective only the last stage measures: the stages before rank without it.

Between stages: every design past a stage's cutoffs climbs to the next one (one already measured there, in an earlier pass, is not measured there again), so every design gets every objective's number. Only a cutoff, or an estimate, saves a costly stage: with neither, the cheap stage saves no measurement, and task check says so. A pass carrying many designs (a sweep's) then pays the costly stage for each of them, at most budget.tools_at_once at a time. The decision is made on the deepest stage reached, over the designs measured there, each with every objective by then; a design that never reached the stage where an objective is first measured is not chosen: Results lists it as Rejected, "stopped at" its stage (or Pending while its pass may still climb it).

docs.title: Knowledge settings
docs.text:
Field Default Purpose library Empty Files and folders (specs, sources, notes, PDFs), relative to the folder, that join library/ as the loop's library; the AI looks it up when it needs it (flux library) by flux Who summarises the library's papers: flux (FluxAgent) or an agent (its options beside); off turns the library off insights {by: off} Conclusions drawn from the loop's results: {by: rules} (computed, no AI), {by: <agent>}, or {by: off}; flux library insights prints them workbench who digests Who sums up the agents' workbench/ when it changed: off, flux, or an agent ({by: claude, timeout_s: 600} with its options); unsaid, whoever digests the papers ideas flux Who cleans up the ideas notebook before a pass, once it grew: flux (FluxAgent, the default in every loop: no line needed), off, or an agent; {by: flux, open: 20, new: 10} runs it at 20 open ideas with 10 new since the last cleanup (the defaults). It merges repeated ideas (undoable); see Ideas cleanup hidden Empty Files, folders or globs (relative to the folder) the AI agents may not read: tests, checks, a gate's files and their parameters; see Hidden from AI

by: off may have insights, ideas, workbench and hidden beside it, not library. digest, lessons and off are keys of an older document and are refused (the message names the Flux that still reads them); sheet, files and text are unknown keys: a warning, ignored. While knowledge is on, the loop's library/ is read. Each project the loop is linked into has its library inside it, read-only, at library/<project>@<group>/ (<project>@_ for a global project), in the loop's project order, with the project's hidden paths hidden under it: a name with @ at the top of library/ is reserved for them.

docs.title: Hidden from AI
docs.text:
knowledge.hidden lists paths the loop's agents may not read, so no agent games the gate by reading it: the loop's own checks, stages and scripts read these paths as ever, and a check's failure text still reaches the agent.

flow:
  knowledge:
    hidden: [tests/, golden.py, "params/*.json"]

Each path is relative to the loop folder, inside it, and never the document itself. An agent's own hidden: option adds paths for that agent alone. Hidden paths are left out of the library, the knowledge files and the skills. Hiding is no sandbox: for secrets, use the run's sandbox. In the web app, a file or folder is hidden from the Files tab (Actions, Hide from AI), when it is added, or in the configurator's Hidden bubble, in the Graph's Knowledge group.
