Chat can read hidden files to answer you; the loop's own agents cannot.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (front matter name and description, then the instructions). The loop's skills/ folder is used without a word in the document, by the model and every coding agent of the loop, together with the built-in flux-loop-commands (how the loop's results are read with flux loop ...). skills: chooses other folders or turns them off:

skills: off                                  # none, not the built-in one either
skills: [skills, ../shared-skills]           # these folders instead of skills/
skills: {off: [flux-loop-commands, rtl-style]}   # skills/ and the built-in one, these two off
skills: {from: [../shared-skills], off: [old-style]}

docs.title: Objective settings
docs.text:
Each entry is a metric name or a map:

Field Default Purpose metric Required A metric a stage reports (name or name.test for a dictionary metric) direction maximize; a goal written "< 80" or "<= 80" makes it minimize minimize or maximize goal None A limit: at most N when minimizing, at least N when maximizing; also ">= 1000", "< 80" stage The deepest stage for a goal Where the goal is judged (a stage that has the metric: measured there or carried from an earlier one) unit Known for common metrics Display unit aggregate mean How a dictionary's tests make its number: mean, median, min, max, sum tie 0 Relative band within which two designs tie and the next objective decides margin 0 Extra headroom required when a goal is judged on a shallower stage balance false Decide by the best trade-off (the knee) of the goal-less objectives keep None A relative limit: keep this fraction (0..1] of the best gain over above above 0 The reference for keep

How the decision is made: a design that meets every limit beats one that misses any. Among those that meet them, the goal-less objectives decide in the order written (within tie, the next one decides). If none meets every limit, the one missing fewest, then by the smallest shortfall, is reported as the closest, not as a decision. While a stage has refused every design tried there, none has passed every stage yet: no decision is made and no design stands (Results and the Overview say "None has passed every stage yet"). An unmeasured limit counts as missed. With balance, the best trade-off of the goal-less objectives decides. An exact tie goes to the next objective in the order written, limits included (of two designs alike on area, the faster), then to the design made first. goal cannot be combined with keep or balance. A dictionary metric needs no type:: an objective naming it ranks its mean unless its aggregate (or else the dictionary's own _a) says another, or names one of its tests (d.test).

docs.title: Resource hints (needs)
docs.text:
A check or a stage says what it uses at most with needs: {cores: N, memory: G}, memory a plain number of GB. A top-level needs: is the default of every check and stage that says none; unsaid, cores and memory are unlimited: nothing is forced or set aside for a step that does not say them, and its memory is limited only by the loop's sandbox memory (Admin › Runtime › Sandbox, a loop's Settings › Advanced).

needs: {memory: 8}                 # every step of this loop
flow:
  check:
    lint: {run: "{python} {home}/lint.py {artifact}", needs: {cores: 2}}
  measure:
    place:
      run: fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage place
      metrics: [area_um2]
      needs: {tools: [openroad], cores: 8, memory: 48}
  • Where it starts. The machine's cores and memory (less 10% of the memory, at least 4 GB, for the system) are a pool every loop and user shares. A check or measurement -- an agent's probe too -- starts when its hint fits what is free: the pool less the hints of the steps running, and never more than the memory the machine has available. Else it waits ("waiting for room (needs 8 cores, 48 GB; free 2 cores, 30 GB)" on Live), in fair turns between users and loops; a step that has waited 10 minutes is not overtaken by smaller ones. A step counts the larger of its hint and the most its stage used over its last 20 runs. A step that says no cores counts 1 core, whatever it used: it never waits for cores it did not ask for. A step that says no memory counts none, whatever it used: it never waits for memory. A step always starts when nothing else runs.
  • Its builds. FLUX_JOBS is its cores (never above the sandbox's CPU limit): make -j"$FLUX_JOBS". With no cores said, FLUX_JOBS is the machine's cores shared among the loop's tool runs at once (cores ÷ tools_at_once, at least 1), as for any tool run.
  • Never a limit. A step may use more than its hint, up to the sandbox's limits (Admin › Runtime › Sandbox, a loop's Settings › Advanced). When it does, its loop gets one note per step, updated rather than repeated -- "Stage place used 37 GB of memory against a hint of 4 GB." -- with a button, Set memory: 48 (its peak plus a quarter, in 4 GB steps, 8 GB above 32 GB), that writes needs: {memory: 48} on that stage, the rest of the document as written. A note about cores comes only for a step that says its cores, and one about memory only for a step that says its memory (or that ran out of it, below).
  • Out of memory. A step the kernel's OOM killer ends when the machine ran out (no limit of its own reached) runs once more and the note says so; a second kill fails it as any crash. One killed at its sandbox memory limit fails as before, and the note says to raise the loop's sandbox memory.
  • Another machine. Any other key (fpga: true, lab: loopback, vivado: "2025.2") is a capability: the step -- an agent's probe of it too -- runs on a machine joined to the server that has it (Machines: one line adds a machine, an admin's for the server, or one of your own that only your loops use), the same command on the same files, and its numbers come back to the loop as a local step's. Live says where it ran ("… · on runner-1"); a step no machine has waits, saying so. true asks that the machine has the key, a string that it says exactly that (">=2025.1": that version or newer), a number that it has that many (two boards: fpga: 2). Run from a shell rather than from the web, such a step runs on this machine, and its note says no machine here has the key.
  • Other commands. A command the loop runs to write designs can say needs too: flow.design: {run: ..., needs: {fpga: true}}, the baseline's run, a search's run (flow.search: {run: ..., needs: ...}) and the scope's commands (flow.search.scope.needs). A label there sends that command to a machine that has it, as for a stage; the loop's top-level needs: does not apply to them. Work done by an agent or by FluxAgent (a box with by:) always runs on the server: needs there is refused, saying so.
  • Changing needs never makes measurements stale. Cores, memory and every other key only say where a step runs: adding, changing or removing them -- at the top, on a check, on a stage or on another command -- leaves every measurement and check counted as it was, with nothing to accept or measure again. Only a stage's tools is part of how it is measured: listing another program there is a change to the stage. Writing a stage's needs as a list or as a map with the same tools is the same; a map without tools keeps the tools of a stage that says none.
  • In the configurator. A check's or a measurement's Resources row has two fields, cores and GB of memory: left empty they say "unlimited" and Save writes nothing for them. Its Machine labels row adds a label with + Add label: the list offers the labels of the machines your loops may use, each with how many machines have it ("fpga=1 · 2 machines") -- your own machines, and the server's when your groups use the server's settings. A label no machine has yet can still be typed (gpu=2, or a word alone for true): it is kept, marked "no machine has this yet", and its steps wait for a machine that has it. Save writes the labels picked into the step's needs (needs: {lab: loopback}), beside its cores and memory; × takes one away. The loop crafter on this site has no machines to ask: it offers examples and takes what you type.
  • Admin › Activity › Resources shows the pool: cores and memory hinted, used and free, and the steps waiting.

docs.title: Run length, repairs, and concurrency
docs.text:
Field Default Purpose passes 0 A limit on the passes of flux task run without --passes; 0 runs until stopped. A pass is one design, so this is how many designs the run makes, however many run at once. Not in the configurator, and a start from the web never reads it: the Start dialog sets each start's passes, and "until I stop it" means just that tries_per_pass 3 What one pass may work through. A loop builds one design a pass, so this caps its tries that give none and a critic's send-backs; for a search, its rounds: a pass carries one proposal, and a round that gives no design takes the next. Leave it out unless a search needs more; only a search's Tries row sets it in the configurator repairs_per_design 3 Repairs of one design before it is given up designs_at_once 1 Designs at once, wherever: passes at once (each its own design, in its own agent session; passes still counts each; a pass starts as soon as another is measured, and they decide in turn), trunk branches (twice that may wait), a search pass's designs, the re-check's designs. A server limit also applies. Passes of a search run one at a time: the designs at once are inside each pass (what a pass carries) tools_at_once auto Tool steps at once across the whole loop: one pool of this many slots. A design's check, its measurements and its decision run as one tool step that holds one slot from its first check to the end of its decision (a pass's decision that must wait for an earlier pass's to be made gives its slot back before it waits). An agent's probes (flux loop gate, flux loop measure) and estimates take slots from the same pool, each only while its tool runs. Unsaid: half the cores, at most 4, or designs_at_once when more. Use 1 for anything timed, or for a tool that breaks when two of its runs share the machine: no two tools then run at once, checks included. It never holds designs at once, only their tool steps. Each check's and measurement's builds get FLUX_JOBS, its hint's cores. A server limit also applies agent_continues 3 Times a design agent's work is continued past its time limit before its design is handed in as it stands agent_grace_s a quarter of the agent's time limit, 300–600 s A final short turn to get the design past the gate; 0 turns it off tools true Whether FluxAgent calls tools inside its turns (compute, check, history, knowledge); false for a server without tool calls. A coding agent's turns are its own pipeline false true: drafting the next design overlaps the tool steps of the designs before it -- each lane starts its next design as soon as its current design has passed its check, while that design's measurements and decision finish behind it in its tool step, one design behind a lane at most. It never splits a design's check from its measurements. The designs are still decided in order, a design refused at a measurement stays a record later passes can improve on, and so does a design a measurement sends back to be fixed: with pipelining on it is not repaired (its lane is already designing the next one), and flux loop tried says "sent back by : not repaired while pipelining" under it -- with pipelining off it is repaired as before. A stop lets the designs behind finish and be decided. The next design's agent sees a design behind as being measured, its numbers once they land. No effect on a re-check (it drafts nothing: its designs run designs_at_once at once, each one tool step), a search (its pass measures its designs inside it) or a trunk-mode loop (its agents draft while branches run anyway); a server's parallel allowance applies. In the configurator: Extra › Running › Pipelining. Live and flux loop passes say what it would save on your loop once it has three passes

These nine are the whole budget. prototype as a budget key is refused: it is Design's (below). Only tools_at_once and pipeline are type-checked; check the others with care.

A key the budget once had and has no more loads with a warning and does nothing: remove it (a save from the configurator drops it). The prototype's limits and FluxAgent's tool turns are the loop's own; no key sets them.

docs.title: Prototypes
docs.text: A prototype is the algorithm in Python (or SystemC) checked against the golden model before the target design is written. It applies to problems with a golden model, and is said on the box that writes the designs: design: {prototype: false}, design: {by: claude, prototype: systemc} (true, the default, false, python or systemc). Beside a run or a catalog no prototype is written: it is a warning there. Setting it does not create a golden model.

docs.title: Baseline / pass 0
docs.text:
baseline runs the checks and the real measurements on a reference before pass 1, so results can be read relative to it. It is off by default; pass 0 uses no AI and repairs nothing, and does not count toward passes.

baseline: true                                   # the project as it is: your scripts as written
# baseline: {file: baseline.py}                  # an unchanged design file
# baseline: {run: "{python} {home}/baseline.py {artifact}", timeout_s: 600}
# baseline: {metrics: [{metric: area_um2, value: 120}, {metric: fmax_mhz, value: 1000, stage: place}]}
# add only: true to stop after pass 0
Form What pass 0 measures true Your scripts as written; {artifact} is an empty file, so use {home}/... paths {file: F} F (relative to the folder) copied to {artifact}; the original is untouched {run: C, timeout_s: 600} Whatever C writes to {artifact} (contract); if it writes nothing, the project as it is {metrics: [...]} Nothing runs: the values are recorded as the reference
  • metrics entries are {metric, value, stage}: a finite number; stage defaults to the deepest; the metric must be one that stage reports; each stage/metric pair once. Provided values supply no design and are never the decision.
  • only: true ends the run after pass 0 (a tool check without optimization).
  • Reuse: a successful baseline on record stands while the document's baseline: section is unchanged -- whatever else changes (the folder's files, the tools, Flux). To measure it again, the loop's Settings › Record › Re-Evaluate with Rerun baseline ticked (or flux task run ... --rerun-baseline) makes the next start, and only it, run pass 0. A failed one is tried again at the next start. Baselines skip estimates and cutoffs.
  • Baselines are references: drawn as gray lines, the base of relative values, never the decision or a search start.

docs.title: Moved to their own pages
docs.text:
Older links to this page land here.

  • Search settings and policies: Search policies
  • Agent options: Agent options
  • How commands run, placeholders and contracts: Commands and placeholders
  • Each command's contract: Command contracts
  • Built-in tools and Flux presets: Presets
  • The RTL golden model: Golden model
  • Common refusals: Common refusals

docs.title: Run, stop, resume
docs.text: Use this page after creating and configuring a loop. In the web app, the same actions are a loop's Start and Stop (Tour). Replace sums with your loop's folder. Commands use the active Flux environment.

docs.title: Check before running
docs.text:
flux task check sums
flux task run sums --passes 1 --json sums/out/answer.json

task check validates the document, lists the stages and required tools, and reports problems before a run: every file the document names must be in the folder (a missing one is listed with the key that names it and what the folder holds), and the golden model must run. It exits 2 when the document does not load (not a task:) and 1 when something is missing or refused (MISSING:, REFUSED:, or WILL NOT RUN: when a flux/fluxpreset command's words are refused by its own --help). Like a run, it runs in the sandbox; --no-sandbox checks on this machine. It does not execute the candidate checks and measurements. A bounded first run checks the actual scripts and their output.

A folder normally contains problem.yaml. Additional NAME.problem.yaml files describe alternate problems in the same folder and use separate records. When a folder contains several valid documents, specify the file explicitly for unattended runs:

flux task run sums/small.problem.yaml --passes 1

docs.title: Runtime overrides
docs.text:
Values in budget are persistent settings; command-line options override them for one run. Use flux task run --help for the complete command syntax.

Option Effect --passes N Stop after N passes (one design each, however many run at once); default is budget.passes, or until stopped when omitted/zero --tries-per-pass N, --repairs-per-design N Override budget.tries_per_pass and budget.repairs_per_design --db FILE Use a different record --out FILE Choose where the feasible decision artifact is written --json FILE Write the answer and results as JSON --tui Open the terminal task, log, and results view --model NAME, --think, --num-predict N Choose a model, request reasoning, and bound output tokens --role ROLE=NAME Override a role; task check lists available choices --agent orchestrate plan Give the direct model orchestration and planning; all enables both (its tool calls are budget.tools, on by default) --tool-hops N, --hop-share F, --patience N Override model tool rounds, context share, and prototype patience --no-prototype Disable prototype work --skill DIR Add a skill directory; repeatable --replies FILE Supply scripted model replies, useful for repeatable experiments --rerun-baseline Measure the baseline (pass 0) again, though the document's baseline is unchanged --reevaluate At this start, after the baseline: check and measure again every design on the record (those Invalidate set aside, else every one), after a check or measurement changed; then the passes --reevaluate-tabs accepted,failed With --reevaluate: only the designs of these Results tabs (accepted, rejected, failed, pending); all four, or none said, is every design --remeasure Measure again the designs a rejection asked for, then rest --no-sandbox Run on this machine, not in the sandbox (also FLUX_SANDBOX=0)

docs.title: Stop, resume, and keep experiments separate
docs.text:
An unlimited run continues until you stop it. Limits and timeouts can end individual attempts or passes; a satisfied objective or a stalled search does not automatically end the run. Stop with Ctrl-C, q in the TUI, the browser's Stop action, or another terminal:

flux stop sums/out/sums.db        # finish the current pass
flux stop sums/out/sums.db --now  # interrupt immediately

Run the document again to continue its record; unchanged measurements are reused. One run a record at a time: while a loop runs, from the browser or a terminal, a second start of it (the other way too) is refused with not started: this loop's record (sums.db) is being run by pid N (...), naming the run that has it. While a terminal's run has it, the browser's Delete, Rename, Reset, Archive, Replace (import) and Set aside are refused the same way, and Stop says to stop that run where it runs. A run that was killed holds nothing. Changing the objective can reuse observations; changing the measurement changes what can be reused.

A loop run as a trunk stops the same way. flux stop: its agents' turns end, the running branches finish, the designs waiting stay for the next start. --now: everything ends; the designs that were running are kept, and the next start runs them first, then the ones waiting, and its agents go on where they were. --passes N counts hand-ins there; the queue drains after the last.

docs.title: When a measurement still counts
docs.text:
A measurement still counts (for the decision, the ranking, the best and the charts) until one of these changes for its stage: the measure command (its words; spacing, quoting and comments do not count), how its numbers are read (metrics / metrics_re, a dictionary's aggregate), its parameters (the document's params:, when the command takes {params}), its input files (the files and scripts the command uses), or its tools (the build of each program the stage runs or needs). Nothing else of the loop makes a measurement stale: not the prompt, other stages, the checks, objectives, cutoffs, agents and their settings, budgets, names, comments, or files no measurement reads (a README, notes).

A change counts from when the loop judges it: at the loop's next start, or at once when the file is saved on the page (the configurator, the Files editor) and the loop is not running. A file edited elsewhere (a shell, an agent) is judged at the next start; until then every page and flux loop summary say the last judgement, and when it was made ("what counts was judged ... by ...").

When a stage changes, its older measurements stop counting, but nothing is hidden: in Results they keep their numbers and their tab, muted, with a "measured before a change" mark; the decision, the pool, the best and every chart leave them out, as the loop does. The loop's Overview says so on top, in the card a failed start uses ("12 designs were measured before a change to how synth is measured (the measure command and input file a.txt)"), and the loop's owner or an editor chooses:

  • Accept as current: the measurements count again, at once, for the loop and every page (audited);
  • Leave as stale: they stay uncounted and the card is closed for that change; a later change shows the card again;
  • Re-measure: those designs are checked and measured again under today's setup: by the running loop before its next pass, else by a run of its own that starts at once.

For a separate experiment, use a fresh --db or a new folder name. Copying a folder's generated out/ and workbench/ also copies its history and agent files; leave them out for a fresh loop. In the browser, a stopped loop's Settings › Preferences › Archive, reset or delete offers Reset, which asks what to keep. Reset removes generated data while retaining the source document and scripts.

For a process that outlives the terminal:

flux run -- flux task run sums
flux status sums/out/sums.db
flux attach sums/out/sums.db

docs.title: Upgrading older loops
docs.text: Flux never upgrades a document silently. flux task migrate FOLDER shows what would change in a loop's documents and --write saves them (the original kept as <file>.orig). This Flux reads documents from the format of Nov 12, 2026 on, and records from version 7 on: no document step is above that yet, so the command says every document of today current. A record of an older version, or a loop file of an older format, is refused saying the commit that still brings it up -- open the loop with Flux 9957e3728, run flux task migrate --write (and a start, or Compact and check, for its record) there, and export it again. A document saying a key of an older document is refused naming the key and Flux e7a0f9cba, which says what became of it.

docs.title: Moving a loop in one file
docs.text:
flux loop export writes a loop as one .zip, as the web's Settings › Export does (see Export and import); flux loop import replaces a loop's contents from one, with the same checks:

flux loop export sums --loop-only -o sums.loop.zip     # the document, files and library (hidden files too)
flux loop export ada/sums --full -o sums.full.zip      # and the record, workbench, answer, notes (a web loop: USER/LOOP)
flux loop import sums.full.zip --into other --dry-run  # every check, nothing replaced
flux loop import sums.loop.zip --into ada/sums --keep-results --json

LOOP is a loop's folder or USER/LOOP of the web server's data (--data; then a running loop is refused and both are on the audit). Import keeps the loop's name and settings, migrates the file's documents up from the format of Nov 12, 2026 (an older file, a record in it older than version 7, or a newer file is refused, the older ones naming the Flux that brings them up), runs nothing of it, and leaves the loop as it was on any refusal. Exit 0 done, 1 refused, 2 the loop or the file is not there.

docs.title: Read the result and full output
docs.text:
flux loop summary --loop sums/out/sums.db --html
flux log sums/out/sums.db

The report shows measured designs, trade-offs, refusals, and the standing design. The chosen artifact is written under out/ only when a design meets the requirements. An estimated metric or a shallower screening result should not be read as a confirmed measurement.

task run exit Meaning 0 A measured design meets every requirement; the decision artifact is written 3 Correct designs were measured, but none meets every requirement; the report shows the shortfall 1 No design was measured, or the run could not start 130 Interrupted

In the web app, a loop's Live tab shows passes, tools, agent activity, and their output as a graph and a timeline. Its Start picker opens an older start; its tasks and conversations belong to that start. Files, logs, and results provide raw or fullscreen views. History is available while its files and records are retained; resetting a loop clears the generated history.

docs.title: Read a loop from a shell
docs.text:
flux loop reads a loop's results back, one question a command, read-only, so a running loop is safe. Name the loop with --loop FOLDER (a folder, a document or a record file; default: the current folder); every command takes --json. The options are in the CLI reference.

Command What it answers flux loop summary The loop's state: running or not, its last phase, the budget, how many at once, a trunk's queue, its stages and checks; the baseline, the best per objective and the standing pick, each against the baseline flux loop passes [--last N] Each pass: its direction and why, its decision; "checks changed at pass N" where the document's checks or stages changed flux loop notes The people's notes and the decisions' reasons flux loop results [--top N] [--stage S\|all] [--goals] The measured designs ranked by the loop's objectives, meeting or missing the goals flux loop tried [--failed] [--gate G] [--match TEXT] Every design tried: how far it got, its numbers or why it stopped; a draft a stop cut before it was handed in, "stopped before handed in" flux loop show NAME [--rows] One design whole: its pass, its idea, its gate check by check, each stage's numbers or error, what changed since it was judged; --rows: every row of it in order flux loop design NAME [--print] A design's files, written read-only to a folder of yours, one path a line flux loop compare A B ..., flux loop diff A [B] Designs side by side, metric by metric; two designs (or a design and a file) line by line, or one design against the design it was built from (else the baseline); --stat counts the lines flux loop stages Each stage: designs reached, passed, refused, running; how long its rows take flux loop events [--kind K] [--since 2h] The record's events; --since those after a time ago or an ISO time flux loop ideas [--top] The ideas notebook, the best-scored first, with each idea's evidence flux loop starred The designs people starred in Results

A first look at a loop:

flux loop summary --loop sums
flux loop results --top 5 --loop sums
flux loop tried --failed --loop sums
flux loop show '#6' --loop sums

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run inside a container, so neither an agent nor the document's own code (its commands, scripts, golden.py) can touch the rest of the machine. The engine is rootless Podman when installed, else Docker (FLUX_SANDBOX_ENGINE=podman|docker). Without either, these commands stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker.

  • It sees the host read-only: the system, /nix/store, Flux itself, the programs on PATH, and the loop's folder.
  • It writes only the loop's out/ and workbench/ and the loop's own cache. Scratch is gone after the run, and a loop's Scratch /tmp size (Admin › Runtime › Sandbox, or the loop's Settings › Advanced) caps it on disk: write what must last under the loop's out/ or workbench/.
  • Its home holds the agents' configuration and logins for Flux, not your own home: ~/.ssh, other repositories and the Docker socket are not there.
  • Network is the host's by default. FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW=host,domain,10.0.0.0/8 limits HTTP(S) to those destinations; add FLUX_SANDBOX_RAW_NETWORK=1 for direct TCP/UDP to them (needs nft on the host). Behind a proxy, HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY pass in; an allowlist's hosts are reached through it. On a server, its admin sets it (Proxy).
  • Limits: FLUX_SANDBOX_MEMORY in GB (e.g. 16), FLUX_SANDBOX_CPUS, FLUX_SANDBOX_PIDS (default 4096), FLUX_SANDBOX_TMP_SIZE in GB (e.g. 0.5). On a server, its admin's defaults and maximums apply (Sandbox limits), and the server stops the biggest loop before the machine runs out of memory (The memory guard).
  • Off: --no-sandbox or FLUX_SANDBOX=0 runs on this machine as you. Use it only for code you trust, such as the first loop.
  • Where Podman keeps its state: FLUX_SANDBOX_STORAGE names its storage and FLUX_SANDBOX_RUNTIME its runtime folder (by default /run/user/<uid>, else /tmp).

docs.title: When the sandbox cannot start
docs.text:
A start that cannot reach the engine stops with what the engine said and what to do, for example the podman sandbox cannot start: .... Check that the command it names (podman ... info) answers as the account that runs Flux. Flux repairs Podman's own state by itself when no Flux container runs, and says so in the loop's log.

To keep Podman's state in one place, let the account linger (sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>) before its first sandboxed run, or name a folder with FLUX_SANDBOX_RUNTIME (for a system service, in its environment file); keep that folder's path short, as Podman refuses long ones (the error says how long it may be). ... belongs to another account: remove the folder it names as root, or set FLUX_SANDBOX_RUNTIME to a folder of the account's.

docs.title: Compiling
docs.text:
Checks, measurements and an agent's probes often build C or C++ (a Verilator testbench, a simulator, a benchmark). Flux sets three things for every tool it runs, in the sandbox or not, and its built-in checks and measurements use them:

  • Flux clears MAKEFLAGS. A -j inherited from your shell's profile (MAKEFLAGS=-j32) would make Verilator's own make build one file at a time. Never put -j in MAKEFLAGS in a script.
  • Use FLUX_JOBS for a build's parallelism: make -j"$FLUX_JOBS", verilator --build-jobs "$FLUX_JOBS", cmake --build . -j "$FLUX_JOBS", ninja -j "$FLUX_JOBS". For a check or a measurement it is the cores of its resource hint (needs: {cores: 8}), never above the sandbox's CPU limit; with no cores said, and for a tool run outside them, it is the machine's cores shared among the loop's tool slots (cores ÷ tools_at_once, at least 1).
  • ccache is on. Each user has a cache of their own (ccache/<user> in Flux's cache folder, at most 10 GB), shared by all of that user's loops and runs, so a design built again, or the same files in another design's folder, compile in a fraction of the time. No user's run can read or write another user's cache: a shared one would let a run plant a compiled file that another user's build then uses. Each user's first builds fill their own cache. Verilator's builds use it on their own. Another build uses it with CC="ccache gcc" CXX="ccache g++", or with PATH="$FLUX_CCACHE_BIN:$PATH", where gcc, g++, cc, c++, clang and clang++ go through ccache. A build that does neither is not cached. The tool's step in Live says the run's ccache hits and misses; Admin › Activity › Resources says each user's cache's size.

The built-in checks and measurements build with FLUX_JOBS and through your ccache on their own, and within a pass the steps of one design share what they built: rtl measure --stage place after --stage synth at the same clock and settings continues from the synthesised floorplan, rtl power, energy, path and breakdown read a stage already made, and rtl cycles, power and energy run the model the golden test built. To benefit, measure a design's stages at the same --clock-ps. Nothing is shared with another design, loop or user, and none of it changes a number, a verdict or a netlist.

docs.title: System service
docs.text:
A server for a team runs as a system service, set up by one command, as root, from flux/:

sudo python3 scripts/install-service.py -- --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765

Options for flux serve go after --. The service runs neither as you nor from your checkout:

What Where Account flux, a system user (--account) Code its own clone, /opt/flux/src (--src), of main from your checkout's origin (--origin, --branch) Web data /var/lib/flux/web Sandbox home /var/lib/flux/home, the account's HOME, where its agents log in Caches /var/cache/flux Settings /etc/flux/service.env, one NAME=value a line

In order, the command makes the account, lets it use Nix (below), gives it sub-ids and linger (rootless Podman needs both), lets Podman limit its jobs (below), clones the code as the account, creates /etc/flux/service.env (with your proxy settings, below), installs the unit, builds the environment, makes the first admin account when there is none (it asks for a password), and turns the service on. Each step is skipped when it is already done, so it can run again after a fix. For an SSH origin it first makes the account a key and stops until that key is a read-only deploy key of the repository. For an HTTPS origin, see A private repository over HTTPS.

--dry-run needs no root: it says what is there and what is missing, and prints the unit and every step, writing nothing. The service is protected from the out-of-memory killers (--oom-score-adjust, default -500; --memory-low 2G keeps memory for it) and starts at boot. journalctl -u flux.service -f shows it.

At the end the command prints how each agent logs in as the account (codex login, claude setup-token, opencode auth login); a web user logs in in Account › Agents.

A flux serve started by hand is for development only.

docs.title: The environment is built before the restart
docs.text:
Updates go through Admin › Server › Version. An update that changes Flux's toolchain builds its new environment first, while the old server keeps serving, and the server restarts only once that build has finished; a failed build leaves the server running as it was. A code-only update restarts in seconds. Admin › Server › Version shows the build's state.

Updates never stop running loops: they finish on the version they started on, and their next start uses the new one.

docs.title: Host commands as the flux account
docs.text:
flux web-loop and flux web-agent (from the server's machine) must run as the flux account, in the service's prepared environment:

sudo -u flux -H env -C / FLUX_DATA_HOME=/var/lib/flux sh /opt/flux/src/flux/scripts/flux-env.sh run flux web-agent test

Run as yourself, they say "permission denied on …" and print this command.

docs.title: Nix for the flux account
docs.text:
The account runs the daemon's (multi-user) Nix, and the daemon decides two things from /etc/nix/nix.conf. The installer reads both (nix config show, else nix show-config, else the file and what it includes, never your own ~/.config/nix) and sets what is missing itself:

  • May it use Nix? allowed-users must name it, a group of it, or *. When it does not, the installer adds flux to it (your entries kept).

  • Does it get the binary caches? The flake's nixConfig names a cache (its substituters and keys are read from flake.nix). Nix uses it for an untrusted account only when the cache is in substituters or trusted-substituters and its key in trusted-public-keys. Otherwise OpenROAD and the other tools build from source, which takes hours. The installer adds what is missing, for example:

    # Flux: the account that runs Flux and the binary caches its tools come from (written by its installer)
extra-allowed-users = flux
extra-substituters = https://nixchip0.cachix.org
extra-trusted-substituters = https://nixchip0.cachix.org
extra-trusted-public-keys = nixchip0.cachix.org-1:nT5gEHc4661JFHoDukEnF1NFQ0XvS0TE7P370HLm4Ng=
# end of Flux

    It writes this block to /etc/nix/nix.custom.conf when nix.conf includes that file (the Determinate installer's), else to the end of nix.conf, after copying the file once to nix.conf.before-flux. Lines you added yourself are found and left alone. After a change it runs systemctl restart nix-daemon and checks, as the account, that Nix now shows the values. On NixOS (nix.conf made by the system's configuration) it prints the nix.settings to add and stops. With FLUX_INSTALL_BUILD=1 it leaves the caches alone.

  • Can it reach the daemon's socket? This is decided by the files' modes, not by nix.conf. Debian's and Ubuntu's nix package (/usr/bin/nix) makes /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket root:nix-users 0750, so an account outside nix-users gets "getting status of /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket: Permission denied" even when allowed-users = *. The installer reads the folder's and the socket's group and mode. When only their group may reach them, it adds the account to that group (usermod -aG nix-users flux), never to root, wheel, sudo, admin or adm. When only such a group or only the owner may reach them, it stops and says so.

The report also says which nix the service runs: /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin/nix when it is there, else the nix on your PATH (/usr/bin/nix with a distribution's package). It names Nix's version and warns when it is older than the flake needs (Nix 2.4, the first with flakes, for its flake.lock). It also says whether that nix is a client of the daemon. With no daemon socket, Nix is single-user, which cannot serve another account.

Each time it runs, the installer reads the settings again and tries Nix as the account: nix store info from Nix 2.19, nix store ping before it (an older Nix does not know store info), and the other one if the first fails. A daemon that closes the connection ("Connection reset by peer": it has not read its settings since they let the account in) is restarted once. If both still fail, it stops and prints both commands' errors. Listing flux in trusted-users would also do all of this, but a trusted user can do nearly what root can, so the installer never does it.

docs.title: cgroup delegation for the flux account
docs.text:
Rootless Podman limits a job's CPU, memory and processes inside the account's systemd user manager (user@<uid>.service). It can do that only when systemd hands the manager the cpu, memory and pids controllers. The host must use cgroup v2. On an older host that still uses cgroup v1 or the hybrid mode, the installer stops and says to boot with systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1. It never switches the mode itself.

When the account's manager lacks one of those controllers, the installer:

  1. Writes /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/delegate.conf:

    [Service]
Delegate=cpu cpuset io memory pids

    It leaves your files alone when one of them, or systemd's own default, already delegates them. A delegate.conf of yours that delegates too little is first copied to delegate.conf.before-flux. 2. Runs systemctl daemon-reload. 3. Restarts the account's manager, and no other user's, when nothing of the account's runs under it. If something is still running there, it stops instead and asks you to restart user@<uid>.service once that has finished, or to reboot. Then run the installer again. 4. Checks that the manager now has the controllers.

When the controllers are already there, it changes nothing and prints nothing.

docs.title: A private repository over HTTPS
docs.text:
With an HTTPS origin (--origin https://...), the account needs a credential for the clone and for Admin › Server › Version's fetch. The report says whether the account has one for the origin's host and whether your ~/.git-credentials has a line for that host. It never shows a token. The installer first tries git ls-remote as the account, which needs nothing for a public repository. If that fails:

  • It copies only your ~/.git-credentials line or lines for the origin's host into the account's /var/lib/flux/home/.git-credentials (0600, owned by flux) and sets credential.helper store in its ~/.gitconfig. Lines for other hosts are never copied.

  • With --no-git-credentials, or when you have no line for the host, it copies nothing. It prints the steps and stops. To store a token as the account, typed so it stays out of the shell's history:

    sudo -u flux -H bash -c 'read -rsp "Token for github.com: " t; echo; git config --global credential.helper store; printf "protocol=https
host=github.com
username=x-access-token
password=%s

" "$t" | git credential approve'

Use a token of its own rather than a broader personal one: a fine-grained token for this repository only, with Contents: read-only. The server's fetch uses the same stored credential and never prompts either.

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text:
A systemd service gets none of your shell's variables, so behind a proxy its first start times out fetching the flake's inputs from GitHub. The report lists your http_proxy, https_proxy, all_proxy and no_proxy (in either case) by name and the proxy's host:port only; under sudo, which keeps none of them, it reads them from the shell you ran sudo from. A user and password in a proxy URL are never shown. The report also says whether nix-daemon has a proxy. The installer then:

  • writes them into /etc/flux/service.env, each only if that file does not set it already. A proxy URL with a user and password is never written; it names it for you to add by hand. With --no-proxy-env it writes nothing and prints the lines instead.

  • prints, when nix-daemon has no proxy, the lines for its binary cache downloads. It never edits the daemon itself:

    sudo systemctl edit nix-daemon    # add:
[Service]
Environment=https_proxy=http://proxy.example:3128
sudo systemctl restart nix-daemon

  • tries each GitHub input of flake.lock as the account, with those variables (curl, 15 s). A timeout points to a proxy it lacks. A 404 means a private input: Nix needs a token in the account's own ~/.config/nix/nix.conf (access-tokens = github.com=<token>), and the step prints how to store one without it landing in the shell's history.

docs.title: Moving the server's data by hand
docs.text:
Never copy the server's database (flux-web.db) alone while the server runs. Either copy the backup that Admin › Server › Maintenance › Compact and check saved (with backups kept over 0), or stop the server first (Backups and restore). The next start refuses a database with stray files beside it and says which to move aside.

After copying a server's data to new folders by hand, run flux web-move with the service stopped, so the records name the new folders (a dry run first, then the same with --write):

sudo systemctl stop flux.service
sudo runuser -u flux -- env HOME=/var/lib/flux/home FLUX_DATA_HOME=/var/lib/flux \
  FLUX_CACHE_HOME=/var/cache/flux FLUX_ROOT=/opt/flux/src/flux \
  sh -c 'cd /opt/flux/src/flux && nix develop --accept-flake-config --command flux web-move \
    --from-data /home/you/.local/share/flux/web --from-cache /home/you/.cache/flux \
    --from-source /home/you/src/flux/flux'
sudo systemctl start flux.service

--from-source is the folder of your own checkout's flake.nix. A second run changes nothing.

docs.title: Where a loop's files are
docs.text:
folder what is in it out/ the results: designs, measurements, decisions runs/ the log, the notes, the answer, the loop's conversations workbench/ the agents' notes and tools

Everything else Flux writes for a loop is scratch, which the clean-ups may delete.

docs.title: Setup elsewhere
docs.text:
• Installing Flux, the web app and the hardware tools: Install.
  • FluxAgent and the coding agents: Models and agents.
  • Following runs in the browser: Web app.

docs.title: First loop
docs.text:
Build a loop that compares two ways to compute the sum of squares of the integers below n. One design loops over the inputs; the other uses a formula. Flux generates both, tests them against a reference, times them, and writes the faster passing design.

This example needs Python 3.11 or newer. It uses no model and no hardware tools.

docs.title: 1. Install Flux
docs.text:
The Flux source is not public: ask its maintainer for access. Then, from its folder (here flux-repo):

cd flux-repo
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ./flux
source .venv/bin/activate

If Flux is already installed, use your existing environment. Keep that environment active for the commands below. Hardware tools and the web app are covered in Install.

flux task check and flux task run run inside a container, the sandbox, with rootless Podman (preferred) or Docker. Without either, they stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker. This example runs only your own scripts, so you can run it on your machine directly:

export FLUX_SANDBOX=0        # or add --no-sandbox to each flux task command

docs.title: 2. Create the folder and document
docs.text:
flux new sums

Replace sums/problem.yaml with:

statement: Find the fastest correct sum_squares(n) implementation.
contract: >-
  Provide sum_squares(n) for nonnegative integers n. Return the exact integer
  sum of i*i for 0 <= i < n. Keep the function name and signature.
language: python

flow:
  search:
    params: sweep
    space:
      implementation: [loop, formula]
  design:
    run: ["{python}", "{home}/render.py", "{artifact}", "{implementation}"]
  check:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
  measure:
    bench:
      run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact}"
      metrics: [time_ms]

objectives:
  - {metric: time_ms, direction: minimize}

budget: {passes: 2, tries_per_pass: 1, tools_at_once: 1}

The folder name sums identifies the loop and its record; you do not add an id field. space has two choices; the sweep proposes both in its first pass, which checks and times each. passes: 2 is only a cap: the run ends as soon as the sweep has nothing left to propose. tools_at_once: 1 keeps the timed measurements from competing with each other.

docs.title: 3. Write the generator
docs.text:
Create sums/render.py:

import sys
from pathlib import Path

implementations = {
    "loop": "sum(i * i for i in range(n))",
    "formula": "n * (n - 1) * (2 * n - 1) // 6",
}
expression = implementations[sys.argv[2]]
Path(sys.argv[1]).write_text(f"def sum_squares(n):\n    return {expression}\n")

Flux replaces {implementation} with the selected knob value and {artifact} with the path where this script must write the design. {home} is the loop folder; {python} is the interpreter running Flux. See command placeholders.

docs.title: 4. Write the correctness check
docs.text:
Create sums/check.py:

import importlib.util
import sys

try:
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("candidate", sys.argv[1])
    candidate = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(candidate)
    function = candidate.sum_squares
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"did not load: {exc}")
    sys.exit(3)

failures = 0
for n in [0, 1, 2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    expected = sum(i * i for i in range(n))
    try:
        actual = function(n)
    except Exception as exc:
        actual = repr(exc)
    if actual != expected:
        failures += 1
        print(f"FAIL n={n}: got {actual!r}, expected {expected}")
print(f"{failures} failing")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)

This is the gate, the loop's checks: a failing design never reaches the benchmark. Exit 3 means the design could not build or load; exit 1 means it loaded but failed the tests. These six cases are this example's test coverage, not a proof for every possible input.

docs.title: 5. Write the measurement
docs.text:
Create sums/bench.py:

import importlib.util
import sys
import time

spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("candidate", sys.argv[1])
candidate = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(candidate)
candidate.sum_squares(1_000_000)  # warm up

times = []
for _ in range(9):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    candidate.sum_squares(1_000_000)
    times.append((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000)
print(f"time_ms={min(times):.6f}")

metrics: [time_ms] tells Flux which name=value output to read. The objective asks it to minimize that number. The benchmark workload, repetition count, and statistic are your choice; here they make the difference between a loop and a formula easy to see.

docs.title: 6. Check, run, and inspect
docs.text:
flux task check sums
flux task run sums --json sums/out/answer.json
flux loop summary --loop sums/out/sums.db --html

task check validates the document and lists its requirements; it does not run the candidate tests or benchmark. The run executes them in one pass and ends once the sweep has measured every point. The formula should win this workload; the actual times come from your machine.

The run writes, among other bookkeeping files:

File Contents sums/out/sums.py The chosen passing design sums/out/sums.db The record: every design, check and measurement sums/out/answer.json The decision and recorded results sums/out/sums-report.html The report written by flux loop summary --html

Keep the record to reuse previous measurements. To try a separate experiment, copy the loop folder to a new name and omit its generated out/ and workbench/ directories.

docs.title: Change the loop
docs.text:
Add another implementation to render.py and space.implementation: the next run measures the new point in its first pass. You can replace the generator with an agent, change the benchmark, add a second measurement stage, or introduce a limit alongside the speed objective.

Continue with Configure, then Search and agents, or open the loop in the web app. For another starting point, copy a folder from flux/applications/, including its scripts, or use flux new NAME for a blank loop.

docs.title: Agent options
docs.text: The options a coding agent takes in a document. Which boxes an agent may work is in the Document reference; where its model and login come from is in Models and agents.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Beside by: <agent> on any box an agent may work, or on a critic. Beside by: flux or with no by, an agent's option has no effect: a warning, ignored.

Design may list agents (design: {by: [claude, {by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex}], timeout_s: 1800}, under flow: in turn, under trunk: a trunk each): the options beside the list are every agent's, an entry's own are that agent's and win. Each agent's session, warm start and kept sessions are its own.

Option Default Purpose model The agent's own (or its settings) Its model by name, as the agent takes it: {by: codex, model: gpt-5-codex}, OpenCode's provider/model; it wins over every setting. Refused beside by: flux and for your own run: (give it in your command). The older args: [--model, …] still works, but not both at once timeout_s 1800 (or FLUX_<NAME>_TIMEOUT_S) Most seconds for one turn session pass (design: seeded) pass: one session per pass, on design one until the design is admitted; seeded (design only, its default): each design's session a warm start, begun where a shared turn that read the loop first ended -- Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, others start from nothing; fresh (design only): each begun from nothing, as pass there; keep: its sessions kept across passes, one per design at once. The papers' digest, the workbench and the ideas have none. turn, an older value, does nothing: a warning, read as pass; remove it turns 8 With session: keep: the turns a session serves before a new one begins, 1 or more; forever: never renewed for its turns (the agent's own context management keeps it running), a new one only when it cannot be resumed or the document, the agent, its model or Flux changes seed_timeout_s 3600 design only, with its warm start (session: seeded, unsaid): the most seconds that shared first turn may take, 300 to 10800, whatever timeout_s says (Warm starts); refused elsewhere questions decide Who answers a question the agent asks: decide (nobody), flux (FluxAgent; model too), operator. Not on a box whose agent answers in one turn (search, plan, choose, the insights, a critic): nobody answers there, so it is a warning, ignored max_questions 2 Question exchanges per draft (as questions) wait_s 300 Seconds to wait for the operator's answer (as questions) probe {gate: 20, stages: 3} Probes per turn the design agent (design) may run: its current file against the loop's gate, and against its stages; per stage {bench: 2}; false turns them off; elsewhere a warning allow [] Tools the agent may run itself, e.g. [yosys], or all effort The server's thinking by default: the agent's own unless an admin set one How hard it reasons: Claude Code low, medium, high, xhigh, max; Codex none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh (as its model takes them: none and minimal are not every model's); OpenCode minimal, low, medium, high, max (as its provider names them); refused for your own command. It wins over think. FluxAgent takes low, medium, high, max beside by: flux (Effort) think The server's thinking by default true: the agent's effort for thinking; false: its effort for not (Admin › Runtime › Agents) -- the box's Thinking switch; refused for your own command hidden [] More paths this agent may not read, beside knowledge.hidden (Hidden from AI) bin FLUX_<NAME>_BIN, else its kind's (FLUX_<KIND>_BIN, else the kind's program on PATH: claude, codex, opencode) The program to run args None (or FLUX_<NAME>_ARGS) Extra arguments, added before the prompt (the model is model:) output text Your own agent: how its output is read (text, opencode, claude, codex) resume The preset's Your own agent: the command that resumes a session ({session}, {answer}); without it session: keep begins a new session every pass (task check says so) name The program's Your own agent: its name in the record

docs.title: What an agent may run
docs.text: By default an agent does not run compilers, simulators or test runners itself: it checks its file against the loop's own gate and stages (a probe). allow gives specific tools back ([yosys], or all); probe: false turns probes off, so the loop alone checks and measures, and budget.tools_at_once makes probes wait for a free slot like the loop's own runs. The agent's model is set on the machine (FLUX_<NAME>_MODEL or the web's Agents settings), not in the document. Your own agent is by: {run: [my-agent, "{prompt_file}", "{artifact}"]} (agent contract).

docs.title: flux loop
docs.text:
usage: flux loop [-h]
                 {summary,passes,notes,show,ideas,tried,results,compare,starred,events,stages,design,evaluate,diff,export,import} ...

Reads a loop's record and library. It reads --loop (a folder, a document or a
record file; default: the current folder). Reads add nothing to the record and
open it read-only, so a record in use is safe. Every read takes --json: the
data its text is made from, an error as {"error": ...} with exit 2.

positional arguments:
  {summary,passes,notes,show,ideas,tried,results,compare,starred,events,stages,design,evaluate,diff,export,import}
    summary             The loop in short: its status, phase and settings
                        (budget, at once, the queue); the baseline, the best
                        per objective and the standing pick, each against the
                        baseline at the same stage.
    passes              Each pass, oldest first: its search direction and why,
                        what it decided.
    notes               The operator's notes and the decisions' reasons,
                        oldest first.
    show                One design whole: the pass that made it and what its
                        design agent probed, its idea and why, its author's
                        rundown, its gate check by check (each one's verdict
                        and the end of its output), every stage's numbers or
                        error, the checks or stages changed since it was
                        judged or measured, its trace files.
    ideas               The ideas notebook: each hypothesis, its status and
                        the evidence on record.
    tried               The designs tried, oldest first: the stages each
                        reached, its numbers or why it stopped.
    results             The measured designs at one stage, ranked by the
                        loop's objectives, with every metric each has (a
                        dictionary metric's cases as metric.case).
    compare             Designs side by side, metric by metric, the best on
                        each objective marked; how far each got and why it
                        stopped.
    starred             The designs the people starred in Results (their own
                        key designs), oldest star first: who starred each and
                        when, its numbers at the goal's stage, whether it
                        meets the goals. A bookmark: the loop decides nothing
                        with it.
    events              The record's events: without --kind how many of each
                        kind; with it the last N of that kind (decision,
                        conclusion, pass, human_note, idea, checks,
                        decided:...), each in short; --since those written
                        after a time.
    stages              The record stage by stage, in the loop's order: how
                        many designs reached each, passed or were measured,
                        refused, are running; how long its rows took (median,
                        longest); when a design last reached it.
    design              A design's files, written read-only where you read (a
                        folder of yours in the temp folder), one path a line:
                        read and grep them. Asked again, the same files. The
                        name, or the one name it starts or ends: #6, 6.
    evaluate            A draft an agent probed and did not hand in (#p4.2)
                        handed in for the loop to evaluate: Check, Measure and
                        Choose, as any design --). A person's call.
    diff                Two designs line by line; either may be a file. One
                        design: it against the design it was built from, else
                        the baseline, said first.
    export              A loop to one .zip: --loop-only (its document, files
                        and library, hidden files too) or --full (and its
                        record, workbench, answer and notes).
    import              A loop's contents replaced from a .zip (either kind):
                        its document, files and library -- and with a Full
                        file its results.

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit

docs.title: flux library
docs.text:
usage: flux library [QUERY | digest PAPER | outline PAPER | read PAPER [--section S | --around QUERY | --lines A-B | --pages A-B | --from N] | entry ID | insights] [--n N] [--project P] [--topic T] [--loop LOOP] [--json]

The loop's own library/ and every project library it reads
(library/<name>@<group>/), each document by its name there (booth.md,
silicon@hw-lab/x.pdf). With nothing: every document, one line each, then the
accepted knowledge of the projects the loop is linked into -- each project's
topics and its entries' headlines -- as its run's start saw it (never a
proposal). With QUERY: the nearest files (a reference implementation too),
each with its digest or its line and its 3 best passages, and the entries
matching it, whole. digest PAPER: its digest; outline PAPER: its sections with
their pages and lines; read PAPER: a section, the passages around a query, a
range of lines (or a PDF's pages), or from a line on. entry ID: one entry
whole (#12 or 12). insights: what the run has concluded from its record so far
(knowledge.insights: by rules or an agent), as the loop last made it. Every
answer prints about 3000 tokens at most; one cut ends with the command that
continues. What the loop hides from its agents is refused. It reads --loop
(default: the current folder). Plain text; --json for data.

positional arguments:
  QUERY              Words to search for, or digest|outline|read and the
                     PAPER, entry and the ID, or insights.

options:
  -h, --help         show this help message and exit
  --n, -n N          How many documents (and entries) for a query (default 5).
  --project PROJECT  Only one project's entries, by its place (silicon@hw-lab)
                     or address.
  --topic TOPIC      Only one topic's entries.
  --section S        read: one section, by its id in the outline (3.2) or its
                     title.
  --around QUERY     read: the passages best matching QUERY, with a little
                     context.
  --lines A-B        read: lines A to B.
  --pages A-B        read: a PDF's pages A to B.
  --from N           read: from line N on (the list: from its N-th document).
  --loop LOOP        The loop's folder or document (default: the current
                     folder).
  --json             The answer as data: the JSON its text is made from (an
                     error: {"error": ...}, exit 2).

docs.title: flux web-loop
docs.text:
usage: flux web-loop [-h] [--user USER] [--passes N] [--forever]
                     [--document DOCUMENT] [--rerun-baseline] [--now]
                     [--lines LINES] [--json] [--data DATA]
                     {ls,start,stop,status} [USER/LOOP]

Through the running `flux serve`'s control socket: the server starts and stops
the run, as its Start and Stop buttons do, as the loop's owner, each on the
audit "(by host)". The agents and models are the problem's (its flow); a start
takes what the Start dialog does. Not `flux loop`, which reads a loop's
record.

positional arguments:
  {ls,start,stop,status}
  USER/LOOP             start, stop, status: the loop, its owner's name first.

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --user USER           ls: one user's loops.
  --passes N            start: N passes (default: the last start's, as the
                        Start dialog; else 1).
  --forever             start: until stopped.
  --document DOCUMENT   start: which problem, for a loop with several
                        (x.problem.yaml).
  --rerun-baseline      start: measure the baseline again first.
  --now                 stop: at once, the pass abandoned (else at its end).
  --lines LINES         status: the log's last N lines (default 20; 0 none).
  --json                The server's answer as JSON.
  --data DATA           The server's data (default: $FLUX_DATA_HOME/web, else
                        $XDG_DATA_HOME/flux/web; else the system service's:
                        run as its account).

docs.title: flux web-agent
docs.text:
usage: flux web-agent [-h] [--user USER] [--all] [--loop USER/LOOP] [--needed]
                      [--jobs {1,2}] [--json] [--data DATA]
                      {ls,test} [AGENT]

Through the running `flux serve`'s control socket, as `flux web-loop`: ls each
user's agents and whether a start would pass their gate (ready, or needs Test
and why); test runs Account › Agents' Test for them -- the server runs it, in
the user's home with their own settings and sandbox, as the button does, kept
as theirs and on the audit "(by host)"; this command sees no credential. By
default every user and each agent they set up (logged in, or tested before),
and the loops with variables of their own that were tested in their context;
the disabled skipped. One line a Test: ok or failed and why, its seconds; exit
1 when one failed. Not `flux agent test`, which tests this account's own
agent.

positional arguments:
  {ls,test}
  AGENT             Only this agent (codex, claude, ...).

options:
  -h, --help        show this help message and exit
  --user USER       One user's agents.
  --all             test: every user (the default).
  --loop USER/LOOP  test: in that loop's context, its variables (as the page's
                    Test for the loop).
  --needed          test: only the agents whose gate is not ready.
  --jobs {1,2}      test: Tests at once (default 1, at most 2).
  --json            The server's answers as JSON.
  --data DATA       The server's data (default: $FLUX_DATA_HOME/web, else
                    $XDG_DATA_HOME/flux/web; else the system service's: run as
                    its account).

docs.title: flux machines
docs.text:
usage: flux machines [-h] [--mine] [--user NAME] [--role {runner,storage}]
                     [--machine NAME] [--label KEY=VALUE] [--minutes MINUTES]
                     [--url URL] [--json] [--data DATA]
                     {join-code,list,drain,resume,rotate,rename,label,revoke}
                     [name] [new]

join-code: a single-use code (an hour at most) for one new runner, bound to
this server's key's fingerprint, and the install line to run on it (curl
.../worker/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- CODE: it needs Podman 4.9+ and Nix
there, and says what is missing); a server machine serves the loops of users
who get the server's settings, a user's own (--mine) only that user's loops;
list: the machines joined, their capabilities, health, code and jobs; drain
NAME: it finishes the steps it holds and takes no new one (resume NAME: it
takes them again); rotate NAME: it makes new keys at its next heartbeat, the
old ones refused after (no new code); rename NAME NEW: the same machine (its
keys, jobs and history) under a new name, this server's own included; label
NAME --label KEY=VALUE ...: a server machine's labels, all of them (none
clears them), this server's own included; revoke NAME: its key refused from
now on. A step whose `needs` names a key (lab: loopback, fpga: true) goes to a
machine whose capabilities have it.

positional arguments:
  {join-code,list,drain,resume,rotate,rename,label,revoke}
  name                  drain, resume, rotate, rename, label, revoke: the
                        machine.
  new                   rename: its new name (lower-case letters, digits, . _
                        -).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --mine                join-code: a user's own machine, which only their own
                        loops use (--user NAME: whose; default: this account's
                        name).
  --user NAME           join-code --mine: the user whose machine it is.
  --role {runner,storage}
                        join-code: what the machine does (runner: checks and
                        measures; storage: holds the blobs the runners fetch,
                        a server machine).
  --machine NAME        join-code: its name (default runner-N).
  --label KEY=VALUE     join-code, label: a capability the machine gets
                        (repeat; lab=loopback, fpga=2, vivado=2025.2).
  --minutes MINUTES     join-code: how long the code is good (at most 60).
  --url URL             join-code: the server's address, for the line printed
                        (default http://127.0.0.1:8765).
  --json                list: as JSON.
  --data DATA           The server's data (default: $XDG_DATA_HOME/flux/web).

docs.title: flux worker
docs.text:
usage: flux worker [-h] [--role {runner,storage}] [--listen HOST:PORT]
                   [--url URL] [--server SERVER] [--join CODE] [--home HOME]
                   [--label KEY=VALUE] [--jobs JOBS] [--once] [--check]

The first time: --server URL --join CODE (a code from `flux machines join-
code`); the server's key is checked against the code's fingerprint, this
machine's keys are made in --home and kept. After: `flux worker` alone. Each
step runs in a Podman sandbox with the server's sandbox limits for its loop
(FLUX_SANDBOX=0: on this host). Labels (--label lab=loopback, or
<home>/capabilities.yaml) are the keys a step's `needs` can ask for.

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --role {runner,storage}
                        What this machine does (runner: checks and measures;
                        storage: holds the blobs the runners fetch, with a
                        join code of role storage).
  --listen HOST:PORT    storage: where it listens for the runners (default
                        0.0.0.0:8766).
  --url URL             storage: the address the runners reach it at (default
                        http://<its name>:<port>).
  --server SERVER       The Flux server's address (http://host:port), for the
                        join.
  --join CODE           A join code (fx1-...@...), used once.
  --home HOME           Its keys, config and caches (default:
                        $FLUX_WORKER_HOME, else ~/.local/share/flux-worker).
  --label KEY=VALUE     A capability of this machine (repeat; kept).
  --jobs JOBS           Steps at once (each also waits for room in this
                        machine's pool).
  --once                Run one step, then stop (a test, a demo).
  --check               Check this machine can run a step (disk, environment,
                        a container as a job's), then stop.

docs.title: flux ask
docs.text:
usage: flux ask [-h] [--tui] [--file FILE] [--hidden HIDDEN] [--skill SKILL]
                [--author AUTHOR] [--dir DIR] [--checks CHECKS] [--no-run]
                [--questions {decide,operator}] [--wait-s WAIT_S] [--repair]
                [--session SESSION] [--note NOTE]
                [--unfinished {time,error,stopped}] [--think | --no-think]
                [--effort EFFORT] [--model MODEL] [--num-predict NUM_PREDICT]
                [--author-replies AUTHOR_REPLIES] [--no-sandbox]
                [prompt]

positional arguments:
  prompt                What you want, in words (none: the setup screen
                        opens).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --tui                 The setup screen first: the prompt, the files, the
                        skills and the author.
  --file, -f FILE       An input: a spec, code, a reference, a PDF, tests
                        (repeatable; a folder is copied whole).
  --hidden HIDDEN       A path in --dir hidden from the loop's AI agents and
                        an agent author (repeatable): the document gets it in
                        flow.knowledge.hidden.
  --skill SKILL         A skill folder (SKILL.md), or a folder of them, for
                        the author and the designers (repeatable).
  --author AUTHOR       Who writes the problem: flux (FluxAgent, the default),
                        a coding agent preset (opencode, claude, codex), or a
                        JSON agent spec.
  --dir DIR             The working directory (default: ./out/ask_<slug>; its
                        name is the problem's id).
  --checks CHECKS       Repairs of a refused document (default 3).
  --no-run              Kept for old scripts: flux ask never runs the
                        document.
  --questions {decide,operator}
                        operator: an agent author may ask a question, answered
                        in runs/author/inbox.jsonl (the web's page) within
                        --wait-s; decide (default): it decides.
  --wait-s WAIT_S       How long a question waits for its answer (default
                        600).
  --repair              The document is in --dir already, refused: check it
                        and repair it, write nothing new.
  --session SESSION     The agent author's session to continue, when the loop
                        keeps none in runs/author/session.json.
  --note NOTE           With --repair: what the person says to do.
  --unfinished {time,error,stopped}
                        With --repair: how the job before it was cut off; the
                        agent's session goes on though the document passes.
  --think, --no-think   Think, or not (--no-think), as a chat's message:
                        FluxAgent reasons before it writes; a coding agent at
                        its effort when thinking, else its lowest. Unsaid: the
                        admin's default (Admin › Runtime › Agents;
                        FLUX_THINK).
  --effort EFFORT       The author's effort, first, before --think, as a
                        chat's message: a coding agent's, one its kind takes
                        (claude: low..max; codex, opencode: minimal..);
                        FluxAgent's low | medium | high | max.
  --model MODEL         FluxAgent's model, when it authors (--author flux).
  --num-predict NUM_PREDICT
  --author-replies AUTHOR_REPLIES
                        Scripted replies for FluxAgent as the author (tests,
                        dry runs).
  --no-sandbox          Run on this machine, not in the container sandbox
                        (Podman or Docker; also FLUX_SANDBOX=0).

  --json        Print one JSON object: ok, code, the issues (severity, path,
                file, line, message, suggestion, detail, fix) and the text the
                check prints otherwise.

docs.title: flux task run
docs.text:
usage: flux task run [-h] [--skill SKILL] [--db DB]
                     [--tries-per-pass TRIES_PER_PASS]
                     [--repairs-per-design REPAIRS_PER_DESIGN] [--model MODEL]
                     [--replies REPLIES] [--out OUT] [--role ROLE=NAME]
                     [--agent HALF [HALF ...]] [--tui] [--think]
                     [--num-predict NUM_PREDICT] [--passes N]
                     [--tool-hops TOOL_HOPS] [--hop-share HOP_SHARE]
                     [--patience PATIENCE] [--reevaluate]
                     [--reevaluate-tabs TABS] [--remeasure] [--rerun-baseline]
                     [--json FILE] [--no-prototype] [--no-sandbox]
                     file

positional arguments:
  file                  The problem's folder, or one of its documents
                        (problem.yaml, NAME.problem.yaml).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --skill SKILL         A skill folder (SKILL.md), or a folder of them, beside
                        the document's own (repeatable).
  --db DB               Campaign record (default: <document dir>/out/<task
                        id>.db).
  --tries-per-pass TRIES_PER_PASS
                        What a pass may work through: its tries that give no
                        design and a critic's send-backs; a search's rounds
                        (default: the document's).
  --repairs-per-design REPAIRS_PER_DESIGN
                        Repairs of one design (default: the document's).
  --model MODEL         The model name on the endpoint in use: the local
                        Ollama by default, or the server FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL
                        names.
  --replies REPLIES     A JSON list of scripted replies: runs without a model.
  --out OUT             Write the decided artifact here (default: <document
                        dir>/out/<task id><extension>).
  --role ROLE=NAME      Switch who fills one of the four roles, repeatable:
                        --role orchestrator=rules. `flux task check` lists the
                        choices.
  --agent HALF [HALF ...]
                        The AGENT takes these halves: orchestrate (it picks
                        what next, which direction, which improve option, with
                        its reasons on record), plan (it writes the loop plan
                        the pass follows); all for both. The model's tool
                        calls inside its turns are the document's budget.tools
                        (on by default).
  --tui                 The curses screen: tasks, results, log, the r loop
                        toggle.
  --think               Ask the model for its reasoning on every turn.
  --num-predict NUM_PREDICT
                        Output tokens per turn (default 6000).
  --passes N            Stop after N passes. Default: the document's
                        `budget.passes`, else run until stopped (`flux stop`,
                        Ctrl-C, q in the TUI); a pass at rest is followed by
                        one that explores.
  --tool-hops TOOL_HOPS
                        Rounds of tool calls a turn may make.
  --hop-share HOP_SHARE
                        Share of the model's context window a round that may
                        call tools may write (0.5).
  --patience PATIENCE   Prototype turns granted after each new best.
  --reevaluate          At this start, after the baseline: check and measure
                        every design on record again -- the designs the loop's
                        Invalidate all set aside, else every design,
                        invalidated first -- then the passes; a stop keeps
                        what was measured and the next start continues.
  --reevaluate-tabs TABS
                        With --reevaluate: the Results tabs whose designs are
                        measured again, comma-separated -- accepted, rejected,
                        failed, pending: their designs written as a round to
                        measure again, as Re-Evaluate does; what Invalidate
                        all set aside only with pending; all four (or none
                        said) is every design.
  --remeasure           Measure again the designs a rejection asked to (the
                        re-check), then rest.
  --rerun-baseline      Measure pass 0 again though the document's baseline is
                        unchanged (otherwise the one on record stands).
  --json FILE           Also write the answer as JSON: the decision, the
                        frontier, what was refused, the application's own
                        result.
  --no-prototype        No prototype stage: the target directly.
  --no-sandbox          Run on this machine, not in the container sandbox
                        (Podman or Docker; also FLUX_SANDBOX=0).

Exit status: 0 a design meets every requirement (the decision, its artifact
written); 3 correct designs were measured but none meets every requirement yet
(no decision; the closest is reported, no artifact written), or none has
passed every stage yet (a stage refused every design tried there); 1 no design
was measured, the run could not start, or the record could not be written (the
run stopped); 130 interrupted.

docs.title: Commands and placeholders
docs.text: Every command a document names runs the same way, receives the same placeholders, and follows a contract: its arguments, what it prints, its exit code.

docs.title: How commands run
docs.text:
Every command a document names (checks, stages, estimates, the generator, the search, the baseline, the composition) runs the same way, and is said run: (command: there is refused). Your own agent's command differs; see agent command.

  • Written as a list of arguments or one string. A string is split like a shell would split it, but no shell runs: for a pipe or redirection, call one yourself: ["sh", "-c", "cat {artifact} | wc -l"].
  • flux first runs Flux's own CLI with the same interpreter (flux tools ...).
  • fluxpreset first runs one of Flux's presets the same way (fluxpreset rtl measure ...).
  • Working directory is {workdir}, the pass's trace folder, shared by every design in the pass. Name your files with {home}/...; relative paths do not reach the loop's folder.
