  • Environment: Flux's own, with MAKEFLAGS cleared and FLUX_JOBS set: a build's parallelism (make -j"$FLUX_JOBS", verilator --build-jobs "$FLUX_JOBS"), the cores shared among the tool runs at once; ccache's variables when ccache is on PATH. The loop's own checks and stages of one design also get FLUX_REUSE_DIR, a folder of that design's where the presets keep what their tools built so a later stage continues instead of starting again; it goes with the pass. See Compiling.
  • Standard input: inherited from Flux, not data. A command must not read stdin.
  • Output: stdout and stderr are captured separately; checks and stages read both, joined. Line endings are normalised. Live shows the command, its folder, the ends of its output as it runs, and its exit.
  • Timeouts stop the whole process group. A missing program is reported as "not found on PATH" before the run; flux task check lists them.
  • Placeholders are replaced inside every argument, without quoting. At load, a {name} that is neither the loop's nor a knob is refused (an argument containing spaces, such as an sh -c script, is not checked). A placeholder with no value for that command is passed through as written.

docs.title: Command placeholders
docs.text:
Placeholder Value Generator Check, stage, estimate Search Baseline Composition {artifact} Path of the design file (<workdir>/<name><ext>) writes it reads it "" writes it writes the whole {home} The document's folder (absolute) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {workdir} The pass's working folder ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ the compose folder {python} The interpreter running Flux ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {name} The design's name (mul8#3, slice_sieve) ✓ ✓ search ✓ the loop's id {params} Path of a JSON file of params ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {knob} One knob's value (True/False for booleans) search mode ✓ first choices {point} Path of a JSON file of every knob search mode ✓ "" ✓ "" {failure} Why the last attempt was refused (text) drafting "" {attempt} 1, 2, ... drafting 1 {history}, {state} Search history and the search's own state file ✓ {metrics} The stage's declared metrics:, comma-separated, in the document's order; flux task check asks the preset (--check) whether its stage can give them stage only {scope} The scope a pass works on, in search.scope's brief and check {prompt}, {prompt_file}, {session}, {answer} Brief and session, for your own agent

{part} is not a placeholder any more (it was always empty: a loop is one design): a command saying it is refused when the document loads, as any unknown placeholder is. Remove it.

File formats:

  • {params} is params.json in {workdir}: the document's params as a JSON object rewritten for every command.
  • {point} is <artifact>.point.json: the knobs as a JSON object, components nested ({"algorithm": "list_sieve", "prefetch": {"distance": 2}}); an optional component that is off is left out.
  • {failure} is the text itself, not a file: the last 4000 characters of the failing check's output (prefixed failed at <check>: with several checks), or a send-back reason. It is empty on the first attempt.

docs.title: Generator command
docs.text:
design: {run: ...} writes one design to {artifact}. Its stdout is not the design.

Drafting (no space): each draft is checked; if the checks refuse it, the command runs again with {failure} and {attempt} set, up to budget.repairs_per_design times. A failing command (non-zero exit, or exit 0 without the file) ends the repairs at once; so does writing the same design twice.

Search (with a space): the command runs once per proposed point, with that point's {knob}s and {point}. A failing command drops the point; there is no repair. The design is named after its knob values.

# document: design: {run: "{python} {home}/gen.py {artifact} {attempt} {failure}"}
import sys
out, attempt, failure = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]   # failure is "" at first
design = "def count_primes(n):\n    ...\n" if not failure else "...a design that fixes it..."
open(out, "w").write(design)                                         # exit 0

docs.title: Check command
docs.text:
A check reads {artifact} and reports failures. Flux reads stdout and stderr together:

  1. Exit 3 means the design did not build, whatever was printed. For a check named build, any non-zero exit means that.
  2. Otherwise, with count_re (default (\d+) failing): the first match's number is the failure count. With fail_re only: each match is one failure.
  3. With no match: exit 0 passes, any other exit is one failure.

A printed count wins over the exit code: 2 failing with exit 0 fails, and 0 failing with exit 1 passes. The first check with failures refuses the design; its output (last 4000 characters) is what Live shows and what a model or agent gets back to repair. A check's debug output on stderr never fails it unless a pattern matches there.

# document: test: {correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"}
import importlib.util, sys
try:
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("design", sys.argv[1])
    design = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(design)
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"did not load: {exc}"); sys.exit(3)                 # 3: did not build
cases = {10: 4, 100: 25, 1000: 168}
bad = [n for n, want in cases.items() if design.count_primes(n) != want]
for n in bad:
    print(f"FAIL n={n}: got {design.count_primes(n)}, expected {cases[n]}")
print(f"{len(bad)} failing of {len(cases)}")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)

docs.title: Measurement command
docs.text:
A stage reads {artifact} and prints its numbers. It must exit 0; on any other exit its numbers are discarded and the design is refused at that stage. Flux reads stdout and stderr:

  • name=value, at the start of a line or after a space: the first occurrence of each metric counts. value is a number (1.5, -2e3); nan and inf are unmeasured.
  • A JSON object on a line of its own (it may span lines): its keys that are declared metrics are read. A name=value line overrides it.
  • A dictionary metric is name={"test": 12, "other": null} (the last occurrence counts), or a dictionary under its name in the JSON object: each finite entry is name.test, and name one number of them -- the aggregate its objective says, else the dictionary's own _a (gate_count={"AND": 41, "OR": 34, "_a": "sum"}: mean, median, min, max or sum; any other value refuses the measurement), else their mean. _a is no entry. If designs say different _a values, all are made one number by the first one the loop met, and the journal says so. Nothing declares it a dictionary; one no objective names is recorded and shown, never ranked.
  • metrics_re, if given, replaces the name=value patterns: one capture group each.

Exit 0 with no metric found refuses the design ("no metric matched in the output"). A stage that reports only some of its metrics is still recorded with those it did. For timings, set budget.tools_at_once: 1: runs at the same time disturb each other. That holds the measurements to one at a time, checks included: one pool of slots for every check, measurement and probe.

# document: measure: {bench: {run: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact}", metrics: [time_ms]}}
import importlib.util, statistics, sys, time
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("design", sys.argv[1])
design = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(design)
runs = []
for _ in range(5):
    t = time.perf_counter(); design.count_primes(1_000_000); runs.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3)
print(f"time_ms={statistics.median(runs):.3f} time_spread_ms={max(runs) - min(runs):.3f}")

The measurement cache: a design measured once by a stage is not measured again while nothing that stage depends on changes: the design's text (or knobs), the stage's command, metrics and patterns, params, the knobs the command names, the files in the folder (except out/, runs/, workbench/, library/ and the documents), the {home}/... files the command names, and the builds of its programs and needs. Change any of them and it is measured again. Only successful measurements are read back. The memory is the loop's record itself: a record copied or moved keeps it, a new record starts without it.

docs.title: Estimate command
docs.text:
estimate: {kind: command, run: ..., margin: 0.1} runs before the stage, once for each design the cache does not hold, with the stage's placeholders and timeout. It prints the stage's metrics in the same format. A non-zero exit or no numbers means no estimate: the tool runs. A design whose estimate misses a cutoff or a limit by more than margin (a fraction of the limit) is skipped and recorded as refused by the estimate.

# document: estimate: {kind: command, run: "{python} {home}/estimate.py {artifact}"}
import sys
print(f"time_ms={len(open(sys.argv[1]).read()) * 0.01:.3f}")

docs.title: Search command
docs.text:
search: {run: ..., timeout_s: 600} is your own search. Each round, Flux writes {history} and runs the command; the command answers with JSON on stdout.

{history} (search-history.json in {workdir}):

{"measured": [{"name": "w4", "knobs": {"w": 4}, "stage": "bench", "metrics": {"time_ms": 3.1}, "by": "mine"}],
 "refused":  [{"name": "w9", "why": "failed at correctness: 2 failing"}],
 "guidance": "operator notes, if any",
 "round": 3}

{state} (out/<record>.search-state.json) is yours: read it if it exists, write it every round; it survives restarts.

The answer is the last line of stdout that is a JSON object (or the whole stdout):

Key Meaning candidates [{name, artifact, knobs, why, by}]: name required; artifact is the design's text (not a path); knobs reach the checks and stages as {knob}/{point} lessons Lines added to the run's lessons not_established Lines added to the report conclusion What the search concluded, recorded when nothing is decided say A line printed with the round done true: this is the last batch

No candidates also ends the search. Candidates go straight to the checks and stages; the generator does not run for them. A non-zero exit or no JSON ends the search with a note.

# document: search: {run: "{python} {home}/search.py {history} {state}", timeout_s: 300}
import json, os, sys
history, state_path = json.load(open(sys.argv[1])), sys.argv[2]
state = json.load(open(state_path)) if os.path.exists(state_path) else {"next": 1}
tried = {m["name"] for m in history["measured"]} | {r["name"] for r in history["refused"]}
cands = [{"name": f"w{w}", "artifact": f"WIDTH = {w}\n", "knobs": {"w": w}, "why": "next width"}
         for w in (state["next"], state["next"] + 1) if f"w{w}" not in tried]
state["next"] += 2
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(state_path), exist_ok=True)
json.dump(state, open(state_path, "w"))
print(json.dumps({"candidates": cands, "done": state["next"] > 8}))

docs.title: Baseline command
docs.text: baseline: {run: ...} runs once, before pass 1, with the first point (every knob's first choice, overlaid with the first seed). It either writes the reference design to {artifact}, or prepares the project and writes nothing (then the checks and stages run on the project, through {home}/... paths). A non-zero exit records "baseline failed" and the loop goes on.

docs.title: Agent command
docs.text:
Your own coding agent: by: {run: [my-agent, "--prompt", "{prompt_file}"], output: text, resume: [...]}. Write run as a list.

  • Placeholders use Python formatting: {prompt} (the brief; very long briefs become an instruction to read the file), {prompt_file}, {artifact}, {workdir} (the session folder), {name}, {python}, {home}, {workbench}, {probe}; a resume command also gets {session} and {answer}. Write a literal brace as {{ or }}; an unknown name refuses the draft.
  • The brief goes to stdin unless the command names {prompt}, {prompt_file} or {answer}.
  • It runs in its session folder with Flux's environment, plus FLUX_<NAME>_ENV and FLUX_PROBE. Default timeout 1800 s.
  • It writes {artifact}. If it does not, its reply is read: a JSON artifact field, else the largest fenced code block.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words Flux and its web app use, one term each.

Loop. A folder holding a document, problem.yaml, and the scripts and files it names. The folder's name is the loop's id. Flux generates designs, checks and measures them, and decides, pass after pass.

Document. The loop's problem.yaml: what to make (statement, contract), who does each box (flow), what wins (objectives) and how much to spend (budget). See the Document reference.

Start. One launch of a loop, from Start (or flux task run) until it stops. A loop keeps one log and one record across its starts; each start resumes from the record.

Pass. One trip round the loop, one design: choose what to try, make a design, check it, measure it, decide. budget.passes or --passes N caps them on the command line, the Start dialog on the web; without a cap a run goes on until stopped. budget.designs_at_once is how many passes run side by side; budget.pipeline: true lets each start its next design as soon as the current one passed Check, its measurement finishing behind.

Trunk. The other way to run a loop: trunk: at the document's root in place of flow:. A coding agent works in one long session and hands in designs as it writes them; branches check, measure and decide each one meanwhile. See passes or a trunk.

Box. One step of the loop as the configurator's Graph draws it. Setup, before the passes: Plan (plan) and Baseline (baseline). Knowledge, what the agents can look up, a bubble each: Skills (skills), Library, Workbench, Lessons and Ideas (flow.knowledge), Notes (notes) and Hidden (flow.knowledge.hidden). Each pass: Search (search), Design (design), Check (check), Measure (measure) and Choose (choose), whose arrow points into Knowledge. The record is always on and has no box. flow says who works each box.

Check. A command that decides whether a design is correct (flow.check). Checks run in the order written; the first that reports failures refuses the design. Together they are the gate: a design that fails it is never measured.

Measurement. A command that puts numbers on a design that passed the gate. Each measurement is a stage of flow.measure; stages run cheapest first, and a cutoff decides which designs go on to the next.

Design. One candidate the loop made: a file (the artifact) written by a script, a model or an agent, with its checks and measurements on the record.

Design name. Each pass's design takes the next number, a new draft or an edit of the standing design alike: pass 1 primes#1, pass 2 primes#2 (from primes#1), pass 3 primes#3 (from primes#1). The numbers go on after a stop and a restart. Inside a pass, the tries are primes#3, primes#3.2, primes#3.3 ...; the try the gate passes is the pass's design and is named primes#3. A pass none of whose tries passed spends its number, so the numbers can have gaps. Two designs whose texts differ only in spacing or comments are the same design: a draft that repeats a measured one is refused ("the same as primes#1"), and so is one another pass running at once has just numbered ("the same as primes#4, measured by another pass at once"). A draft that repeats a design whose numbers are stale (an edit changed how a stage measures) is not refused: it is that design again, under its own number, measured again where its numbers are stale ("primes#2 again: its numbers were stale"). A search's points (arch=ripple) keep names of their own. A draft an agent checked or measured itself without handing it in is a probed draft, primes#p4.2 (pass 4, its second): Results lists it folded under its table, "unverified", never counted, with Evaluate to have the loop check and measure it as a design of its own.

Standing design. The design the next pass builds on: the last decision on the record (with nothing that meets every limit, the closest). A run started again keeps it.

Decision. The design that meets every limit and is best on the objectives. Flux writes it under out/. When none meets every limit, the closest is reported, not decided. While a stage has refused every design tried there (a time limit too short, a tool that crashes), none has passed every stage: there is no answer yet and no design stands; the loop says so until a design passes every stage. "Then earliest" after its Decided by means another accepted design ties it on every objective: the one made first (measured first) is the decision.

Record. Every design, check and measurement a loop made, with where it came from, kept in out/. A rerun reuses it.

Campaign. The command line's word for one line of work inside a record, named after the loop. --campaign on flux loop summary, flux stop and the others picks one; by default, the latest.

Objective, limit, preference. An objective is a metric and a direction. With a goal it is a limit (at least or at most a value); without one it is a preference, compared in the order written.

Front, knee. The front (Pareto frontier) is the set of designs no other design beats on every objective at once. The knee is where improving one objective starts to cost much more of another.

Knob, space. A knob is one setting with a list of choices; the space is all of them (flow.search.space). A point is one choice for every knob.

Search. How the next points are chosen (flow.search.params): sweep, montecarlo, gradient, anneal, genetic, pareto, phases, or FluxAgent or an agent proposing them (by: flux beside the space). See Searches.

Policy. Sets the search's emphasis (flow.search.policy): adaptive (the default), explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations.

FluxAgent. Flux's own language model, on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, as a worker: flux in a document (design: flux, {by: flux}), a chat or --author; model, its old name, is the same. It can propose points, write designs, review the document, digest papers and answer in Chat.

Agent. A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or one a server adds) that writes files. It runs on its own model settings, never on Flux's. See Models and agents.

Critic. A second opinion on a box: Search (the direction picked for a pass), Check (each design its checks passed), Measure (a stage's numbers) or Choose (the pick), each set in its box's panel in the configurator's Graph. Its rejection is a verdict: the direction is picked again, the design fails, the numbers are marked, or the pick is made again. See critics.

Author. In flux ask and New loop › Agent, FluxAgent or an agent that writes the document and its files from your prompt.

Knowledge, library. What the model and agents can look up besides the document: the loop's library (library/, the files flow.knowledge.library lists, the projects'), read on demand with flux library, and the insights drawn from the loop's results (flux library insights).

Ideas notebook. The hypotheses the loop's model and agents proposed, each with the designs that tested it, kept across passes (Results › Ideas). The ideas cleanup merges repeated ideas into one; a merged idea is kept, folded under the one it was merged into. Each idea has a number, said "idea 3" (oldest first), so it is never taken for design #3.

Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md (a name, a description, then instructions) that the model and agents can load. The loop's skills/ folder is read by default.

Workbench. The agents' own folder beside the document, workbench/: tools they build and notes they keep, shared by the loop's agents and kept across runs.

Chat. A conversation with an agent or FluxAgent that belongs to no loop, in the web app's Chat tab. It may read your loops (read-only) and keep tools and notes in your chat workbench, one folder for all your chats, as the admin allows and you switch on. See Chat.

Hidden from AI. Paths the loop's agents may not read, such as the gate's tests (knowledge.hidden). The loop's own commands still read them.

Golden model. A short Python file, usually golden.py, that says what a hardware design must compute (PORTS and golden(**inputs)), not how. See Presets.

Prototype. The algorithm written first in Python (or SystemC) and checked against the golden model before the hardware design is written.

Baseline. A reference measured before pass 1 (pass 0), such as the design you have today. Results can be read relative to it; it is never the decision.

Preset. One of Flux's own checks and measurements, run as fluxpreset NAME. See Presets.

Archived loop. A stopped loop kept read-only, its working files deleted to free disk: its results, document, files, workbench and Chat stay. The loop lists show it under Archived; Unarchive makes it editable again. See Archive.

Sandbox. The container flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run in, so a loop's code and agents cannot touch the rest of the machine. See Run, stop, resume.

ULP. A unit in the last place: the gap between two neighbouring floating-point numbers. "Within 1 ULP" means at most one step from the exact result.

ASAP7. A free, predictive 7 nm process design kit from Arizona State University. Flux's area, timing and power numbers are on ASAP7, not on a commercial process.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Flux's own checks and measurements. A document runs one as fluxpreset NAME ...; nothing is copied into the loop's folder. flux tools lists the catalog entries below, and the configurator offers them as a check's Type or a measurement's Tool under Flux presets. In a shell, fluxpreset alone lists the presets and fluxpreset NAME --help describes one.

Each entry gives its title, catalog id and role, the command a document writes, and its parameters with their defaults. A {name} in a command that is not one of the loop's placeholders is a parameter.

docs.title: golden
docs.text:
The golden test for RTL: the design against a golden model's vectors. It prints the failing vectors and N failing of M, and exits 0 (pass), 1 (fail) or 3 (did not compile). --extra F.sv adds a module the design instantiates; --lib PATH reads shared HDL in place, as rtl's below. The golden model's format is below.

fluxpreset golden DESIGN --golden golden.py [--extra F.sv] [--lib PATH ...] [--module M]
  • Test against a golden model (rtl-golden, a check): fluxpreset golden {artifact} --golden {golden} Verilator runs the module on golden.py's vectors and counts the wrong outputs. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing. Needs verilator.

docs.title: rtl
docs.text:
Hardware checks and measurements on the ASAP7 process: lint with Verilator, measure with OpenROAD-flow-scripts. rtl measure runs the flow to the stage asked and prints one line, fmax_mhz=... area_um2=... power_w=... cell_count=... logic_count=... gate_equivalents=... path_ps=... worst_slack_ps=... (stat only area and counts, adding gate_count; route adds drc_errors and wirelength_um, its timing and power estimated from global routing; final is the same line, signed off on the parasitics extracted from the routed wires).

--metrics a,b,c asks for metrics by name: the line then has exactly those, in that order, and stage=. One flow run serves them all. fluxpreset rtl metrics lists the names, each with where it is read from and the earliest stage that has it:

From Metrics stat area_um2, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, gate_count; the area classes of rtl breakdown: area_seq_um2, area_arith_um2, area_xor_um2, area_buf_um2, area_logic_um2, flop_count synth fmax_mhz, power_w, path_ps, worst_slack_ps, clock_period_ps; the critical path of rtl path: path_levels, path_cell_ps, path_wire_ps; tns_ps, hold_slack_ps, power_dynamic_w, power_leakage_w, die_area_um2, utilization_pct place wirelength_est_um route drc_errors, wirelength_um final buf_count

Some of these are only ever asked for by name:

  • tns_ps: the total negative slack, 0 when timing closes. Beside worst_slack_ps it says whether one path fails or many.
  • hold_slack_ps: the worst hold slack. The clock is ideal before route.
  • power_dynamic_w and power_leakage_w: power_w split into what switching costs and what the cells leak idle.
  • die_area_um2 and utilization_pct: the die, and how much of the core the cells fill at that stage (area_um2 is the cells alone); the two to read when tuning --utilization.
  • wirelength_est_um: the placer's wire estimate, the routed wirelength_um without paying for routing; the same number at later stages.
  • buf_count: the buffers in the finished design. The flow counts them only at the end, so final alone gives it.

Area, cells, power and timing are read at the stage asked. logic_count and the area classes come from synthesis, which every stage runs first. An unknown name, or one the stage cannot give (drc_errors at place), is refused before anything runs: error: drc_errors needs --stage route (asked: place) -- known at place: .... A metric that was asked for but cannot be read fails the run. The catalog's stages run --metrics {metrics}, and Flux fills in the metrics the document's stage lists. flux task check asks the preset (--check, which runs nothing) and refuses a stage that lists a metric its stage cannot give.

Three counts of the logic stand beside cell_count (every mapped cell at that stage):

  • logic_count: the cells of the synthesised netlist less the sequential ones (flops, latches, clock gates) and the buffers, inverters and tie cells, the classes rtl breakdown groups by. Every stage reads it from synthesis, before OpenROAD adds buffers and resizes cells.
  • gate_equivalents: the usual post-synthesis figure: the standard-cell area of the synthesised netlist over the area of the library's reference 2-input NAND, ASAP7's unit-drive NAND2x1 (0.08748 um2, read from the standard-cell LEF). Flops and tie cells count; macros and memories do not. It is the same number at every stage: the buffers and resized cells placement adds, and physical-only cells (tapcells, fillers), are in a later stage's area_um2 but not in gate_equivalents.
  • gate_count: technology-independent. Yosys runs synth -flatten -noabc, then abc -g AND,OR,XOR,MUX, and each combinational gate counts as one: a 2-input AND, OR or XOR, a 2:1 MUX, a NOT. Flops and buffers do not count. It is a dictionary by gate type, gate_count={"AND":41,"OR":34,"XOR":31,"MUX":0,"NOT":0,"_a":"sum"}; its _a makes its one number the total, so an objective needs no aggregate:. stat prints it by default. At the other stages it is printed when asked for, and it costs an extra Yosys pass.

--advanced-gates, a flag that is off by default, synthesises the design to complex cells: AOI and OAI gates, XOR and XNOR, majority, full and half adders, in all their sizes, with multipliers built as Booth multipliers and adders built from full adders. It usually gives a smaller area and less power; timing changes too, most often for the better, so measure both if timing matters. Every number of the run comes from that netlist: area_um2, power_w, cell_count, fmax_mhz, the critical path, logic_count, gate_equivalents and rtl breakdown's classes. rtl measure, breakdown, fmax, power, energy and path take it; the catalog lists it as advanced_gates under each of those entries' options, and a document adds it to the stage's run line. Without the flag the flow and its numbers are exactly as before. On adder16's behavioural adder at place (333 ps), the area goes from 16.6 to 12.2 um2; on an 8x8 multiplier (625 ps), from 38.0 to 33.9 um2, power down by a third.

With the flag, gate_count also counts with complex gates. Without it the count is the one above. With it, Yosys runs synth -flatten -noabc, then extract_fa (full and half adders), then abc -g AND,NAND,OR,NOR,XOR,XNOR,ANDNOT,ORNOT,MUX,NMUX,AOI3,OAI3,AOI4,OAI4 and opt_clean, and the netlist is read. Each of these is one gate:

Key One gate AND, NAND, OR, NOR, XOR, XNOR a 2-input gate ANDNOT, ORNOT A & ~B, A \| ~B MUX, NMUX a 2:1 mux, inverted or not NOT an inverter AOI3, OAI3, AOI4, OAI4 ~((A&B)\|C), ~((A\|B)&C), ~((A&B)\|(C&D)), ~((A\|B)&(C\|D)) AO3, OA3, AO4, OA4 the same without the inversion: an AOI or OAI whose only reader is a NOT, counted with it as one gate (ABC has no such type) FA a full adder: the sum and the carry of three bits HA a half adder: of two bits, or of three with one constant

The adders are found before ABC runs, and ABC leaves them whole; an adder of several bits counts one per bit. There is no MAJ: Yosys extracts a carry only beside the XOR of the same bits, so a majority on its own stays AOI and OAI gates. The inverters extract_fa adds where the logic had the other polarity count like any NOT. Every key is printed, 0 when absent, with _a as before, and the same design always gives the same counts. On adder16's ripple-carry adder, the count without the flag is {"AND":31,"OR":15,"XOR":31,"MUX":0,"NOT":0} (77), and with it 15 FA and 1 HA (16).

fluxpreset rtl lint DESIGN
fluxpreset rtl measure DESIGN --stage stat|synth|place|route|final --clock-ps N [--metrics a,b,c] [--advanced-gates] [--utilization P] [--hierarchy] [--seed N] [--check]
fluxpreset rtl metrics [--stage S] [--json]
fluxpreset rtl cycles DESIGN --golden golden.py
fluxpreset rtl equiv DESIGN --reference ref.sv
fluxpreset rtl breakdown DESIGN [--advanced-gates]
fluxpreset rtl fmax DESIGN --stage synth|place|route|final [--steps 6] [--advanced-gates]
fluxpreset rtl power DESIGN --golden golden.py --stage place [--advanced-gates]
fluxpreset rtl energy DESIGN --golden golden.py --stage place [--advanced-gates]
fluxpreset rtl path DESIGN --stage synth|place|route|final [--advanced-gates]

breakdown, fmax, power, energy and path take --utilization, --hierarchy and --seed too.

docs.title: What is passed to the flow
docs.text:
Three options set what the flow is given. All are off by default, and the numbers are then exactly as without them. Put one in a stage's command when you need it: a stage's whole command is what identifies its measurements, so another seed is measured afresh.

Option What it does --utilization P How full the floorplan's core is, in percent (40 by default). A lower one gives a larger die and easier routing. Nothing changes at stat or in breakdown, which stop at synthesis. --hierarchy Keeps every module instead of flattening: each is synthesised apart and nothing is optimised across a boundary. Placement still works on all the cells at once. Cell counts and areas are the whole design's; gate_count stays that of the flattened design. --seed N Another random start for global placement, global routing and detailed routing, to see how much of a result is luck. It reaches those steps only, so stat and synth do not change. Seed 1 is what global placement does anyway.

docs.title: Other HDL beside the design (--lib)
docs.text:
The design stays one file with only the agent's own modules. Shared IP and a baseline's modules live elsewhere in the loop's folder and are passed beside it, read in place, never copied:

fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --lib {home}/ip --lib {home}/baseline/fifo.sv --stage synth --metrics {metrics} --clock-ps {clock_ps}

Every rtl command (and golden, and measure --check) takes --lib PATH, repeatable, read in the order given and before the design:

  • a .sv or .v file; a .svh or .vh header adds its folder to the include path;
  • a folder: its .sv and .v files (not its subfolders), sorted by name, the folder on the include path;
  • a .f filelist: one source per line, +incdir+DIR or -I DIR for includes, -f FILE for a nested list, paths relative to the list; // and # start comments, any other option is refused.

Verilator, Yosys and OpenROAD-flow-scripts (its VERILOG_FILES and VERILOG_INCLUDE_DIRS) read them; --module names the top as before (lint takes --module too, the design's first module by default). A design that defines a module (or interface, package) that a --lib file also defines is refused, exit 3, before any tool runs: the design redefines module fifo of ip/fifo.sv: instantiate it, don't copy it. There is no override. equiv reads the libs on both sides; the reference's own definitions win, so a self-contained reference proves as before. A missing path is exit 3 (measure --check: exit 2, so flux task check names it). The catalog entries list lib under options with no default: a run line has it only when a document adds it.

  • Lint for hardware defects (rtl-lint, a check): fluxpreset rtl lint {artifact} Verilator's hardware defects only: latches, multiple drivers, combinational loops, blocking/non-blocking mixes, implicit nets; width and style warnings are not defects. It also refuses what does not parse. Reports N failing. Needs verilator.
  • Area and cells (ASAP7) (rtl-stat, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} --stage stat --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts' synthesis: the mapped cells' area and count, the logic cells among them, NAND2 gate equivalents, and Yosys's technology-independent gate count (2-input AND/OR/XOR, 2:1 MUX, NOT); nothing timed, the cheapest screen. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports area_um2, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, gate_count. Needs yosys, openroad, make.
  • Synthesise and time (ASAP7) (rtl-synth, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} --stage synth --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to its floorplan: the netlist timed unplaced, seconds. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Place and time (ASAP7) (rtl-place, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} --stage place --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to detailed placement, timed with wire estimates: tens of seconds. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Route and time (ASAP7) (rtl-route, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} --stage route --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to routing: timing after global routing, minutes. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Sign-off timing and power (ASAP7) (rtl-final, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --metrics {metrics} --stage final --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts through detailed routing and its finish: timing and power with the parasitics extracted from the routed wires (OpenRCX), plus DRC errors and wirelength: the slowest stage and the closest to silicon. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, logic_count, gate_equivalents, path_ps, drc_errors, wirelength_um. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta. Give it a generous timeout_s (the crafter suggests 3600): a stage's default is 600 s.
  • Clock cycles (Verilator) (rtl-cycles, a stage): fluxpreset rtl cycles {artifact} --golden {golden} A clocked design run on golden.py's vectors, each started when the last is done: its latency in cycles (the most, the fewest) and the mean cycles per result. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports latency_cycles, latency_min_cycles, cycles_per_result. Needs verilator.
  • Equal to a reference module (rtl-equiv, a check): fluxpreset rtl equiv {artifact} --reference {reference} Formal equivalence with Yosys (a miter of the two, proved by SAT; a clocked pair by induction): passes when they are equal for every input, else prints a counterexample. Parameters: reference ({home}/reference.sv). Reports N failing. Needs yosys.
  • Where the area goes (ASAP7) (rtl-breakdown, a stage): fluxpreset rtl breakdown {artifact} --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts' synthesis, its cells grouped: sequential, adders, XORs, buffers and inverters, the rest of the logic; and the flops. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports area_seq_um2, area_arith_um2, area_xor_um2, area_buf_um2, area_logic_um2, flop_count, area_um2. Needs yosys, openroad, make.
  • Fastest clock that closes (ASAP7) (rtl-fmax, a stage): fluxpreset rtl fmax {artifact} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} --steps {steps} A few OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs, each at the period the last one's slack says, until the fastest clock that closes timing at that stage is found: costly, and the honest fmax. Parameters: stage (synth), clock_ps (1000), steps (6). Reports fmax_closed_mhz, closed_period_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • Power from the design's own switching (ASAP7) (rtl-power, a stage): fluxpreset rtl power {artifact} --golden {golden} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} Verilator runs golden.py's vectors and records the switching; OpenROAD reads it on the synthesised or placed design and reports power: internal, switching, leakage. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py), stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports power_w, power_internal_w, power_switching_w, power_leakage_w. Needs verilator, yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • Energy per result (ASAP7) (rtl-energy, a stage): fluxpreset rtl energy {artifact} --golden {golden} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} The power the golden vectors' own switching draws, times the time one result takes (its measured cycles at the clock): energy per result and energy-delay product. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py), stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports energy_pj_per_result, edp_pj_ns, power_w, cycles_per_result. Needs verilator, yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • The critical path's anatomy (ASAP7) (rtl-path, a stage): fluxpreset rtl path {artifact} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD's worst path at the stage: how many cells it crosses, and how much of its delay is in the cells and how much in the wires -- whether to cut logic or wire. Parameters: stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports path_ps, path_levels, path_cell_ps, path_wire_ps, slack_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, sta, make.

docs.title: systemc
docs.text:
A SystemC design as SystemVerilog: ICSC translates it, so every RTL preset can judge it. Alone it checks that the module translates; --then "golden --golden g.py" or --then "rtl measure --stage stat" runs that preset on the translation.

fluxpreset systemc DESIGN.h --top M --golden golden.py [--then "golden --golden golden.py"]
  • SystemC translates to RTL (ICSC) (systemc-translate, a check): fluxpreset systemc {artifact} --top {top} --golden {golden} ICSC translates the SystemC module to SystemVerilog: passes when it does, and when the ports are the golden model's. Parameters: top (top), golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing.
  • SystemC against a golden model (systemc-golden, a check): fluxpreset systemc {artifact} --top {top} --golden {golden} --then "golden --golden {golden}" ICSC translates the SystemC module, then Verilator runs the RTL on golden.py's vectors. Parameters: top (top), golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing. Needs verilator.

docs.title: cases
docs.text:
The golden test for Python: the design's function called on cases and compared with the expected value or a reference function's (floats within --tol). Cases come from a JSON table ([args] or {"args", "kwargs", "expected"}), the reference module's CASES, and --random N draws of its inputs(rng).

fluxpreset cases DESIGN.py --call F [--reference ref.py[:F]] [--cases cases.json] [--random N] [--tol R]
  • Compare with a reference function (python-cases, a check): fluxpreset cases {artifact} --call {call} --reference {reference} --random {random} Calls the design's function on cases (a JSON table, the reference's CASES, random inputs from its inputs(rng)) and compares each result with the reference function's or the expected value. Parameters: call (main), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (100). Reports N failing.

docs.title: ccases
docs.text:
cases for a C or C++ function: the design built as a shared library and called through ctypes with a scalar --sig, against a Python reference.

fluxpreset ccases DESIGN.c --call F --sig "long(long,long)" --reference ref.py:F --random N
  • Compare a C function with a reference (c-cases, a check): fluxpreset ccases {artifact} --call {call} --sig {sig} --reference {reference} --random {random} Builds the design as a shared library and calls one function (a scalar signature) on cases, each result compared with a Python reference function's or the expected value. Parameters: call (main), sig (int(int)), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (100). Reports N failing. Needs cc.

docs.title: pytest
docs.text:
Your pytest file against the design: the design is copied as design.py beside your tests, and the failing tests are counted.

fluxpreset pytest DESIGN.py --tests test_design.py

The design is imported as design.

  • Run your pytest file (python-pytest, a check): fluxpreset pytest {artifact} --tests {tests} Runs your pytest file with the design importable as design; counts the failing tests. Parameters: tests ({home}/test_design.py). Reports N failing.

docs.title: accuracy
docs.text:
How far an approximation is from its reference, as a measurement, not pass or fail. max_ulp counts float64 steps.

fluxpreset accuracy DESIGN.py --call F --reference ref.py:F --random N
  • Accuracy against a reference (python-accuracy, a stage): fluxpreset accuracy {artifact} --call {call} --reference {reference} --random {random} Calls the design's function and a reference on the same cases and reports how far apart they are: absolute, relative and ULP error. Parameters: call (main), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (1000). Reports max_abs_error, mean_abs_error, max_rel_error, mean_rel_error, max_ulp.

docs.title: timebound
docs.text:
A time budget as a check: a Python function slower than --max-ms (the fastest of --runs) fails before the costly benchmark runs. A run stuck past the budget is stopped.

fluxpreset timebound DESIGN.py --call F --args "(1000,)" --max-ms 50
  • Within a time budget (python-timebound, a check): fluxpreset timebound {artifact} --call {call} --args {args} --max-ms {max_ms} Times one call of the design's function on a large input and fails a design slower than the budget, before the costly benchmark. Parameters: call (main), args (()), max_ms (1000). Reports N failing.

docs.title: bench
docs.text:
Time a Python function: the design loaded, f(*args) timed over --runs after --warmup. time_ms is the median. Exit 3 when the design does not load, 1 when it raises.

fluxpreset bench DESIGN.py --call F --args "(1000,)" [--runs 5] [--warmup 1]
  • Time a Python function (python-bench, a stage): fluxpreset bench {artifact} --call {call} --args {args} --runs {runs} Loads the design, calls one function with your arguments, times it over several runs. Parameters: call (main), args (()), runs (5). Reports time_ms.

docs.title: prog
docs.text:
Build a program with --build ({out} is the program it builds), then time, count, size or watch it. It prints name=value lines and exits 3 when the build fails.

fluxpreset prog time|count|memory|size --build "c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}" [--run CMD]
  • Program size (prog-size, a stage): fluxpreset prog size --build "{build}" Builds the program and reads its sections with size: text, data and bss bytes. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}). Reports text_bytes, data_bytes, bss_bytes. Needs size.
  • Program run time (prog-time, a stage): fluxpreset prog time --build "{build}" --run "{run}" --runs {runs} --warmup {warmup} Builds the program and times it over several runs (hyperfine when present). Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run, runs (10), warmup (1). Reports time_ms, time_ms_stddev, time_ms_min.
  • Instruction count (Valgrind) (prog-count, a stage): fluxpreset prog count --build "{build}" --run "{run}" Builds the program and counts instructions and cache misses with Valgrind's cachegrind: deterministic. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run. Reports instructions, d1_misses, ll_misses, branch_mispredicts. Needs valgrind.
  • Program peak memory (prog-memory, a stage): fluxpreset prog memory --build "{build}" --run "{run}" --runs {runs} Builds the program and runs it: its peak resident memory as the kernel counts it, the most over the runs. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run, runs (3). Reports peak_rss_kb.

docs.title: sanitize
docs.text:
A C or C++ program built with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and run: each distinct memory error, leak or undefined behaviour it hits is a failure.

fluxpreset sanitize --build "cc -O1 -o {out} {artifact}" [--run CMD]
  • Memory and undefined-behaviour errors (c-sanitize, a check): fluxpreset sanitize --build "{build}" --run "{run}" Builds the program with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and runs it: each memory error, leak or undefined behaviour it hits is a failure. Parameters: build (cc -O1 -o {out} {artifact}), run. Reports N failing. Needs cc.

docs.title: complexity
docs.text:
How complex a design's source is, read and not run, in any common language (lizard). With --max-cyclomatic N it fails each function over N.

fluxpreset complexity DESIGN [--ext .c] [--max-cyclomatic 15]
  • Source complexity (complexity, a stage): fluxpreset complexity {artifact} Reads the design's source (any common language) and counts its lines of code, functions, cyclomatic complexity and tokens; nothing is built or run. Reports loc, functions, cyclomatic_max, cyclomatic_mean, tokens, max_function_loc.
  • No function too complex (complexity-limit, a check): fluxpreset complexity {artifact} --max-cyclomatic {max_cyclomatic} Fails each function whose cyclomatic complexity is over the limit. Parameters: max_cyclomatic (15). Reports N failing.

docs.title: scaling
docs.text:
How a command's time grows with the problem size: timed at doubling sizes ({n}; --input "gen {n}" feeds its stdin, --build makes {out} first), start-up time taken off, fitted as time ~ n^k. scaling_exponent is about 1 for linear, 2 for quadratic. With --max-exponent K it is a check.

fluxpreset scaling [--start 1000|--sizes A,B,C] [--input "gen {n}"] [--build "cc -o {out} {artifact}"] [--max-exponent K] -- CMD {n}
  • How time grows with size (scaling, a stage): fluxpreset scaling --start {start} -- {command} Times the program at doubling problem sizes and fits time ~ n^k: the exponent says how it scales (1 linear, 2 quadratic), the constant factor aside. Parameters: start (1000), command ({artifact} {n}). Reports scaling_exponent, scaling_r2, time_at_max_ms, max_n.
  • Scales no worse than n^k (scaling-limit, a check): fluxpreset scaling --start {start} --max-exponent {max_exponent} -- {command} Times the program at doubling sizes and fails when time grows faster than n to the given power. Parameters: start (1000), command ({artifact} {n}), max_exponent (1.5). Reports N failing.

docs.title: repeat
docs.text:
Any measurement run several times with its noise taken out: each metric's median and NAME_spread_pct.

fluxpreset repeat --n 5 [--warmup 1] -- CMD
  • Median of several runs (repeat, a stage): fluxpreset repeat --n {n} -- {command} Runs any measurement several times and prints each metric's median and its spread, so one noisy run does not decide. Parameters: n (5), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: derive
docs.text:
Metrics made from other metrics: a command's own numbers plus formulas over them (arithmetic, min, max, abs, sqrt, log, exp).

fluxpreset derive --expr NAME=EXPR [--expr ...] -- CMD
  • Metrics from formulas (derive, a stage): fluxpreset derive --expr {expr} -- {command} Runs any measurement and adds metrics computed from its numbers, such as area times delay or throughput per watt. Parameters: expr (adp=area_um2*path_ps), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: regress
docs.text:
A performance gate: a measurement run again and compared with a recorded baseline file. --record writes the file, --tol is the allowed percent, --higher names metrics where more is better.

fluxpreset regress --baseline base.json [--tol 5] [--record] -- CMD
  • No worse than a baseline (regress, a check): fluxpreset regress --baseline {baseline} --tol {tol} -- {command} Runs any measurement again and fails when a metric is worse than the recorded baseline by more than the tolerance. Parameters: baseline ({home}/baseline.json), tol (5), command. Reports N failing.

docs.title: extract
docs.text:
Any tool's output as name=value, so a tool that does not speak Flux needs no script: JSON, CSV or text, picked with --pick PATH=name (a dotted path, a column or a regex group).

fluxpreset extract [--format json|csv|regex] --pick PATH=name -- CMD
  • Numbers out of any tool's output (extract, a stage): fluxpreset extract --format {format} --pick {pick} -- {command} Runs your tool and reads its JSON, CSV or text output, printing the numbers you pick as name=value. Parameters: format (json), pick (value=metric), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: champsim
docs.text:
A cache prefetcher in ChampSim, on your traces. stats runs the prefetcher and the run without it on every trace and says why it wins: coverage (the share of misses removed), accuracy, lateness.

fluxpreset champsim build|check|run|stats ARTIFACT --traces DIR [--warmup N --sim N]
  • Build the prefetcher into ChampSim (champsim-build, a check): fluxpreset champsim build {artifact} Compiles a prefetcher header into ChampSim; reports the first compiler error. Reports N failing. Needs pythia.
  • Smoke-run the prefetcher (champsim-check, a check): fluxpreset champsim check {artifact} --traces {traces} Builds the prefetcher and runs it on one trace; refused when it issues no prefetches. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces). Reports N failing. Needs pythia.
  • Simulate on your traces (ChampSim) (champsim-run, a stage): fluxpreset champsim run {artifact} --traces {traces} --warmup {warmup} --sim {sim} Runs an .ini or a prefetcher header on every trace; the geometric-mean IPC speed-up over no prefetcher. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces), warmup (10000000), sim (15000000). Reports geomean_speedup. Needs pythia.
  • Why the prefetcher wins (ChampSim) (champsim-stats, a stage): fluxpreset champsim stats {artifact} --traces {traces} --warmup {warmup} --sim {sim} Runs it and the run without it on every trace: L2 misses per kilo-instruction with and without it, the share of misses it removed (coverage), and how many of its prefetches were used, late or useless. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces), warmup (10000000), sim (15000000). Reports l2_mpki, l2_mpki_baseline, pf_coverage, pf_accuracy, pf_late, pf_useless, pf_issued_pki, geomean_speedup. Needs pythia.

docs.title: asl
docs.text:
A PTO-style spec's AVS tests, from a spec checkout kept in the loop's folder. tests lists a unit's tests (by id or mnemonic); run runs them with ASLRef as the spec's release suite does, on --jobs threads, each failing test a line then N failing of M. --out FILE writes each result as JSON. Needs aslref on PATH or --aslref.

fluxpreset asl tests|run UNIT... --spec {home}/spec [--jobs N] [--out FILE]
  • The spec's AVS tests pass (asl-avs, a check): fluxpreset asl run {unit} --spec {home}/spec Runs a PTO-style spec unit's AVS tests with ASLRef, through the spec's own runner, from the spec kept in the application's folder. Each failing test a line, then the count. Parameters: unit (TADD). Reports N failing. Needs aslref.

docs.title: ndf
docs.text:
A PTO-style spec's normative clauses, read with the NDF tool. list gives each unit with its clauses by modality and its test count; clauses UNIT prints a unit's clauses; scope UNIT lists the unit and every unit that depends on it; check UNIT --results FILE reads asl run --out and counts each MUST clause failed or uncovered.

fluxpreset ndf list|clauses|scope|check UNIT --spec {home}/spec
  • Every MUST clause covered and passing (ndf-contract, a check): fluxpreset ndf check {unit} --spec {home}/spec --results {results} Reads a PTO-style spec unit's NDF clauses (the NDF tool, from the spec in the application's folder) and the AVS results fluxpreset asl run --out wrote: each MUST clause that failed or has no test is a line, then the count. Parameters: unit (TADD), results (avs.json). Reports N failing. Needs ndf.

docs.title: pto
docs.text:
A pyCircuit design checked against a PTO-style spec's ASL model, unit by unit. The design is one combinational datapath for the spec's elementwise units, with ports op (8 bits, from fluxpreset pto ops), dtype (5), a, b (64), y (64) and fault (1). Each wrong vector is a line, then N failing of M; --build-only only builds, --measure prints vectors_failing, units_passing, units. Needs pycircuit and aslref.

fluxpreset pto ops [--names]
fluxpreset pto ref UNIT...
fluxpreset pto check DESIGN --units UNIT... [--dependents] [--build-only|--measure]

Each takes --spec {home}/spec.

  • The design matches the spec's ASL model (pto-check, a check): fluxpreset pto check {artifact} --units {units} --spec {home}/spec Builds a pyCircuit design (pycircuit, the C++ model) and drives it with each unit's reference vectors -- the spec's own answers from ASLRef, cached per spec -- one wrong vector a line, then the count. The interface: fluxpreset pto ops. Parameters: units (all). Reports N failing. Needs pycircuit, aslref.

docs.title: Without a preset
docs.text:
• Test script (python-test-script, a check): {python} {script} {artifact} A Python script beside the document runs the design on known cases and prints N failing. Parameters: script ({home}/check.py). Reports N failing.
  • Any command (custom-check, a check): {command} Any command; it prints N failing (or say count_re / fail_re), or its exit code decides. Parameters: command. Reports N failing.
  • Timing script (bench-script, a stage): {python} {script} {artifact} A Python script beside the document runs the design and prints time_ms=.... Parameters: script ({home}/bench.py). Reports time_ms.
  • Any command (custom-stage, a stage): {command} Any command; it prints name=value for each metric it measures, listed as the stage's metrics. Parameters: command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: One interface
docs.text:
Every preset keeps the same interface:

Arguments fluxpreset NAME [SUBCOMMAND] ARTIFACT [--option VALUE ...]: the design file first, every other input an option with a default stdin Never read stdout A check: each failure on a line of its own, then N failing (or N failing of M) last. A measurement: name=value for each metric it reports stderr Diagnostics for a person; never the count or the numbers Exit code 0 passed or measured; 1 failed, or the measurement could not be taken; 2 wrong arguments; 3 the design did not build, parse or load Files Only in a temporary folder of its own; never in the loop's folder

docs.title: Golden model
docs.text:
fluxpreset golden, rtl cycles, rtl power, rtl energy and systemc read a golden model: a Python file that defines PORTS and golden(**inputs).

PORTS = [
    {"name": "x", "dir": "in", "bits": 16, "unsigned": True},
    {"name": "y", "dir": "out", "bits": 16, "unsigned": True},
]

def golden(x):
    return {"y": x}
Setting Purpose COUNT Random vectors (default 32), besides generated corner cases SEED Random seed VECTORS Input dictionaries, the whole set when given (no corners, no random vectors); expected outputs still come from golden() EXHAUSTIVE Every input combination (at most 20 input bits) CLOCK The clock port of a clocked design, e.g. "clk" LATENCY Cycles from start to done for a clocked design TOLERANCE_ULP Map of floating-point output port to allowed ULP error; absent means exact

Match the ports and clocking in the contract and the design. Floating-point bit-pattern ports are unsigned; reinterpret their bits in golden() rather than converting the integer to a float. A loop's Python prototype is checked against the same file.

docs.title: Common refusals
docs.text:
flux task check says each issue of the document on a row of its own: the file and line it was written on, the document path, what is wrong and the nearest known word:

not a task: the document does not load: problem.yaml: flow.plan.by is off | flux | claude | codex | opencode or an agent of your own ({run: [...]}), not 'codx'
  WARNING problem.yaml:25 flow.measure.bench.timout_s -- not a stage setting, ignored; did you mean `timeout_s`?
  ERROR problem.yaml:16 flow.plan.by -- No agent called `codx`. Did you mean `codex`? The loop won't start until this is fixed.
  • A warning is a key nobody reads (a typo, a box or setting the loop does not have) or a setting with no effect where it is said (an agent's option beside by: flux, questions on a box whose agent answers in one turn, by beside Design's run). The key is ignored and the loop loads and runs; a run's start log says the same rows.
  • An error is a value the loop cannot run with. The document does not load: flux task check prints not a task: and the reason, the rows, and exits 2.

An error's row says it plainly, as a warning's does ("No agent called claud. Did you mean claude? The loop won't start until this is fixed."); the loader's own words follow not a task: above the rows. flux task check --json prints them as data: {ok, code, issues: [{severity, path, file, line, message, suggestion, detail, fix}], output} -- detail an error's words as the loader raised them, fix the change that makes the issue go when there is a safe one ({kind: replace, from, to} a word on its line, {kind: remove} its line, for a setting that does nothing). The web's Check and Direct edit offer each fix as a button (Use claude, Remove).

An error's row as flux task check and the web's Check say it (each ends "The loop won't start until this is fixed."):

Message (start) Fix No agent called `codx`. Did you mean `codex`? A by: that names no agent, or a box's word that is its by said short (plan: codx); the row suggests the nearest `swep` is not something `search` takes: it is a search (sweep, ...), a list of phases or `module:Class` A word the key does not take; the row lists the ones it does and suggests the nearest A document does not say its `id`: it is its folder's name Rename the folder instead `statement` must be a non-empty string: what is to be made Say what is to be made REFUSED: `problem.yaml` names 1 path the loop folder does not have (the check's text, with what the folder holds) Add the listed file to the folder, or fix the key that names it 'notes.md' is not a file or folder beside ... (knowledge.library) Add the file, or list what is there `check` is never delegated to an agent: it establishes facts check and measure are commands only `{...}` is not something `design` takes: it is "flux" (FluxAgent), {run: [...]}, {catalog: [...]} or {agent: ...} One form only `flow.design.command` is not a key of a document: a command a document runs is said `run:` (and search's, baseline's, an estimate's, an agent of your own's by: {command: ...}) Say run: flow.design.agent.session is `pass` (one session per design until it is admitted ...) or `keep` Write pass or keep, or remove session from design `dse` is `search` / `extract` is `knowledge: {insights: {by: rules}}` Old names: search and knowledge.insights Who works it is by Write knowledge: {by: claude} or {by: off} `budget.parallel` is a key of an older document, which this Flux no longer reads: open the document with Flux e7a0f9cba, which says what became of it, and export it again (any key) A key an older document said, whose meaning moved (budget.parallel, flow.knowledge.digest, flow.measure.<stage>.command, parts:, ...). Open the document with Flux e7a0f9cba: it names what replaced the key. A key that only named something gone (cache:, brief:, knowledge.sheet, ...) is an unknown key instead: a warning, ignored; one that does nothing (budget.finalists, flow.calibrate, ...) is a warning, "does nothing in this Flux: it was retired (remove it)" Generator says {nope}, which is neither a knob of `flow.search.space` (...) nor the loop's (...) A misspelled placeholder, or a knob not in the space `flow.search.space` knobs (...) are said by no command Name a {knob} or {point} in a command, or generate with a command A stage needs `metrics` (...) or `metrics_re` Say what the stage prints `wavee` is not a setting of gradient (its settings: ...) (at search.params.gradient.wavee, a phase's at search.params[1].wavee) An option the search does not have; the message lists its settings (search settings) `critic` is reserved -- it names the box's critic A check or a stage cannot be called critic: it names the box's critic `sweep` is a search, not an intent: `search: sweep` policy: names a policy, search: a search `explore` is an intent, not a search: `policy: explore` Say it under policy:; beside it search: names the algorithm `policy: tune` is the intent beside the phase's search: say the search too A phase says its search: {search: gradient, policy: tune} (or search: model) Its points are picked by a search (...) or proposed by FluxAgent or an agent (search.space) Add params: sweep (or another search), or by: flux `baseline` takes file OR command OR metrics One source per baseline not a task: `problem.yaml` is not a mapping of keys The file is a list or a single value; start from flux new NAME

A missing file is listed with the key that names it and what the folder holds. A refused document never runs; flux task check FOLDER shows the same message before you start.

docs.title: Searches
docs.text: What flow.search takes as a search. Search and agents explains when to use which.

docs.title: Space and seeds
docs.text:
flow.search is one form, {by: <who decides>, policy: <name>, params: <how the points are picked>, space: {...}}:

Said What runs nothing, or {by: rules} the rules pick each pass's direction and the kind of work, no AI {by: flux}, {by: tools}, {by: claude} FluxAgent, FluxAgent with its tools, an agent decides ({by: given} is the rules, under that name) {by: ..., policy: explore} (no space) the same, with that policy {params: sweep, space: {...}} that search walks the space; by beside it has no effect (a warning) {policy: explore, params: gradient, space: {...}} the search, with that policy {by: flux, space: {...}}, {by: claude, policy: explore, space: {...}} FluxAgent (or the agent) proposes the points, with that policy {run: ...} your own search (below)

The bare word is shorthand: search: explore is {policy: explore}, search: sweep {params: sweep}, search: claude {by: claude}; a list is {params: [...]}. A space with neither a search nor FluxAgent or an agent to propose its points is refused, and so is a word under the wrong key: a search under policy: ("sweep is a search, not an intent: params: sweep") or a policy name under params:. A search without a space walks nothing. A search tries points of a space of settings ("knobs"):

search:                                             # under flow:
  params: {gradient: {steps: 16, patience: 2}}     # or: params: gradient
  space:
    algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
    wheel: {values: [0, 1], when: {algorithm: [list_sieve]}}   # only moves for list_sieve
    prefetch:                                       # a component: prefetch.on, .distance, .degree
      optional: true
      distance: [1, 2, 4]
      degree: [1, 2]
    variant: {values: [baseline], from: "variants/*.py"}       # plus file stems found at load
  seeds:
    - {algorithm: list_sieve, wheel: 0}            # measured first; the first seed is home
  • space: knob to an ordered, non-empty list of scalar choices. A map with values takes when: {knob: choice or [choices]} (the knob only moves when the condition holds; otherwise it sits at its first choice) and from: glob (adds the stems of matching files, relative to the folder, read at every load). A map with neither is a component: its knobs are named component.knob; optional: true adds component.on. Order numeric choices: local searches step to neighbours.
  • seeds: points measured first; a missing knob takes its first choice.
  • A space must reach a command: some command names a {knob} or {point}, or the generator is a command or a catalog. A model or agent generator with a space searches settings only and does not write designs.
  • Component knobs reach commands through {point} only; {component.knob} is not substituted.

docs.title: Searches
docs.text: params Options and defaults sweep batch_size: 0 (the whole walk at once) montecarlo samples: 24, batch_size: 8, seed: 0 gradient steps: 16, wave: 0 (all moves), patience: 1, budget: 0 (no cap), reach: adjacent (or any) anneal steps: 32, seed: 0, temperature: 1.0, cooling: 0.9 genetic population: 8, generations: 6, seed: 0, mutation: 0.3 pareto budget: 24, wave: 6, reference: [], scale: [], reach: adjacent; needs two objectives: with one, the search says so in the log and walks nothing (no search, by: flux) FluxAgent proposing points: batch_size: 4, rounds: 8, shown: 40; written {by: flux, ...} (model, its old name, too) or {by: claude, ...} for an agent control keep: []: compare home with only these incumbent knobs kept a list, phases phases in order, each {search: ..., policy: ..., ...its options} (default gradient; search: model FluxAgent proposing the phase's points); {phases: {phases: [...]}} is the long form; phases do not nest module:Class a search policy class of your own, beside the document adaptive, explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations Not searches: said policy:, which sets the search's emphasis (default adaptive) run Your own search: search: {run: ..., timeout_s: 600} (contract)

docs.title: Options every search takes
docs.text:
Every search and phase also takes name (a label), knobs (move only these), hold (keep these fixed; both accept globs such as prefetch.*), metric and direction (its own target; default the first objective), floor ({metric, at} or {metric, keep, above}: designs below it are refused), margin (minimum improvement, default 0) and policy (as above; a phase's was dse before Oct 27, 2026). batch is another name for batch_size. An unknown option is refused where it was written (flow.search.params[1].wavee), naming the search's settings.

A search's batch_size is how many designs one pass carries; a search without one says it its own way (what a pass carries). budget.designs_at_once is how many of them are made and checked at once. Finishing a finite walk does not stop an open-ended run: cap it at Start, with --passes N on the command line, or with budget.passes in the document.

docs.title: Write a loop with an agent
docs.text: Describe what you want, give it your files, and let an author write the loop: the document, its checks and measurements, and a golden model where one fits. The author is FluxAgent or a coding agent. You review what it wrote, then run it: nothing runs until you ask.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
flux ask "a signed 8x8 multiplier in SystemVerilog, the smallest that makes 1 GHz placed on ASAP7" \
  --file spec.pdf --author claude

The author writes the loop into ./out/ask_<slug>/ (--dir DIR to choose; the folder's name is the loop's id). It checks its own draft with flux task check and repairs what the check refuses, up to --checks times (default 3). A coding agent proves its gate before it hands the loop over (its decisions say what it proved; FluxAgent runs nothing: see FluxAgent as the author). The author also writes decisions.json: each decision it took and a one-line reason. A later flux ask on the same --dir continues the same agent's work (see One session per loop).

It stops there and says how to run the loop: flux task run out/ask_<slug>/problem.yaml (--passes N, --tui as for any loop). The author never runs the loop itself. flux ask --tui (or no prompt) opens a setup screen for the prompt, files, skills, author and folder: its Start has the author write and check the loop.

Option Effect --file PATH An input: a spec, code, a reference, a PDF, tests (repeatable; a folder is copied whole) --author WHO flux (FluxAgent, the default), claude, codex, opencode, or an agent of your own --hidden PATH A path in the loop hidden from AI: the author and the loop's agents may not read it (repeatable) --skill DIR A skill folder for the author and the designers (repeatable) --think, --no-think, --effort LEVEL How hard the author thinks, as in a chat: the levels are its kind's, FluxAgent's low to max --questions operator The author asks you before it drafts (see Ask me when unclear), each round answered within --wait-s seconds (default 600) --repair The loop in --dir was refused: check it and repair it, writing nothing new (--note says what to do)

See the CLI for every option.

docs.title: In the web app
docs.text:
New loop › Agent walks through four stages:

  1. Ask: the loop's name, the agent, what the loop should do, and the files it should read. Mark a file Hide from AI to keep it from every agent (a gate's tests, for example). Ask me when unclear (ticked by default) makes the agent ask you before it drafts. Thinking and Effort work as in a chat's composer: the levels are the picked agent's.
  2. Drafting: its conversation, as Chat shows an agent's: its words, its thinking and commands folded under one line, and the check's verdict and your answers. Under it, the files it wrote (each written, yours or removed, a lock before one hidden from AI), the check's last word, and a muted line of the job's numbers: its agent's tool calls and the checks it ran. It updates as the agent works: no need to reload. Its questions show inline as one card. If its check refuses the draft, Try again sends it another round, or write a note telling it what to do in the message box Chat uses (Enter sends).
  3. Review: its decisions, grouped by the configurator's steps, each with its reason. Keep one, Change it in the configurator at that step, or Keep the rest. A change asked of the agent (the message box under the decisions) shows as a diff on the document.
  4. Ready: flux task check on the draft. Make loop, or Open in Configurator to edit it first. Nothing runs until you start it. Tick Run one pass first to start one ordinary pass when the loop is made: it goes to the deepest stage, so a costly stage costs what it costs.

The draft exists as a loop from Drafting on; this browser remembers it, so you can come back. A new loop's agent starts from flux new's baseline (a README of what each folder is for, and library/). When it ends, its copy comes back exactly: what it wrote or changed, and a file the copy began with that it removed or renamed leaves the loop too (shown removed among the job's files); its scratch files never come back. A loop's Settings › Problem › Agent asks an agent to change an existing loop the same way.

docs.title: Ask me when unclear
docs.text:
Ticked, the agent asks before it writes anything. It lists what your ask leaves open or what it would have to assume: the objectives and their goals, the limits (a clock, area, latency, a budget), the measurement stages and their tools, which file is the spec or the golden model, and who designs. It asks every one that would change the document at once, up to four questions, each with its choices and the one it would pick marked Recommended. The card has a chip per question, You decide, a free answer, and the time it waits (10 minutes, then the agent decides). Your answer goes back into the agent's session and it drafts by it; its decisions say which answer decided what. While revising (a change asked in Review, or Settings › Problem › Agent), it asks when the change is ambiguous, and makes a clear one without asking.

A question reaches you whole: a long one is folded behind Show all, never cut. Unticked, the agent asks nothing: it decides and records each assumption in its decisions.

docs.title: One session per loop
docs.text:
A coding agent (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) keeps one session per loop. The first draft starts it. Every later job on the same loop resumes it: a change asked in Review, Try again or a note on a refused draft, an edit from Settings › Problem › Agent. You set nothing for this, and two loops never share a session.

The agent's conversation says which it was, first: Session: resumed session (turn 3), or Session: new session (why). A new session starts only when the loop has none yet, when you pick another agent or its model changed, when the loop's folder moved, or when the agent can't resume the session (it no longer has it, or it truly outgrew its context). Then it starts from the whole brief and the loop's files, not from what it remembered, and the conversation says so.

docs.title: When a turn is cut off
docs.text: A job is finished when the agent ends its own turn, not when the document passes: revising a loop that works, the old document passes from the start. A turn that reaches its time limit or exits with an error is continued in the same session, up to --checks times. If that isn't enough, the job ends as The agent did not finish: what it wrote is kept, and Try again continues the session. Stop ends a job the same way.

docs.title: FluxAgent as the author
docs.text: FluxAgent writes the loop as it writes files in a chat: it reads and writes the files of the draft's folder itself and checks the draft with Flux's own check (flux task check's rules and answer), fixing what it says and checking again until the draft passes; a draft still refused when its turn ends comes back to it, as to any author, up to --checks times. It stays in the draft's folder: no path outside it, no hidden name (.x), no path hidden from AI. It runs nothing, so it does not prove the gate on a sample design the way a coding agent does. Drafting shows its steps as a coding agent's. It keeps no session between jobs.

docs.title: Check what it wrote
docs.text:
An author's loop is a first draft. Before a long run:

  • Read the checks: do they test what you care about, on enough inputs?
  • Read the measurements: the right workload, the right stage, tools_at_once: 1 for timings?
  • Read the objectives: the limit you meant, in the right direction?
  • Run one pass (flux task run FOLDER --passes 1) and read the report.

Configure explains each part of the document, and Knowledge, skills, hidden paths what the agents read.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Flux is a Python package. The command line needs Python 3.11 or newer; the web app, the hardware tools and the sandbox are optional extras.

Before installing, try the web app in your browser: take the guided tour or create a loop step by step in the Preview app.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The Flux source is not public: ask its maintainer for access. Then, from its folder (here flux-repo):

cd flux-repo
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ./flux
source .venv/bin/activate
flux selftest --no-model

flux selftest checks this machine: a script-driven loop, the tools on PATH, and, without --no-model, the model endpoint and a coding agent. It prints PASS, FAIL or SKIP per check.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run inside a container, so a loop's code and its agents cannot touch the rest of your machine. Install Podman (rootless, preferred) or Docker. Without either, these commands stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker.

For code you trust, such as the first loop, run on your machine directly:

export FLUX_SANDBOX=0        # or --no-sandbox on each command

What the sandbox sees, writes and reaches is in Run, stop, resume.

docs.title: Web app
docs.text:
pip install -e "./flux[web]"
flux user add me --admin
flux serve

Run flux user add as the user who should own the loops' files. flux serve prints its address (by default http://127.0.0.1:8765/); open it and sign in. The Web app pages walk through it, and Server and admin covers running it for a team. A flux serve started by hand is for trying Flux and for development; a server for a team is installed as a system service with one command, sudo python3 scripts/install-service.py (System service).

docs.title: Hardware tools
docs.text:
Loops that synthesise, place or simulate hardware need Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD and the other packaged tools. They come with Flux's Nix development shell. Install Nix and enable experimental-features = nix-command flakes in ~/.config/nix/nix.conf, then:

cd flux
nix develop --accept-flake-config
flux selftest --no-model

The first entry may build or download tools. The shell also carries the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode (Models and agents). The shell puts Flux itself on PATH; no pip install is needed inside it. Keep your loop folders wherever you like and pass their paths to Flux.

docs.title: Models and agents
docs.text: A loop whose designs come from a script needs no model. For a model or a coding agent, see Models and agents.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• First loop: a complete loop from an empty folder, in Python only.
  • Loop crafter: build the document in your browser.
  • Write a loop with an agent: describe what you want and let an agent write the loop.

docs.title: Tour
docs.text:
flux serve is a shared server with accounts. Each user has loops; each loop is a document and its files, and runs on the server, sandboxed. You check, start and stop loops, follow them live, and read their results in the browser. Install starts one.

To see it first, the Preview app runs it in your browser: take the guided tour or create a loop step by step.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
The first page lists your loops: their state, their designs as Results' tabs count them -- "2 / 12 / 30" is 2 accepted this start, 12 accepted, 30 in All (the accepted and the rejected), its tooltip adding the failed and pending ones -- and the decision's main measurements (the first objective when none is marked main in Settings › Measurements), each green or red against its limit. The Overview's Acceptance rate is the same share: the Accepted tab's designs of All. Beside its state, each loop names its design agent, the one that works its Design box (design in the document), the slowest part of a pass: FluxAgent, claude, codex, opencode or an agent your admin added. It is tinted while the loop runs and plain while it rests. A document saved in Flux names its new agent at once; one changed another way (an agent, the command line) within a moment while some page looks at the loop. Search, filter by state, and sort by activity, name or decision. Each state in the filter is led by the mark its rows' pill draws, in its tone: Running the turning ring, Idle, Never run and Archived a ring, Failed a cross; All only its word. Shared with me lists loops others shared with you or your group, with what you may do in a few words ("ask · edit · run"). Archived loops are under their own Archived chip (Archive).

The list is drawn at once from the loops' states; a loop whose numbers changed shows a small turning ring in its Designs and Best cells until they come, a moment later.

When you see a group's project, the list opens with a row of project tabs above the search: All, one per group project and In no project, each with its count beside it in grey. The chosen tab is bold and underlined. Under the tabs, the search takes the row's room and the state filter sits beside it. A count of 0 is dimmed, in the tabs and in the state filter, and still a choice: a project with no loop yet says "No loops yet" with a link to the project, where you link one. With many projects the tabs scroll sideways, a fade on the side that hides more; on a phone the search takes its own line and the state filter scrolls under it. The tab you chose is kept in this browser across reloads; the arrow keys move between tabs. When you see no group project, there are no tabs. The list stays flat, each loop once: while All is chosen, a Project column names each loop's first group project (a link to it) and "+N" its others (Groups).

docs.title: New loop
docs.text:
