New loop offers five ways to make one:

Way What it does Configurator A form in six steps, the same as the Loop crafter Create or upload An empty loop, or one from a folder, files or a .zip you drop or pick, or from a problem document pasted (Paste YAML) Direct edit Write the YAML yourself Agent An agent writes the loop from your prompt and files (Write a loop with an agent) Clone A copy of an existing loop, with its problem but none of its runs

docs.title: A loop's page
docs.text:
A loop has six tabs, and its run buttons in its header: Start (▶) at rest, Stop (■) and Restart (↻) joined while it runs, each with its word, beside the header's other buttons. The same buttons are at the end of each row of the Loops list as small square icons; hover one (or focus it) for what it does.

Tab What it shows Overview Its state, the decision and its objectives, the best designs, a best-so-far chart, a note to the running loop and its agent's question Live What the run does now, every pass of it, as a graph or a timeline (Live) Results Every design measured, charts, ideas and the library (Results) Agents Every model and agent turn, newest first and a page at a time as you scroll: where it was taken (pass, box, try) and how its try came out, prompt, reply, tool calls, time and tokens; a turn of a box whose sessions are kept across passes says its lane and "resumed (turn k of K)" or "new session" with why; a design that began as a warm start says "warm start", and the turn they began from "shared first session" Files The loop's files and the agents' workbench (Files and settings) Settings Preferences, sharing, maintenance, and the problem itself (Files and settings)

An agent that writes or revises the loop's problem shows its strip at the top of the Overview while it works, and after it ends until something else has taken over: the loop started, the document changed, the draft made a loop, or six hours gone. Hide from Overview on an ended strip hides it for good, on every device, until the next agent job. Its history stays in Settings › Problem › Agent.

The Overview draws each card as soon as what it shows is read: the state at once, the notes, the workbench and the agents' usage next, the cards of results (the decision, the charts, the recent designs) once the results' summary comes, each a placeholder meanwhile (its title and a few grey lines, a small card its label and a turning ring). The summary is kept by the server and made again as each pass ends; while a loop runs, a look between two of its passes may show it as it was a moment ago, read again a second later. Settings and Live read the same summary; only Results reads every row.

The Decision card is one line, then the numbers: the decision's name and its pill (✓ accepted; ! closest while no design meets every requirement, ✗ failed), "ties with #229" when another accepted design has its very numbers, and "last pass 17 min ago" at the right; hover the pill for why it was chosen -- the rule and its limits ("Decided by: smallest area_um2 at fmax_mhz >= 1000") and the stage it was measured at. Under it a big tile for each main measurement (Settings › Measurements' Main; each objective when none is main), its change from the reference in percent (the latest baseline at its stage, else the accepted designs' P10 for an objective minimized, P90 for one maximized; its value when there is none), green or red by its limit, then Best 3: the rank, the design (the decision with its orange trophy) and each main measurement's change (each objective's when none is main), a row opening Results. The decision says one percent on its tile, its Best 3 row, Results and the Loops list: every one is compared with the same reference. Results › opens Results; the table's own tools (columns, Relative) are Results'. Best draws a chart per main measurement under one legend for the card (Baseline, accepted, failed, decision), each titled by its best and its change from the baseline -- "best cycles (-12.9%)", or "best cycles 6189" with no baseline; fullscreen the same, larger. The Overview's charts (Best, the Pareto front) draw a starred design as any other point, with no Starred in the legend: the stars are Results › Graphs' and the tables'.

Starred designs is a card you add yourself (Account › Profile › Customize, a column's Add menu; it is in no default layout): a tile for each design starred by hand on this loop, the latest starred first, three to a row (one on a phone). A tile names the design with its marks (the decision's trophy, the hand star) and its standing under it (decision, accepted, failed, ...), then each main measurement's change from the reference in big figures with its value under it -- red where it misses a limit, green where it is better. The decision's tile is edged in Flux's orange. A click opens the design in Results; Results › opens the table. With nothing starred the card says how: open a design in Results and press Star. Who starred a design and when is in Results (hover its star), not on the card.

The Overview reads only what its cards show: a card your layout does not show costs nothing.

Small cards. The Overview's top row shows five by default: State, Designs measured, Passes, Last improvement and Working now. Account › Profile › Customize (the Overview layout) adds, removes and orders them -- Agents, Objective, the tokens, cost and the others under "Add small card" -- up to 10 in all ("7 of 10" beside the list), or none; past five they wrap onto a second row (five to a row on a wide screen, three on a narrower one, two on a phone). Defaults in the editor gives the five back; a layout you saved keeps its cards. Hover a card for what its number is and what it is made of. The newer ones:

Card Shows Last improvement When the best design by the loop's objectives (the first, then the next on a tie; the decision when no objective ranks) last got better -- "42 min ago" -- the design, the pass it was made in, and the passes ended since with no better one Pass speed The median wall time of the latest 20 passes ended (a pass's first task to its last), how many ran at once at most, and passes an hour over that stretch Working now The agents and models at work this moment in the running start, and each box's designs at work ("11 design · 3 check · 2 measure"); "idle" when the loop is not running Idea queue The ideas queued for testing, those with an evaluation, and those proposed and neither tested nor queued Uptime How long this start has run, and the starts today (its tooltip says how many followed another, by your clock) One metric One metric's best among the accepted designs and its change from the baseline ("−12.9%", "best 6189 vs baseline 7105"; a percentile of the accepted designs when there is no baseline). Its metric is the one you type under the small cards in the layout editor -- in every loop that measures it -- else each loop's first objective Stage funnel How far the designs got, each at its latest attempt: made → passed the checks → measured on the last stage (each stage in the tooltip)

Last improvement, One metric and Stage funnel are made by the server with the summary, for the cards your layout shows; Pass speed, Working now and Uptime from the running start's journal and the loop's starts, in a small read of their own that a running loop's Overview makes again every few seconds -- a layout without them reads neither.

Start asks how many passes to run -- one design each, however many run at once -- or Until stopped. A trunk document's start asks for designs instead and says what runs under them, which count its hand-ins: "trunk: 2 agents (claude (opus), codex), 3 branches at once, 6 may wait" (each agent's model when its document says one). A loop of several problems (problem.yaml and each NAME.problem.yaml) asks which: every one is listed, one that does not load shown but not to pick, said under the menu with why and a Direct edit link that opens it in Settings › Problem; the menu shows as soon as there are two, even when only one loads, and starts on the one last started (on the first that loads when that one does not). It runs flux task check first when the inputs changed; if the check fails, the button reads Start anyway. A start resumes from the record, and the page stays where it is: started from a row of the Loops list (or Admin › Loops › All loops), the list stays, the row turns running and a notice says Started with an Open link to the loop, so several loops start one after another without leaving the list; started from a loop's header, the tab you are on stays. A refused start says why where you pressed it. A failed loop's Start says Start again; while an agent is still writing the problem, Start waits.

Stop and Restart take effect after the current pass. Once one is asked, only that button is tinted red, with a small hourglass (after its word in the header, in its corner in a row), and the page says when it happens ("Stops after pass 4"). The loop keeps its blue running pill -- it still runs until the pass ends -- and a small amber pill before it shows the stop's square or the restart's arrow; point at it to read "Stops after pass 4" or "Restarts after pass 4", in the header and in the Loops list alike. The other button still works, so a stop can become a restart and back. Hover or focus the tinted button and it turns solid red: press it again to do it now. It asks first, then abandons the pass, and the button stays solid red until the process ends.

docs.title: A loop's Chat
docs.text:
Chat, on every tab of a loop, opens a panel with one conversation about the loop (it was called Talk before; old #/app/NAME/ask and #/app/NAME/talk links still open it, and #/app/NAME/chat/ID opens on that conversation). Its one bar at the top holds the conversation's name, which opens the list of the loop's conversations, by when each last moved, with + New chat, a spinner on one being answered, and the more menu's Delete where you may; then Open in Chat (the open icon, beside Close in one toolbar), which opens the conversation in the top bar's Chat, with its Settings and the loop's Chat workbench; then Close. While the loop's agent asks you something, the Chat button has a dot in the agent's colour; pointing at it shows the question. Below is that one conversation and its message box: Ask puts a question (why it stalls, which design is best, what to try next) to an agent or FluxAgent, which reads the loop and its results and changes nothing. Thinking & commands under an answer shows how it was made. In the message box Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line. The loop's chats share a Chat workbench, where their agents keep tools, notes and attached files, for those who may edit the loop: a file an answer wrote, listed under it, opens in Chat's page (A loop's Chat workbench). It is not the loop's own workbench/, and the loop's runs never see it.

The Overview has a card for Note to the loop: while the loop runs, a note you send there reaches the loop's agents at its next step (under trunk:, each trunk agent at its next turn), and then at every step or turn while it stands. Its box is one line, as Chat's: Enter sends (the arrow at its end too), Shift+Enter adds a line; a loop at rest has no box (nothing would read the note before its next start), the list stays. The notes sent are listed under it, newest first, one line each -- these are the loop's latest notes (there is no separate Latest notes card): a dot, the note's text and how long ago it was sent. The dot is filled once the loop has read the note, as its record says ("Read at pass 14", or "Read" when the pass is not known: passes at once, or a re-check), and a ring while it waits for the loop's next step. A note cut to its line opens whole when pressed. The latest three show, and N more the rest of the latest twenty. Whoever may edit the loop removes one with its bin (on hover, always on a touch screen): a note the loop has not read yet never reaches it, and one it read is gone from the agents' next messages.

When the loop's agent asks something, the Agent asks card shows its question with its choices, You decide and a free answer; your answer goes as a note. Under it are the questions already answered, newest first, one line each: the question, your answer or pick, and how long ago -- the latest three, and N more the rest of the latest twenty. A question counts as answered by the first note sent while it waited (one the agent decided itself is not listed). With nothing asked and nothing answered the card is not shown.

The two are cards of the Overview, last by default: move or hide each under Account › Profile › Overview layout as any other (a layout saved before they existed gets them at its end; one that had the older single note card, or Latest notes, shows the two cards in its place). The question's line above the tabs, and the bell, lead to Agent asks; with that card hidden, the line's Answer opens the question in a dialog, answered there.

Chat, in the top bar, is the same kind of conversation bound to no loop: it may read all your loops and keep tools and notes in your workbench (Chat). Its rail also lists your loops under Loops: go into one to open and continue its conversations there (Loop chats).

docs.title: Everywhere
docs.text:
• Top bar: Chat · Loops · Groups · Admin (admins only). Groups shows your groups, their members and projects, and the global projects (Groups). These pages, and your Account, start with their content, not a title that repeats the bar: New loop (a plus and Loop) is at the end of the Loops list's search bar (or in the empty list), Admin's tabs and Groups' tabs are at the top.
  • Theme: system, light or dark, from the top bar; remembered in this browser.
  • Your name: at the bar's end, a button with a person drawn, before Log out; it opens your Account. A long name is cut short (its whole in the tooltip); while an admin views as a user, it is that user's name, tinted in the warning's colour above the Viewing as banner.
  • Bell: a run ends or fails, an agent asks a question, a loop is shared with you.
  • The browser tab names what is open and what it is, never the sub-tab: a loop "cpu_tune — Loop" on every tab of it, a chat "CPU block diagram — Chat" (no chat open: "Chat"), a project "RISC-V — hw-team" (its group after it), a group "hw-team — Group", Admin's page "Users — Admin", the list "Loops", your Account's "Agents — Account". A long name is cut by the browser. A dot on the tab's icon says the most urgent thing about what is open: pink when something waits for you (the loop's agent asks you, a chat's answer asks, a change it proposes waits for Accept), else red when the loop failed, else blue while the loop runs or the chat answers; no dot when idle. On the Loops list, Groups, Admin and your Account the dot is pink while a loop of yours or one of your chats asks you, and absent otherwise.
  • Pages update by themselves. What a page shows is read again when the server says it changed: a pass ends, a design is measured, a note, an answer or a file comes, an agent drafting a loop writes a line, asks or writes a file, someone saves the problem or a setting. Only the part that changed is read again; the cards and lists stay where they are, with your scroll, open folds and selection. Nothing is asked while nothing changes. Something you are editing (the configurator, Direct edit) is never replaced: a line says Changed on the server with Reload. A tab left alone pauses its updates; come back, or move the mouse over it, and it catches up at once with what changed meanwhile.
  • Long lists come a page at a time. The audit, Maintenance's History, a loop's agent turns, its ideas, a folder of many files and Live's past starts show at once the rows that fill the window (and half as many again); scrolling to the list's end brings the next ones, twice as many each time, a spinner while they come and "N of M" while more are left. A list that fits comes whole. New rows (an audit line, a turn, a task run) join at the top while you look, and the rows you scrolled to stay.
  • Raw and Fullscreen on files, logs, results and agent turns.
  • Addresses name the view, so a link opens it: #/app/NAME/live/timeline, #/app/NAME/settings/problem?step=graph.
  • On a phone the account items move to the menu button (three lines), and lists and tabs stack; on a narrow one the bar's links draw smaller so all four fit beside the bell and the menu.

The Preview app runs the same pages in your browser on sample data.

docs.title: Run a server
docs.text:
flux user add ada --admin       # the first account, on the server's machine
flux serve                      # http://127.0.0.1:8765/
Option Effect --host HOST, --port PORT Where it listens (default 127.0.0.1:8765); put a TLS proxy in front for others --secure-cookie Send the session cookie over HTTPS only, behind a TLS proxy --data DIR The server's data (default $XDG_DATA_HOME/flux/web): accounts, keys, every user's loops --max-running N Runs at once per user --no-sandbox Runs on the host, not sandboxed: for a single trusted user only

flux user add and flux serve must name the same data folder; both print it. Run them as the user who should own the loops' files.

  • Data: the data folder holds the server's database, secret.key (which encrypts keys and secrets) and every user's loops. Back up the database and secret.key together (Admin › Server › Maintenance can) and the loop folders separately; never copy the database alone while the server runs (Backups and restore).
  • Limits: a loop holds up to 100,000 files and 8 GB; one upload, 900 files and 256 MB.
  • Restarts: a restarted server finds its running loops again; their containers keep running while it is down. For a team, sudo python3 scripts/install-service.py (from flux/) installs it as a system service (System service); a flux serve started by hand is for development.
  • Behind a proxy: the pages keep a live connection to the server; a TLS proxy in front must not buffer it (for nginx, the server already sends X-Accel-Buffering: no).
  • Slow requests (over 0.5 s; FLUX_SLOW_S sets it) are logged, and the latest 50 are listed in Admin › Activity › Resources under Slow requests.
  • Worker processes: the server makes its heaviest pages -- a loop's results and its Overview, a design's detail, the ideas, the Agents tab's transcript, Files and the configurator's file list -- in a few processes of its own (2 to 4, by the machine's cores; 40-130 MB of memory each), so a large page being read does not slow the others. The start says how many (flux serve: view workers: 4), and so does Slow requests in Admin › Activity › Resources. FLUX_VIEW_WORKERS=N sets the number; 0 makes every page in the server itself. A worker that stops is started again at once; a page that was waiting for it says so and can be loaded again.
  • Before a login the server serves only the sign-in page and the files it needs; every other page of the app waits for a session. A sign-in page left open goes to the app once the browser has a session (a login in another tab), and a logout in one tab takes the browser's other tabs to the sign-in page.
  • Updates and the browser: after an update a page loads the new version once; a page left open goes on with its own. Restart the server after its files were changed from another machine sharing the folder.

docs.title: Loops from the server's machine
docs.text:
flux web-loop lists, starts, stops and reads the web's loops from a shell on the server's machine. It never runs a loop itself: it asks the running server, which starts and stops the run as its Start and Stop buttons do, with the same limits, pause, checks, audit and live pages.

flux web-loop ls                          # every loop: owner/loop, state, last start, the agents its problem names
flux web-loop ls --user cedric
flux web-loop start cedric/nlu            # as the Start dialog: the last start's passes, else 1
flux web-loop start cedric/nlu --forever  # until stopped; --passes N, --document F, --rerun-baseline
flux web-loop status cedric/nlu           # running pass N or idle, the last start, the log's last lines (--lines N)
flux web-loop stop cedric/nlu             # at the end of the pass; --now abandons it

A loop is USER/LOOP, its owner first. Each request acts as the loop's owner: the run is theirs, on their running limit, and each audit line it writes ends "(by host)". The agents and models are the loop's problem's (its flow, Settings › Problem); a start takes only what the Start dialog takes. --json prints the server's answer; --data names the data folder, as for flux user. Without --data the data folder is $FLUX_DATA_HOME/web, else your own (~/.local/share/flux/web); when no server answers for that one and a system service is installed, it is the service's, as its unit names it (/etc/systemd/system/flux.service's FLUX_DATA_HOME: /var/lib/flux/web).

Run flux web-loop as the account that runs flux serve: whoever can reach the server this way is its admin. When no server answers, the command says where it looked and what was there, or "permission denied on …" with the command again as the server's account. For the system service with its own account (flux):

sudo -u flux -H env -C / FLUX_DATA_HOME=/var/lib/flux sh /opt/flux/src/flux/scripts/flux-env.sh run flux web-agent test
sudo -u flux -H env -C / FLUX_DATA_HOME=/var/lib/flux sh /opt/flux/src/flux/scripts/flux-env.sh run flux web-loop ls

flux-env.sh run runs it in the service's prepared environment (/var/lib/flux/env, no Nix evaluation), env -C / starts it in a folder the account can read.

docs.title: Agents' Tests from the server's machine
docs.text:
A start waits for each agent its problem names to have passed its Test for the loop's owner, of the configuration as it is now ("Codex not set up for cedric yet (its configuration changed since its Test)"). A new program for an agent (a Codex update) is a new configuration: every user who uses it needs a new Test. flux web-agent runs that Test for them, through the running server, as flux web-loop does:

flux web-agent ls                         # each user's agents: ready, or needs Test and why; the last Test
flux web-agent ls codex --user cedric
flux web-agent test                       # every user, each agent they set up: one line each, ok or failed, its seconds
flux web-agent test codex --needed        # only those whose gate is not ready; --jobs 2 for two at once
flux web-agent test codex --user cedric   # one user (an agent named: tested even if never set up)
flux web-agent test codex --loop cedric/nlu   # in that loop's context, its variables

It is the same Test as Account › Agents' button: the server runs it in the user's own home with their own settings, variables and sandbox, and keeps the result as theirs; flux web-agent sees no credential. "Set up" is logged in, a key, endpoint, model or variable of their own for the agent, or tested before (the admin's Test of the server's configuration counts too); a disabled user is skipped unless named. The loops whose own variables run an agent otherwise, and that were tested in their context, are tested again in it. A Test ends by itself after 420 s and says why; a failed one says what the page says and makes the exit 1. Each Test is on the audit as the user's "agent test", ending "(by host)". A Test answers even while loops are busy, and is not counted in the usage; a failed Test is listed in Admin › Loops › Failures.

Admin › Server › Maintenance › Test agents runs the same Tests on a schedule (below).

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
flux user manages accounts from the server's machine:

flux user add bob --invite --url https://flux.example   # a link for bob to choose a password
flux user list
flux user role bob admin
flux user link bob                                      # a password reset link
flux user rename bob robert                             # everything of bob's, re-keyed
flux user delete robert --transfer-to cy                # robert gone, his loops cy's (or --delete-loops)

A link works once, for a week; there is no mail. In the app, Admin › People › Users does the same: a row per user with the Admin, Create, Run and Internals boxes, a Limits cell (how many of their loops run at once, empty for the server's default, and an Active switch: off disables the account, after asking), their groups as pills (× leaves one, + searches the others), Last active, their usage behind Show usage, and a ⋯ menu with View as (the app as they see it, read-only), a reset or invitation link, Rename and Delete (Deletes). Headers sort, and the order is remembered. flux user role bob admin makes bob an admin; user takes the flag away.

A new password logs the user out everywhere: one set from a link, by flux user passwd or by an admin in the app ends all their sessions (for the last two, a notice tells the user at their next login); one changed on their own Account ends all but the session that changed it.

  • Admin is the user's own. An admin administers the server and may do anything with every loop. An admin cannot clear their own Admin box; an admin has Create, Run and Internals.
  • Internals ("See how Flux works") is the user's own too, off until an admin ticks it in Admin › People › Users; each change is on the audit trail. It shows the agents' prompts and thinking, their commands, Flux's own skills, a diagram's source, the workbenches, the loop's whole log and record, and why a search took its direction. Without it, a loop's owner included, a person sees each turn's reply and its actions as counts and time (Live); a Chat proposal says what it changes, where and why, and someone who has Internals accepts it. An admin always has it. No group or project role gives it.
  • Credentials are a group's. Each group is set to Server settings (runs use the server's model, agent and variable settings beneath the user's own) or Own settings (members bring their own settings and agent logins). A user gets the server's settings when any of their groups gives them; in no such group, or in no group at all, they use their own. Admins follow the same rule. A new group starts with own settings. Your Account names the group that gives you the server's settings; Groups in the top bar shows it per group (Groups).
  • Groups: a user is in no group, one or several. Admin › People › Groups lists each group with its member count, its Credentials, Server settings (who gets the server's settings through it, or through another group), Open projects (the level its open projects give its members unless a project says another; Asker by default), and a pencil (Rename) and a bin (Delete) at the row's end. A group unrolls to the member grid under its name: a row per member with a Level (see the words), the Member column every member has, a box per word (hover a column's name for its meaning) and × to remove them. The All members row on top gives a word to everyone or takes it from everyone (a dash: some have it). People (with a plus) is under the table; a new member starts as Member. On a phone a member is a block: the name and ×, the level, then the words three to a line. A project's members and a loop's Sharing are the same grid.
  • Permissions of the account, whatever the groups: Create loops and Run loops and agents. A user in no group still creates and runs their own loops.
  • A membership's words -- curate, manage, create (Member, Maintainer, Lead) -- act on the group's projects, never on a loop: being in a group gives nothing on any loop (see the words).
  • Archive, reset, delete, rename and transfer stay with the owner and the admins. A loop is reached in two ways only: its owner (or one with share on it) shares it with a user or a group, or links it into a project. What someone may do with it is the union of their row, their groups' rows and what the projects it is linked into give them. Ask and Run also need Run loops and agents.

docs.title: The words
docs.text:
One vocabulary for loops, groups and projects: the loop words view, ask, edit, run act on loops -- one shared loop, or the loops linked into a project; share is a loop's own (whoever holds it chooses who else gets the loop, giving at most what they hold). The place words act on a group or a project: link (link one's own loops into a project), curate (review a project's knowledge, keep its library), manage (members, levels, access, title; rename, archive, delete) and, on a group only, create (make projects; the maker is the project's Lead).

A loop is reached in two ways only: a share (to the person, or to a group of theirs), or being in a project it is linked into -- one of its members, with their level there, or a member of its group when the project opens to the group. A group membership carries no loop word: being in a group gives nothing on any loop by itself.

Place Words Loop share view · ask · edit · run · share Group membership curate · manage · create Project level view · ask · edit · run · link · curate · manage Global project level curate · manage

Levels are one ladder in every place, cut to each place's words; a mix that matches no level reads Custom:

Level Words Loop Project Group Global project Member none -- yes yes yes Viewer view yes yes -- -- Asker view · ask yes yes -- -- Contributor view · ask · edit · run · link yes (no link) yes -- -- Maintainer Contributor and curate, create (on a loop: view · ask · edit · run · share) yes yes curate · create curate Lead every word -- yes curate · manage · create curate · manage

A loop's levels stop at Maintainer; its Owner row is shown, never given. A word that acts on a loop brings view with it.

Why a place has no box for a word (the grids leave these out):

Place Word Why not Loop share link covered by share: linking needs share on the loop (its owner has it) and link on the project Loop share curate a loop's record is not curated: what it teaches reaches a project's curators Loop share manage its owner's only (rename, transfer, archive, delete): the Owner row, never given Loop share create loops are made on the account (Create loops) Group membership view, ask, edit, run a loop is reached through a share or a project one is in, never a membership Group membership link linking is a project's word: its members' level, or its open level Group membership share a loop's own: a group never shares its members' loops onward Project level share a loop's own: a link is consent to the project only Project level create projects do not nest Global project level view its visibility gives it: everyone a public one, its members a private one Global project level ask, edit, run, link a global project gives nobody a word on its loops; who links is its join rule

Who manages a group or a project gives anyone a level or words up to their own there; admins any. The open levels are set by the group's managers (a membership has no loop word to bound them) and by a project's own managers within their words.

What a group gives. On the loops linked into its projects, only what each project's group access says: invite (the default for a new project) gives nothing on its loops and is private: hidden from the group's members until they are added (its managers and curators see it); view gives every member view on it and its loops; open gives every member the project's open level (the group's default, Asker unless set, or the project's own) -- that level, nothing more. Its words reach every project of the group, whatever its access: curate curates them, manage manages them and the group's members, create makes projects.

Global projects. A global project is public (everyone sees it, its library and its knowledge) or private (only the members an admin or its managers add, and admins, see it; elsewhere it is not found). Its members hold only curate or manage (Member, Maintainer, Lead). Nobody sees another person's loops linked into it but admins and its managers; in a private one its members do not see the other members either. Who links loops into it is its join rule (everyone, or admins), and in a private one only its members. There is no curator group: a curator is a member with curate.

docs.title: Renames
docs.text:
Only an admin renames a user: Admin › People › Users, the row's ⋯ › Rename (or flux user rename). Everything that holds the name moves with it -- the user's folder (loops, chats, home), their sandbox caches, their loops' settings, variables, shares and result columns, the shares other owners gave them, their runs' paths, scheduled changes naming them, chats that focus on their loops, the questions they asked, their usage. It is refused while anything of theirs works: a run of their loops, an agent writing or answering about one, a chat answer, a login or an agent test. There are no redirects: links to the old name stop working, so everyone their loops are shared with is told once, with the new link, and so is the user. Their sessions stay; they log in with the new name from then on. The audit keeps the old name where it was written, with one "rename user" entry.

Admin › People › Groups, a group's pencil (Rename), renames a group; its members, their permissions and its shares stay (they are kept by the group's id), and its members are told. Names are one whatever their case; _ is reserved and / is not allowed (a project is addressed <group>/<name>). As a project's rename, it is refused while a loop linked into one of its projects runs (or an agent writes it, or answers in it); its projects' members and the owners of their loops are told once too, with the group's page.

docs.title: Deletes
docs.text:
Active off (in Limits) disables a user: logged out, unable to log in, everything kept. ⋯ › Delete is the hard one, for admins only. Its dialog says what the user holds -- their loops (and whom each is shared with), the projects only they manage, the loops shared with them, their groups and sessions -- and asks where their loops go: transferred to another user (each moves as a transfer does, with its files, record, runs and projects; its shares cleared; a name the other user already has becomes <loop>-<user>, shown before you confirm) or deleted (as the loop's own Delete). Then their account goes with everything kept for them: sessions, invites, notifications, memberships, project levels, the shares to them, their own model settings, variables and agents' keys, their Overview layout, scheduled changes for them, their folder (chats, home, agents' logins) and sandbox caches. The audit keeps their name where it was written, with one "delete user" entry; the usage log, transcripts and others' chats stay as history. It is refused while a loop of theirs runs or anything of theirs works (as a rename), for yourself and for the last enabled admin; you type their name to confirm. Whom their loops were shared with is told, and so is the user who got them. flux user delete NAME --transfer-to USER (or --delete-loops) does the same from the server's machine.

Groups › Delete is refused while the group has a project, archived ones too: the dialog lists them, each a link to its page to delete it. Otherwise it says the members, the loops shared with the group and, first, the members who get the server's settings through this group alone: they change to their own. You type its name to confirm; its memberships, the loop shares made to it and its settings go, and its members are told. Its members keep their accounts and loops.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Think of a group as an organisation and a project as one of its repositories: the project has its own members, and loops are linked into it. A project belongs to one group, addressed <group>/<name>, or is global, addressed _/<name> and shown "global / …". Names are letters, digits, - and _, one per group whatever their case; titles are free. The Groups page lists a group's projects and makes new ones, and each project has a page of its own: its loops and its members. flux project on the server's machine manages them:

flux project create hw/nlu --title "NLU operators"                    # --access invite|view|open (invite)
flux project create _/techniques --visibility private --join admins  # global: admins only (public by default)
flux project member _/techniques cy maintainer                        # a global project's: member, maintainer (curate) or lead (curate, manage)
flux project access _/techniques public                               # a global project's visibility: public or private
flux project member hw/nlu bob contributor                            # a level, or view,ask,link ... or none (a Member)
flux project member hw/nlu bob remove
flux project access hw/nlu open viewer                                # what the group's members get: open, at Viewer (group: the group's)
flux project rename hw/nlu nlu-ops                                    # the old address stops working
flux project archive hw/nlu-ops                                       # --undo unarchives
flux project list --all
flux project delete hw/nlu-ops --yes

Levels are the words' ladder cut to a project's words (view, ask, edit, run, link, curate, manage); the one who makes a project is its Lead. A Member (no words) sees the project and its members, nothing more. Group access, per project, says what the group's members get without being its members: invite (private: hidden from them until they are added, but for the members whose group membership curates or manages; the default for a new project), view (they view it and its loops; every project made before reads so) or open (each gets its open level, nothing more). There is no joining: a project's own members are added by those who manage it; anyone may leave a project.

What someone may do with a project is the union of: what its group access gives, their membership of its group (curate and manage on every project of the group), their own level as its member, and a global project's view (everyone a public one, its members a private one). Its contents -- its files, its knowledge, its chats -- are its own members' alone (and admins'): neither its group access nor a membership's curate and manage reads any of them (Groups). Rights only add up: nobody loses a right because of a project. Admins may do everything. Members with create make the group's projects; only admins make global ones and choose whether each is public or private and who may link loops into them; a global project's members (curate or manage) are added by admins and its managers. Archiving hides a project from the lists and freezes it until it is unarchived. Every change is in the audit.

Admin › People › Projects lists every project, the groups' and the global ones, archived ones too: its title (a link to its page) and address, its group, how many loops are linked into it, how many members it has and the size of its library of its limit ("6 B of 2 KB", over in warn when it holds more). A global project's Visibility (Public or Private) and Who links loops (everyone, admins only) are set in its row; each row's tools open it, rename it (a pencil), archive or unarchive it (a box, its arrow up when archived) and delete it (a bin) -- quiet icons that show while the row is pointed at or holds the focus, always on a phone or a touch screen; each says what it does to which project when hovered, and asks first as before. A row with more actions than four, or one without a clear icon (a user's View as, a scheduled change's Turn off), keeps its ⋯ menu. New global project is under the list.

Library limits. Library limit for every project, above the list, is the most a project's library may hold unless its row's Limit says another; both are numbers of GB (5, 0.5), saved as they change, and empty means the next one down: a row empty takes every project's, that empty takes a loop's room, 8 GB. A change is on the audit as "library limit". Past its limit a library takes no upload or edit that would grow it; one over it keeps its files and cannot grow.

A project's library is browsed and changed from its page as a loop's files are: view browses; edit, curate or manage changes; manage hides paths from the agents. It holds what a loop may (100,000 files, 8 GB).

docs.title: Loops in projects
docs.text:
A loop is in no project, one or several, in an order its owner sets. Linking a loop is its owner's consent; the project's roles then decide. Only its owner (or an admin) links it: into a group's project where they hold link, or into a global project (anyone -- a private one's members only -- unless its join rule is admins); an archived project takes none.

  • On every loop linked into a group's project, each of its members gets their roles' loop words -- view, ask, edit, run -- and the group's members what its access gives (view, or the open level). This adds to what shares give, never takes away (a group membership gives no loop word); ask and run still need the account's Run loops and agents; curate, link and manage stay the project's. An archived project gives none until unarchived.
  • A global project gives nobody any right on a loop. A user sees only their own loops in it; admins and its managers see every one.
  • Each link keeps a learning consent: whether the project may learn from its runs (the collector). On by default for a group's project, the owner's to switch; off for a global one, where only an admin or one of its managers turns it on and the owner may turn it off.

A loop renamed or transferred keeps its projects; a loop deleted leaves them; a project deleted lets its loops go and tells their owners. On the server's machine:

flux project loop bob/adder                          # its projects, in order
flux project loop bob/adder set hw/nlu _/techniques  # exactly these, in this order (none: no project)
flux project loop bob/adder add hw/dsp               # one more, last
flux project loop bob/adder extract hw/nlu off
flux project loop bob/adder remove hw/dsp
flux project loops hw/nlu                            # the project's loops

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
Account is in four tabs, as Admin's: the address keeps the one open (#/account/agents), so a link or a reload lands on it; #/account alone opens Profile.

  • Profile: a line that names your groups and links to the Groups page, your usage, your password, desktop notifications, and the Overview layout used on every loop. Changing the password asks for the current one (wrong ones count and lock as a login's do) and logs out your other sessions.
  • Agents: a tab per agent -- its login, Test, model, variables and your own instructions -- and All agents, the variables every agent of yours gets.
  • Machines: your own machines (Add my machine) and the server machines your loops may use (Machines).
  • Shared links: every read-only link you made of a chat, a loop's conversation or a design (Share): what it shows (a link to it), who may open it, when it closes, how often it was opened, with Copy and Revoke; a link whose right you lost says stopped.

An agent is used only once its Test passed for whoever starts the loop. A Test runs at once, whatever your loops hold: it waits for no turns at once and no running limit (Agents' Tests). A login runs the agent's own login command in the sandbox, in a small terminal; Claude Code's token is stored encrypted and never shown again. An agent never runs on FluxAgent: without settings of its own, it uses its own configuration and login (Models and agents).

docs.title: Admin
docs.text:
Admin has five tabs, each of sub-tabs; each tab opens on the sub-tab last looked at in this browser.

Tab Sub-tab What it holds Loops All loops Every user's loops (a loop is archived from its own settings); pause new starts, stop or restart them all after their pass Failures Failed starts and agent Tests People Users Users and permissions, invitations, View as Groups Every group, its members and credentials Projects Every project Runtime Agents FluxAgent and each agent: program, login, model and key, seconds per turn, token prices, turns at once on its endpoint (every loop's turns; an agent's Test takes none), whether Ask may use it, thinking by default, its instructions; + Add agent Machines Every machine that measures steps, this server's own first, then the server's and users' (a user's tagged with its owner): how many cores, how much memory and how many of each device are in use, each machine's labels (edited in its row), size, health, jobs, Flux version and when it was last heard from, Rename, Drain/Resume, Rotate keys and Revoke (this server's own: its labels and Rename); the steps waiting for a machine; join codes not used yet (Cancel); + Add machine Sandbox Limits (CPUs, memory, processes, scratch: a default and a maximum), the network (open, or an allowlist), the PATH directories mounted, what every user's home starts with Chat What users may use in Chat (the tab, network beyond the base allowlist, the workbench, loop access), the hosts a chat may also reach, FluxAgent on the web, overrides per group and user (Chat) Activity Resources CPUs, memory and disks over time (this server's, or a joined machine's), the tool pool (the cores and memory the running checks and measurements hint, use and leave free -- a step that says no cores counts 1 -- and how many wait for room: resource hints), the sandbox containers, each loop's disk and caches Usage Usage and cost by user and agent (the knowledge collector's calls as their loop's), the disk now Endpoints How each endpoint did, and the hosts the network refused Audit The audit trail: the whole trail, newest first, a page at a time as you scroll; What, Who and the search narrow it on the server, their counts over every entry, said once the first page has come Server Version The commit the server runs, updates waiting on origin/main, Update and Roll back (Version) Old data Loops' documents of an earlier form, with Migrate all; what the migration of the commits behind would do to them; data only legacy code reads (Version) Maintenance Scheduled clean-up tasks, each on or off, with Run now; scheduled changes of a setting

An address of an earlier Admin page (a bookmark, #/admin/users, #/admin/insights) opens where that page is now.

Keys are stored encrypted and never shown again. With nothing set, runs use the machine's own configuration (~/.config/flux/flux.env, and each agent's own).

An agent with no endpoint URL runs on its own providers and login, and its Model can still be picked: with From the agent on, the field lists what the agent itself offers on your login (two people can see different models from the same agent; Admin › Runtime › Agents lists with the admin's own). The login is never kept, shown or logged; only the list is. Default (the agent's own) leaves the choice to the agent. An agent that is not logged in says so, with where to log in (Account › Agents); with the box off, any model name can be typed. The refresh button asks again.

Which model a turn uses: Admin › Runtime › Agents sets the server's model, Account › Agents your own, which wins; a loop's variable wins over both, and a document's own model: over everything. Every turn gets it: the loop's, Chat's, New loop's author and the Test.

An agent's panel says its program as runs find it, with its version, or what was looked for ("claude is not on the runs' PATH"). Users are offered only agents whose program is found -- in the chat, Ask, New loop › Agent and the configurator's agent menus, where one a document names that is not found shows (not available). An agent added under a name of its own runs its kind's program unless its Program (or FLUX_<NAME>_BIN) names another, and its login, Test and runs use that program too.

docs.title: Thinking by default
docs.text:
Each agent's panel in Admin › Runtime › Agents, and FluxAgent's, says whether it Thinks by default: where a loop's box does not say (think: beside by: flux or an agent, an agent's effort:, Thinking) and as the Think switch of a chat's composer starts for it (Chat). An agent also has the effort it works at when thinking and when not, from the levels its kind takes; its own leaves it to the agent. FluxAgent has its own four efforts -- low, medium, high, max (Chat); built in is high thinking and medium not.

Thinks by default Effort when thinking when not Each agent on its own its kind's lowest (low, or minimal) FluxAgent off built in (high) built in (medium)

Untouched, agents work at their own effort and FluxAgent answers straight. What wins, first to last: a chat's Think, the loop's box, this default. Saved at once and audited (thinking by default); a run, a chat or an ask started afterwards takes it.

FluxAgent's panel also has Structured answers, on unless turned off: a loop's turns ask the model for answers in a fixed shape. Turn it off for a model server that cannot do that; every loop on this server then gets plain answers. It is saved and audited with the row above.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: Each agent's panel has Instructions: text given to that agent with every task, wherever Flux uses it -- a loop's boxes, a loop's Chat, Chat, New loop › Agent, its Test. FluxAgent takes none. OpenCode ships with a default; Default brings it back once changed or cleared. The others have none. At most 4,000 characters; saved as typed and audited (agent instructions); a run, a chat or an ask started afterwards takes them. Each user may add their own under Account › Agents (the server's shown above, read-only), after the server's: a loop's turns take its owner's, as they take the owner's settings.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The tab charts the machine Over time (CPU, memory, disks, kept for thirty days, beside every loop's tokens per second), lists the Sandbox containers with their CPU, memory and processes, and each loop's disk (Disk per loop). Whose says what each container is: a loop's (its link; Stop ends the loop after its pass), Chat · user (a user's chat sandbox; Stop ends its answers and removes it), Login · user or Agent test · user. A container no process runs any more is left behind, with Kill; the scheduled clean-up removes those itself. A Compiler caches line says what the tools' compiler cache holds -- one cache a user, each kept under its cap by ccache -- with each user's size. The container CPU and memory charts sum each minute's containers as read; a minute's tooltip says when one of them could not be read (it ended first), and a minute with none read is a gap. A container that ended since the last minute -- a tool's, which may live only seconds -- adds the CPU it used that no earlier minute counted; it adds nothing to memory, which is what the containers hold at the minute.

With machines joined (Machines), a picker above the cards shows This server or one of them: a runner's CPUs, CPU used, load, memory and disks, and over time its CPU, load, memory, disks, its steps' containers and how many steps run; the storage machine's disks and the bytes it served. Each machine sends its figures with its heartbeat, about every 15 seconds; they are kept as the server's own, for thirty days. A machine away sends none: its charts stop there and its card shows its last figures, said to be old. On Admin › Runtime › Machines a machine's name opens its view.

Orphan caches lists the sandbox caches no loop of this server owns: a deleted loop's, and those not the web's -- made by a flux task run from a shell (named by its document's id, like demo.primes) or a user gone. They hold scratch, agent sessions and tool caches, rebuilt when needed; no result is ever in a cache. Each row says whether Clean disk removes it at its next weekly pass (goes at the next clean) or why it stays: a process works in it, or it was used in the last 14 days. The line above the table says when Clean disk next removes them; Clean now runs that part alone, after a confirmation listing each cache it deletes. Delete on a row removes that one cache whole, whenever it was used.

A cache whose files belong to another account cannot be deleted by the server: its row says whose and gives the command to run and as whom -- podman unshare rm -rf <cache> as the service's account when its own sandbox containers wrote them, else sudo -u <owner> rm -rf <cache>. Clean disk leaves such a cache and says so in its result.

Slow requests lists the latest 50 requests over FLUX_SLOW_S (0.5 s) since the server started. A machine's request that waits for a job (up to 25 s) is not counted for its wait. Its heading also says where the heavy pages are made: in 4 worker processes, 60 MB each, or in the server (FLUX_VIEW_WORKERS=0).

docs.title: The memory guard
docs.text:
Each sandbox has its own memory limit, but nothing limits all of them together. When the machine runs short of memory (RAM above the high mark, 95% by default, with swap full or filling), the server stops the loop that uses the most memory now, then the next biggest while the machine is still short (until RAM is under the low mark, 90%). A chat's sandbox or another sandbox the server started can be the biggest too: its answers then end saying why.

A loop stopped this way ends failed, killed mid-pass (the passes that ended before are kept). Its Overview's Why it stopped says so, for example Stopped to free memory: the machine was at 96% (30.7 GB of 32.0 GB); this loop used 11.4 GB, the most of any. The stop is in its log and the audit (memory guard), and its owner gets a notice. It is not started again: its owner or an admin starts it when there is room.

The Server card shows Memory used and Swap used, the guard's marks and the last thing it stopped. Edit (the pencil) turns it on or off and sets the marks (from 50% to 99%, the low mark under the high one, the swap mark in percent of the swap); a change is audited (memory guard settings).

docs.title: The sandbox scratch cap
docs.text:
A loop's sandbox scratch holds its passes' working files (measurement folders, place-and-route files, the agents' folders); it can grow to many gigabytes. Its cap is the loop's Scratch /tmp size: the loop's own in its Settings › Advanced (admins), else the server's default in Admin › Runtime › Sandbox › Limits, held to the server's maximum (see Sandbox). No Scratch /tmp size: no cap, nothing is deleted.

Maintenance › Clean disk keeps each scratch under its cap, every five minutes, deleting the oldest pieces first; it never deletes recent files, a running loop's current work, or the baseline's and the decision's files. What it deleted is said in the loop's log, in Maintenance's history and in Disk per loop's Scratch /tmp column (trimmed 4.2 GiB today). A loop's Settings › Maintenance › Clean disk does it now, asked first. A file trimmed away is said no longer kept.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
Six tasks keep what grows on disk and in the server's tables, each by age or by count, and a seventh removes what updates leave behind:

Task What it does Its setting Clean disk Reaps sandbox containers no process runs (every minute), keeps each loop's sandbox scratch under its Scratch /tmp size (every five minutes), tells the admins when a disk has little space left (hourly), removes pass folders older than the days set (a run's newest stays, running loops too), a loop's sandbox cache once it has not run for 14 days, a deleted loop's cache and a cache no web loop owns once nothing touched it for 14 days (never one in use; see Resources › Orphan caches); ticked, also what FLUX_TMPDIR holds that nothing touched for the days set and no process uses (shared by everything on the machine: off until ticked) older than (days), 3; Flux's temporary folder too Condense history A loop's log over 50 MB and its task journal over 20 MB keep their recent part, the older part gzipped beside them; transcript turns older than the days set keep only what usage counts. Running loops too. A loop's results, ideas and decisions are never touched older than (days), 14 Compact and check Compacts the server's database and every loop's record, checks them read-only, loads each stopped loop's document and says which do not load; with backups kept over 0, saves a copy of the server's database and secret.key in the data folder's backups/ (accounts, settings and run metadata; loop files, outputs and sandbox caches are not included), the latest kept backups kept, 0 (no backup) Prune server tables Expired sessions and invitations; login failures, notifications and the refused-host log (Activity › Endpoints › Network refused) older than the days set; audit lines older than theirs older than (days), 30; audit (days), 365 (0: all kept) Prune run history Each loop keeps its latest starts in the server's run list; older rows go (a running start never) keep, 200 Test agents Off until turned on: the agents' Tests, below none Clean leftovers Off until turned on: what updates leave behind once done with, below. Never a record none

Each runs on its schedule (Clean disk every minute, Compact and check weekly, the others daily, by default); within a task, each piece runs at most as often as the table says. Running loops are never touched but where the table says, archived loops only by the checks and compaction, and every run is audited. Orphan caches' Clean now runs one part of a task alone; that part's clock moves, the task's does not.

What edits a loop's record is the loop's own, in its Settings › Record, asked for and never scheduled nor run over the loops from here: Prune stale records (the rows measured before a change to how their stage is measured: the loop no longer counts them), Prune empty starts (starts that did nothing: their row, and for the latest its log and journal), Prune failed designs, Invalidate all (every design set aside) and Re-Evaluate (the next start measures again the designs of the Results tabs ticked: Pending by default; Accepted, Rejected, Failed, all four for every design; and pass 0; see Results). Each asks first; the loop must be at rest, but Re-Evaluate, which only marks the next start.

Prune failed designs asks at which stage: the loop's checks and stages in flow order (its first stage chosen), each with how many designs failed there, or Any stage. It removes the designs in Results' Failed tab whose latest attempt failed at that stage, with their history and files. Accepted, Rejected and Pending designs are never touched, nor the baseline. The confirmation reads, for example, Deletes 143 failed designs (stage gate) in bob/x: their rows, their designs' text and the pass files only they have ... Cannot be undone.

Test agents (off until turned on; e.g. daily at a time) runs the same Tests as flux web-agent test does by default: each user's agents they set up (logged in, a key of their own, or tested before; disabled users left out), and their loops' Tests in their context, and Admin › Runtime › Agents' Test of the server's own configuration of each agent that has a shared endpoint or credential, as the admin who asked (a schedule's: the first admin). Each result is kept as that Test's, so a start's gate reads it, and is on the audit as the user's "agent test", ending "(by maintenance)". Two Tests run at once. A Test takes no turn at once on its endpoint and no running-loop limit, as above. A Test already running (a button's, the daily retest) is left and said "being tested already". The task's result says each Test, failed first: whose, which agent, ok or why not, its seconds; its Edit dialog lists the last run's Tests one per row. One failed Test makes the run failed. A user whose Test passed before and fails now is told, as the daily retest tells them.

Clean leftovers (off until turned on; run it after an update, or weekly) removes what Flux's own updates leave behind once they are done with it, on every loop at rest or on one (a loop's Settings › Maintenance too):

Left behind By Removed when problem.yaml.orig, NAME.problem.yaml.orig beside a loop's document a document migration (an update's start, Old documents › Migrate all, flux task migrate --write) keeps the original the document is there, loads, and is at today's format, and the last update's Roll back would not put it back files in the data folder's kept/ (lines.json, hashes/*.json) the server, for its next start, named for its code made by other code than the server runs now (never read again), or half-written by a process gone over an hour ago

It never removes a record or any file of one: a record's copy before a bring-up (out/.NAME.db.before-vN) and an SQLite side file (-wal, -shm, -journal) of no record are listed in its confirmation as kept, with their size, for you to delete by hand once satisfied. It never looks into a running loop (said, left alone), nor at a loop's results, ideas, decisions, workbench, library or inputs. Its confirmation is a table: a row per loop and kind, with how many files, their size, and whether they go or are kept and why (its document does not load, the last update's Roll back puts it back). Each file removed is on the audit (the loop, the file, its size), and the task's result says the totals. The prepared environments are not its: each update's prepare keeps the current one, the previous one and those a running loop is on, and removes the rest.

Maintenance has three tabs, each with a filter box and chips that narrow its rows:

Tab What it lists Tasks The seven tasks: running first, then queued, failed, done and off. Chips: Running, Queued, Failed, Off Schedule Your scheduled changes (below), soonest next run first. A chip per setting or kind History Every run of a task or a change, newest first: what, when, by whom (the schedule, the server's start-up, or an admin's Run now), how long it took and its result, a page at a time as you scroll. Chips: Failed, Schedule, Run now, counted over every run kept; the chips and the filter narrow it on the server. The last 1000 runs are kept

On a phone each row is two or three lines: its name with its buttons, then its schedule and last run, then its result.

Each task's row ends with Run now (the play, named "Run ") and a pencil (Edit, its options). One task runs at a time. Run now (on every loop, or on one) runs the task at once when nothing else runs; otherwise it joins a queue, first come first run, and the row says queued · 2nd with Cancel. Asking again for a task already queued or running adds nothing. Scheduled runs join the same queue. A running task shows a spinner and how long it has run. A restart drops the queue, and the schedule asks again. Resetting, renaming, transferring or archiving a loop is still refused while a task runs, never between two. A task's result says each of its pieces; one that fails is said so, the next still runs, and the run is failed.

Run now asks first when a task deletes or rewrites data. The confirmation names the task, says what each of its pieces does with its settings and on how many loops, how many of them are running, and ends Cannot be undone. where that is true, for example Deletes pass folders older than 3 days in 12 loops (3 running) ... Cannot be undone. Cancel runs nothing. The same question comes from Edit › One loop › Run, naming that loop, and from a loop's own Settings › Maintenance and Settings › Record. On one loop, Clean disk trims its scratch, removes its old pass folders and deletes its sandbox cache (however recently it ran, unless it runs); Condense history condenses its log, journal and transcript; Compact and check compacts and checks its records and loads its document. Clean disk, the loop's cache and a cache's Clean in Resources delete no history: a loop's journal lives in the loop itself.

Counts are cheap ones: the loops, the running ones, the run rows, the stale rows and the backups. What would take a scan, such as sizes or a loop's files, is described without a number. A task asks nothing when a count shows it would delete nothing: no old run rows, no stale row, no backup past the number kept, or no loop at rest to act on. Test agents only reads and runs at once, as does Re-Evaluate, which only marks the next start and can be cancelled from the loop's Settings. A scheduled change's Run now asks first when it is a Stop loops and loops are running. It names them, and says whether they stop now or after their pass. The schedule itself never asks. No flux command runs a maintenance task.

A task runs every so many minutes, hours or days, or daily at a time on the days picked, or on a cron expression (the same form as a scheduled change's, below). A task at a time of day runs once when its time comes; a time already past when it is set waits for its next day.

docs.title: Backups and restore
docs.text:
Back up server database saves the server's database and secret.key in backups/server-<time>/, while the server runs and writes go on.

To restore a backup, stop the server and move the database's files (flux-web.db and any flux-web.db-wal and flux-web.db-shm beside it) aside, keeping them until the restored server runs well. Then put the backup's flux-web.db and secret.key in the data folder and start the server. Never copy a database in while the server runs. A start that finds a database and stray files that do not belong together is refused, with a message naming the files and the fix; nothing is deleted. A start after a crash reads the database's own -wal back, even one a crash cut mid-checkpoint. When a start is refused, copy all three files together to a folder of their own before moving any of them: the -wal holds committed changes.

docs.title: Scheduled changes
docs.text:
A scheduled change does one thing at a time of day. + Schedule asks first for its kind, then that kind's fields, then when:

Kind What it does Turns at once Sets one endpoint limit: turns at once of an agent's endpoint, or requests at once of FluxAgent (the limits under Admin › Runtime › Agents), checked as that form checks it: a whole number, 0 for no limit. An agent's Test takes no turn Pause starts Pauses new starts with a reason (up to 200 characters), or resumes them. Running loops go on. While paused, starts, owners' restarts, Restart all and a pending restart after a pass are refused with the reason Running limit A user's running-loops limit (0–64, or default), or the server's default (0–64, or default: the --max-running flag). New starts only Stop loops Stops the running loops after their pass: every loop, one user's, or one loop. Now (off by default) stops them at once, the current pass abandoned Start a loop Starts one loop as its owner, with the options of its last start, for 1–1000 passes or until stopped. Refused, and shown as a failed run, when the loop is gone or archived, its owner is disabled or may not run loops, starts are paused, the owner is at their limit, or it already runs

When is daily at a time on the days picked, or, under Advanced: cron expression, five cron fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week. */15 9-17 * * 1-5 means every 15 minutes from 09:00 to 17:59 on weekdays. The form says the schedule in words and its next times. Times are the server's own, and its time zone is shown beside the field.

For example, to leave the shared endpoint to people by day and give it to the loops by night, add two changes to Claude Code's turns at once:

Change When Claude Code turns at once → 1 daily at 08:00, Mon–Fri Claude Code turns at once → 4 daily at 20:00, every day

A night of runs, for example, takes three changes, every day: Start a loop at 20:00 until stopped, Pause starts at 20:05 with the reason nightly runs (no one else starts one), and Stop loops at 07:00, every loop after its pass, with Pause starts set to Resume starts at 07:30.

Each change is a row with its schedule, next run, last run and result, Run now (the play, queued like any task), and Edit, Turn off/Turn on and Delete in its menu. A change takes effect at the next turn of every loop, running loops too. Lowering the limit stops no running turn: running turns finish, and new turns wait until fewer than the new limit run.

A stop or a start happens at its time only: one missed while the server was down is not done when it starts. The pause, each user's limit and the default limit are settings. When the server starts, each setting gets the value of whichever of its changes came last (at or before now), so a server that was down at 20:00 still has the night's value. If two changes of one setting were both missed, only the later one is applied. Adding, editing and deleting changes is audited, and so is every change made. A run that found the value already set is not recorded. The audit reads, for example, scheduled: Claude Code turns at once → 4 (was 1).

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text: Every run is sandboxed unless a loop's Settings › Preferences › Advanced (admins) says otherwise. The network is open, or an allowlist of hosts, domains and address ranges; HTTP(S) goes through the server's proxy, and raw TCP/UDP is a per-loop choice. The command line's equivalents are FLUX_SANDBOX_NET=allowlist, FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW and FLUX_SANDBOX_RAW_NETWORK=1 (Sandbox).

docs.title: Allowlists
docs.text:
Every allowlist (the sandbox's, Chat's, a loop's extra hosts, an agent's hosts and FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW) reads the same way:

Entry Allows dl.acm.org that host only *.acm.org or .acm.org acm.org and every subdomain (dl.acm.org, www.acm.org, a.b.acm.org) 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.20, ::1 the addresses in the range, or that address localhost this machine (127.0.0.1, ::1)
  • Separate entries by new lines, commas, semicolons or spaces. # starts a comment to the end of the line.
  • Case, a trailing dot and a port do not count (DL.ACM.org.:443 is dl.acm.org); a pasted URL keeps its host.
  • * alone is refused: choose open (or Chat's Open) instead.
  • Saved, the list is kept one entry per line, and the page says how it reads, for example Understood as: acm.org and its subdomains · arxiv.org only.
  • A page that redirects to another domain (a sign-in or a CDN host) is refused by that host's name. Recently blocked under the list names the hosts refused lately; a click adds one. The agent's error says the same: flux sandbox: refused www.acm.org (not on the network allowlist -- add www.acm.org or *.acm.org).
  • Lists kept before this rule, when a name also allowed its subdomains, were rewritten once as *.name, so they reach what they reached.

Limits restrict every sandbox the server starts: a loop's runs and checks, a loop's Chat, Chat answers, the author agent, agent Tests and logins. For CPUs, memory, processes and scratch /tmp:

  • Default is what a sandbox gets when its loop sets none.
  • Maximum is the most a loop may ask for. A higher ask is clamped to it, never refused, and a loop that sets nothing is held to it too. The run's log says memory 8 GB clamped to 1 GB by the server.
  • Empty is no limit (processes: 4096).

CPUs are a positive number such as 2 or 0.5, at most this machine's count. Memory and scratch are numbers of GB, such as 128 or 0.5 (the fields say GB); memory is at most this machine's RAM. The page shows both. Scratch /tmp also caps the loop's sandbox scratch on disk (the sandbox scratch cap). A change is audited (sandbox limits). It applies to sandboxes started after it; running ones keep their limits. A loop's Advanced (admins) shows the server's default and maximum under each field, and clamped to 1 GB by the server when its value is above the maximum. On a server started with --no-sandbox, the limits are shown read only.

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Proxy is what runs, agents, Chat, logins and the author agent reach the network through, and Flux's own calls to the model endpoints. It applies with or without the sandbox.

  • From the host (the default) takes the first place that names one: the server's environment, /etc/environment, /etc/environment.d/*.conf and ~/.config/environment.d/*.conf, then what the server user's login shell exports (a systemd service often has none of a profile's). The page says which, for example From /etc/environment: HTTP http://proxy:3128 · not for .corp.example.org.
  • Set here takes an HTTP proxy, an HTTPS proxy (each http://host:port, with user:password@ if it asks) and a not through it list, read like an allowlist (new lines, commas, semicolons or spaces; # comments): a host, .domain or *.domain (it and its subdomains), an IP or a CIDR. Empty fields are no proxy. Switching to set here starts from the host's values.
  • Credentials are stored encrypted and shown as http://***@proxy:3128; a URL left as shown keeps them.
  • The server and its sandboxes get HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY in both cases (localhost always added to NO_PROXY); an allowlisted sandbox reaches its allowed hosts through this proxy, directly for those its not through it list names.
  • In effect says the proxy and where it came from. A change is audited (sandbox proxy, the credentials masked) and applies to what starts after it: running loops keep theirs.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Admin › Runtime › Chat says what users may use in Chat. The admin allows features; each user then switches them on or off per chat, within what is allowed.

Feature Allowed Default Chat tab The user has Chat in the top bar. Off, every other feature is off too. on Network beyond the base allowlist A chat may also reach the hosts listed under Network beyond the base allowlist, or any host when it is Open. off Workbench A chat may read and write the user's workbench. on Loop access A chat may read the user's loops, their own and those shared with them, read-only. on
  • For everyone sets the server's value. Overrides sets a value per group and per user: default, on or off. A user's value beats their groups', which beat the server's; of a user's groups, one that turns a feature off wins. Add a user adds a user's row.
  • A chat always has the sandbox's base allowlist (Sandbox): the hosts listed there, the agents' hosts and the model endpoints. Agents need it, so there is no "off". Allowed with no hosts listed and not Open, the feature stays off, and users see why. On a server whose sandbox network is open, chats have the open network.
  • The hosts beyond the base are an allowlist (Allowlists): *.acm.org lets a chat reach acm.org and all its subdomains. Recently blocked names the hosts chats were refused lately.
  • A feature that is off is greyed in the user's chat, with the reason: turned off by the admin on this server, for the group …, or for you.
  • Changes apply from each chat's next message. They are audited (chat permissions), as are chats made and deleted (chat created, chat deleted).

FluxAgent on the web sets how FluxAgent's web tools work. A chat gets them only when its Network is on. They reach the hosts above, or any public host when the network is Open, and never a private or local address.

Setting Default MB each 50 1 to 500. A larger download is refused. Seconds a fetch 60 5 to 300. Ports beyond 80 and 443 none For example 8080. Other ports are refused. Web search None SearXNG (its address, for example https://searx.example.org), or Brave Search (its subscription token).
  • With None, FluxAgent has no web_search: it searches papers (search_papers) and fetches addresses it knows. search_papers asks export.arxiv.org and api.openalex.org, so list them above (they are suggestions, not allowed by default).
  • The search provider is reached as set here, on any address and port, whatever the hosts above say.
  • The Brave key is stored encrypted and never shown again. Type a new key to replace it, or Remove key. Changes are audited (chat permissions: search key set), without the key.
  • Each answer's fetches are audited as chat web: the hosts and the sizes read, the searches, the refusals.

Limits per answer bound a coding agent's answer: Minutes (default 8, 1 to 60) and Tool calls (default 40, 5 to 400). An answer stopped at a limit keeps what the agent wrote; with nothing written it fails, saying which limit it reached.

Diagram tries (default 5, 0 to 10) is for every answer, FluxAgent's too: how many times a ```diagram block that doesn't draw is sent back to its agent to be fixed before the answer is shown as it is (Chat). 0 never sends one back. Each try is a turn of the agent, under the limits above.

Attached files bound the files a user attaches to a message, in Chat and in a loop's Chat: MB each (default 50, 1 to 2048) and Files a message (default 10, 1 to 50). Any type is kept as it is: in the user's workbench (uploads/) or with the answer (Chat › Attached files).

How Think starts in each composer is each agent's and FluxAgent's own: thinking by default, in Admin › Runtime › Agents. (A server where Chat's earlier Think on by default was ticked has FluxAgent thinking by default.)

Each answer runs as a loop's Chat answers do: in the sandbox, under the server's limits, with the user's model and agent settings, and the agents offered for Ask (Admin › Runtime › Agents).

Sandbox sets how long a user's chat sandbox is kept idle (minutes, default 30, 0 to 240). A user's answers run in one sandbox, started by their first message and kept between messages, so the next answer starts sooner; it ends once no answer has run in it for this long. Several chats of the user share it, and so do answers written at the same time, under one set of limits. 0 gives each answer a sandbox of its own.

A sandbox is started again when what it is started with changes: these settings (the network beyond the base, its hosts), the sandbox's (limits, network, PATH, the proxy), the agents' and the model's settings, and, when the server restarts, Flux's code or the server's environment. An answer running at that moment is stopped and written again on the new ones, its message kept and one answer kept, saying restarted: the admin changed the chat settings (or the sandbox settings, the proxy, the agents' settings) or restarted: Flux was updated. One the user may no longer have answered ends stopped, saying why. A finished answer is never touched; the next one simply starts on the new settings. The limits per answer and this time apply from the next answer and start nothing again.

docs.title: Sharing
docs.text:
Under Admin › Runtime › Chat, Sharing governs the read-only links users make of a chat, a loop's conversation or a design (Share):

  • Links for anyone (on): off, no one makes a link for anyone, and those already made stop opening (turned on again, they open again). Links for the people signed in to this Flux are not touched.
  • The longest a link for anyone lasts (90 days): 1, 7, 30 or 90 days, from when it was made; a link made for longer stops at that age.
  • Each user with links, how many, and Revoke: every link of that user deleted at once.

Links are rate-limited, and a link that does not open looks the same whatever the reason. The page is built with the maker's rights as they are then, so a lost right, a deleted chat or loop, a disabled user stop it at once. Viewing as a user cannot make, copy or revoke a link. The audit's Shared links group lists each link made and revoked, the revocations by an admin, these settings, and each open by someone signed in.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variables apply in order: the server's (Admin › Runtime › Agents › All agents), the user's (Account), each project the loop is linked into, in the loop's order -- its first project wins (Groups › Variables) --, the loop's (Settings › Preferences). Secrets are stored encrypted. The sandbox's own variables, PATH, HOME and the model settings cannot be set this way.

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
Admin › Server › Version says which code the server runs and updates it. Updates follow main and are fast-forward only.

  • The head is a row of five tiles, as the Overview's top row (five across, then three, two and one on narrower screens):
