  • Running: the commit the server started on -- its short hash -- and its subject's first line (cut short; the whole on hover).
  • Update: "Up to date", or "3 commits behind origin/main" in amber with Update to its commit, with what it follows and when it was checked ("origin/main · checked 2 min ago"); the refresh tool at its label's end is Check now. It says too when an update is queued (with Cancel), when an environment is building or failed to build, when the check failed or main has diverged, and just after an update. Its tooltip, and Update's dialog, say how the server restarts.
  • Up: how long the server has run ("57 min"), and since when.
  • Checkout: the branch (amber off main) with clean or how many files changed (listed on hover), and the clone's path.
  • Nix: the toolchain's locked revisions. Under the system service the prepared environment the server started on, and the previous one, are on hover; a line says when one is building or failed.

Under the row, what does not fit a tile: when the checkout has moved since the server started (with the restart command), documents waiting for a run's end, a check that failed, a build and the end of its output, a diverged main, then the commits behind (what their migration would do is on Old data). - Updates: opening this tab runs git fetch origin main in the server's clone when a check is due -- none made yet, a day after the last (an hour after one that failed) -- in the background at the lowest priority, and lists the commits behind origin/main. A main that has commits of its own has diverged and cannot be updated. The tab opens at once with what was last found, saying when ("checked 3 h ago"); a spinner shows while a check, or a read of the checkout, runs behind it, and the tab redraws when it ends. Check now (the refresh tool on the Update tile) checks at once (seconds; longer on a machine behind a proxy); pressed while a check runs, it waits for that one. A check that fails (no network) keeps the last good one -- its list and its Update button -- and says when and why it failed. The checkout itself (its commit, branch and changed files) is read again in the background when its HEAD, a ref or its index moved, or when the tab is opened a minute after the last read; Update and Roll back always look at the checkout as it is. - Documents (Server › Old data, while commits are behind): a dry run of flux task migrate over every loop's documents, by origin/main's code when it can run here: which documents would change and which need a hand. Nothing is written. A document that names an agent an admin added (Admin › Runtime › Agents) loads as it does for its runs: the dry run, the migration after an update and Admin › Server › Old data › Migrate all know the server's added agents. - Old documents also offers a rewrite no update makes on its own: a document that still names the boxes the older way (orchestrate, generate, test, select, feedback, and Search's search) is listed, and Migrate (or Migrate all, or flux task migrate --write) writes the Graph's names (search, design, check, choose, notes, and params) in place, its comments and order kept. It is only an offer: a document left as it is loads, starts and runs exactly the same, and a rewritten one is the same loop (nothing is measured or started again). - Update is refused off main, with changes in the checkout, or when main has diverged. Updates never stop running loops: they finish on the version they started on, so no loop is stopped or waited for. After the fast-forward the server restarts. When it starts on the new code it first migrates every idle loop's documents: a document is written only when it loads, and the original is kept as <file>.orig. A running loop's documents are migrated when its run ends (or just before its next start); the tab lists them as waiting. A loop started while the checkout had changes holds an update until it ends; the tab names it. - The environment first: under the service units, when an update changes Flux's toolchain, Update builds its environment first, in the background. The checkout and the server are not touched meanwhile. The update is queued: the tab says "Building the environment for …" and follows the build, and the History lists it. Once the environment is built, the update is applied (fast-forward, the environment made current, the restart). A failed build moves nothing: the queued update is dropped, and the tab shows the end of Nix's output. A queued update builds its environment ahead in the same way, so the switch is quick. A code-only update needs no build and goes at once, as before. A rollback reuses the previous environment that is kept, or builds it first in the same way. - Roll back returns to the commit the last update came from, as long as the checkout is still where that update left it. It is refused with changes in the checkout, or while a loop runs on the checkout itself. Documents that update migrated and nobody changed since are put back from their .orig; a renamed one is listed for a hand. A running loop's are put back when its run ends, as above. Then the server restarts. - Old data (Server › Old data, under the loops' old documents and the dry run): whether this server still holds data of older formats that a future Flux will no longer read, checked without changing anything. Today nothing is left to look for: the card says No legacy code waits on a check now: there is nothing to look for. A document or record older than this Flux reads is refused where it is opened, naming the Flux that still brings it up (below). - Records after an update: a loop's record has a version. The first time a newer Flux writes to a record -- the loop's next start, or Compact and check, which opens every loop's record at rest weekly -- it brings the record up once, keeping a copy beside it; every row, decision and rejection stays as it was. A running loop's record is left until its run ends; one that cannot be brought up is left as it was and said. - Older backups, exports and records: this Flux reads records from version 7 on and documents and loop files from the format of Nov 12, 2026 on. An older one -- a backup from before, an old export, another server's record -- is refused with the commit that still brings it up: open it with Flux 9957e3728 (a checkout of that commit, or a server on it), import or start it there so its record and documents come up (Compact and check, or Admin › Server › Old data), export the loop again, and import the new file here. Nothing older is converted here, and nothing is guessed. A document saying a key of an older document is refused naming the key and the Flux that says what became of it; open it there, fix it, and export it again. Its record's designs and measurements stay readable. - History: who, when, from and to, and the result of each update, queued update, migration (at the start, or "after its run"), document put back, and rollback, also in the audit trail.

The system service ends itself after an update and systemd starts the new code; no sudo is involved. A server started by hand (development) says to restart it, and it has no prepared environment: an update moves the checkout at once.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: Chat, in the top bar, is a conversation with an agent or FluxAgent that belongs to no loop. Ask it about your loops, a paper, an idea; let it write a script or keep notes for next time. It is there when an admin gives it to you (Admin › Runtime › Chat).

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
Your chats are in a slim rail at the left and the open conversation is in the middle. The Settings panel opens at the right from the sliders at the top right (the head's toolbar: a loop's or a project's conversation has the open icon before them, to the loop or the project).

The rail's top row has three tabs: Chats, your own conversations, Loops, the conversations held on your loops (Loop chats), and Projects, the conversations held on your projects (Project chats); then the + button and Close. Click a tab, or focus one and use the arrow keys (Home and End too). A link to a chat opens Chats, a link to a loop's conversation opens Loops inside that loop, a project's Projects inside that project; otherwise the rail shows the tab you last chose in this browser. A tab with a question waiting for you inside shows the dot.

  • + starts a chat where you are: on Chats a chat of your own; inside a loop or a project, a chat on it (when you may ask there). On the Loops or Projects list, with none open, it is greyed: pointing at it says to open a loop (a project) first, and clicking it puts you in the search box.
  • Chats lists them under a Search box (it keeps the chats whose title has the words), under Pinned first, then Today, This week and Earlier, each a one-line card with how long ago it last moved at its right, the open one outlined -- the cards a loop's or a project's conversations have too. A chat whose answer is still being written shows a spinner in place of its age; one whose answer ends in a question for you shows a dot in the agent's colour (pointing at it says who asks and what), and so does the top bar's Chat while any of your chats waits on you. Close hides the rail and the menu button (three lines) brings it back. On a phone the rail opens over the conversation from the menu button.
  • A chat's more menu (three dots), shown on hover and for the open chat, has Pin (or Unpin), Rename and Delete. A pin is yours alone: it keeps the chat under Pinned whenever it last moved. Deleting removes its messages and answers; the workbench stays.
  • Open any chat to go on with it: each answer reads the conversation before it.

Your messages are on the right and answers under them. Under each answer one line names the agent and how long it took, and Thinking & commands (the terminal icon at the line's end) shows how the answer was made, as in a loop's Chat. When an answer writes or changes files in the workbench, they are listed under it (↳ designs/adder8_csel4.sv). Click one to open it in the panel.

Answers are drawn as Markdown. A code block shows its text exactly as written, and Copy (two sheets) in its corner copies that text. Its fences work as in CommonMark: a block opened with ```` (four backticks) or ~~~ stays one block even when it holds ``` fences, so an agent can hand you a whole Markdown file to paste. A block still being written runs to the end of the answer.

Pictures show in the answer. ![caption](/workbench/plots/speed.png) shows a picture from the workbench, and in a loop's or a project's chat ![caption](library/figs/x.png) shows one from its library. The picture is no wider than the column. Click it to open it in the viewer; Open (a new tab) and Download are on its corner when you point at it. A link to a workbench picture keeps its link and gets a small preview under its line. A ```svg block is drawn as a picture, with Fullscreen, Show the source and Copy on it. PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and SVG are shown.

The viewer shows a picture or a drawing over the page, fitted to the window. Zoom with the wheel, a pinch, the head's zoom buttons or the keys + and -; drag to move it; Fit (or 0, or a double click) fits it again; Esc or the close button leaves. In the chat itself a drawing always fits the column's width: nothing scrolls sideways. Anything else is never fetched: an address on the web, a data: or javascript: address, a path outside the workbench or the library, or a file that is not there. It stays as its words and its address, as text.

A ```diagram block is a diagram Flux lays out itself. The agent writes a few lines of YAML that only name the parts and pick a kind. Four are ready-made arrangements: a pipeline (stages in columns, pipeline registers between them, edges going back in lanes under the row), a cycle (steps of equal size in a row, each leading to the next, back edges under it, an optional band under all of them), an architecture (rows of cards and groups of cards, each card a name, a muted line and an icon) or layers (bands stacked top to bottom, a bus joined to every box next to it). The fifth, blocks, composes the same building blocks freely: boxes, stores (memory, a cache, a database), states, start and end dots, buses, and groups inside groups. Flux places them from the edges ("A -> B": B after A, along the flow, right or down) and from a few place: lines the edges don't say ("Registers under Execute"); a group may set its own flow, or lay its blocks out as a row, a column or a grid. An edge that closes a loop runs back round the outside; the longest chain runs on one straight line, its branches beside it; a chain too long for the column wraps into rows, each turning back under the one before; a bus runs across the flow, so flowing right it stands up. The same kind draws a state machine (states, a start dot, an edge from a state back to itself) and a flow chart (a question is a diamond, @decision, its answers the labels of the edges leaving it, by its corners). Two kinds are not boxes and arrows: timing, a waveform strip (a clock and signals over cycles, one word a cycle: 0 1 . x A0 z, a value of several words quoted, phases named over their cycles, arrows from one signal's edge to another's: valid@2 -> ready@4: handshake), and memory, a memory map (address ranges stacked, highest at the top, each with its size and its first and last address, the holes between them said, a region's own regions drawn inside it); a strip may leave cycles out (~12), run a gated clock (c) and group its signals under headings. A strip also draws a plan: tasks over weeks, each a bar, the months over them. Two more: sequence, who talks to whom (participants with their lifelines, messages one under another, replies dotted, frames such as alt and loop), and register, a register map (each register a row at its offset, its fields by bit, reserved bits narrow). The last, network, draws a network's topology by its name and size (topology: mesh 8x8, a torus, a ring, a tree, a fat-tree, a butterfly, a Clos, a hypercube, a dragonfly), a route computed or given as a highlighted path, and blocks attached beside a mesh's nodes (attach: {R00: [MC0 @storage]}). A sankey shows amounts that split and flow, each written From -> To: amount: every flow a band as wide as its amount, every part a bar with its name and its total beside it, the parts ordered so the bands cross as little as they can; its bands take their source's role (or branch's) colour, or, once any part has a tone (Refused @bad, Decided @ok), the tone of where they end; percent: source or percent: total adds shares. On a phone it runs top to bottom, and it is drawn again for the column's width when that changes. Under any kind, a range names many parts at once (R00..R33, In0..In7), and an edge's width is a tag (@wide, @narrow) said in the legend. In blocks, a block may name its ports (an edge meets Adder.a), A, B -> X, Y is one bundle through a junction (as is a crossbar written edge by edge), a start dot says its name, a state machine of six to fourteen states going round is drawn as a tall ring (a column folded in two; flow: down keeps the column), and layout: ring puts states round a wide rectangle. Under any kind, legend: says what a tone, a role or a dotted line means. A part may say its role -- @compute, @storage, @interconnect, @io, @control or @external -- and is drawn as a soft tint of that role's hue, the same hue for the role everywhere in Flux (a store, a bus, and a cpu, db or memory icon have theirs without saying); @accent highlights what the answer is about, on as many parts as that is, and a box's outline is drawn plainly enough to read in either theme. A cycle, say:

kind: cycle
title: The loop
steps: [Search: What to try, Design: Make it, Check: Verify it, Measure: Evaluate it, Choose: Select it]
back:
  - Check -> Design: Failed check
legend: {bad: a failed check goes back}

Flux places every box on that kind's grid (or, for blocks, in even ranks along the flow), sizes it so its text fits, routes the edges at right angles around the boxes and puts each label where nothing else is, so the drawing is never too wide for the column and nothing overlaps. A blocks drawing too wide flowing right is drawn flowing down; too wide either way, its error names the widest group and what to change. Text widths come from a fixed table, so the same YAML draws the same everywhere. It is drawn like an svg block, as a picture in the page's colours with the same tools, and drawn again in dark. Save to the workbench writes the drawing as plots/<name>.svg and its YAML beside it as plots/<name>.diagram.yaml. A block with a mistake is not drawn: its errors take the drawing's place, each on its own line and saying where and what ("edge 3: unknown box 'Excute' (did you mean Execute?)"), with the YAML folded under them. Ask to fix puts a message asking the agent to fix it in the message box, without sending it.

Flux checks each diagram block before the answer is shown, in Chat and in a loop's Chat, whoever answers. A block that doesn't draw is sent back to the same agent with its errors, to be corrected. Until the block draws, this goes on up to 5 times (Diagram tries in Admin › Runtime › Chat; 0 turns it off). Meanwhile the answer's row says Fixing the diagram (2 of 5)…. A block that draws takes the failing one's place, and the earlier attempts are not shown. After the last try the answer is shown as it is: the block's errors where its drawing would be, and under it the line Flux sent this diagram back to be fixed 5 times; it still does not draw. Once every block draws, one that reads badly -- a name cut to fit, labels numbered for want of room, two edges on one line, a label nearer another edge than its own, a graph too dense to read -- is sent back once more with what reads badly; what comes back takes its place only if it draws and reads no worse. Nothing in a diagram block is ever drawn on top of something else. An edge that would run through a box goes round it. When a label finds no clear spot, the diagram is laid out again with more room. A label that still has none becomes a small number on its line, and a key under the drawing gives each number, its words and its edge. A pipeline too wide for the column has its names wrapped, its gaps narrowed and a stage's boxes stacked. If it is still too wide, it is drawn wider and shown fitted to the column; open it full size to read it. A diagram that can't be drawn clean even so is not drawn: its errors say where and what to change ("too many labelled edges in the EX1 column ... move details to a table, or split the diagram"). A block still being written shows as its code until its fence closes. Its names are drawn as text: nothing of the block becomes markup.

A ```figure block is a figure of cards and containers written in HTML, for a drawing no kind of diagram block fits (a floor plan, say), with a container's cards in a grid, each a title, a muted line and an icon, and arrows between them. Its root <figure width="760" height="534"> gives the size it is drawn at. It is drawn like an svg block, as a picture in the page's colours with the same tools, and drawn again in dark. Flux's own classes stand in for colours and layout (card, group, group dashed, the tones, tint-1 to tint-6, grid cols-3, an icon by name with <i data-icon="cpu"></i>, an <svg class="wires"> for its arrows). Before it is drawn, everything that could run or reach out is removed: scripts, event handlers, frames, images, forms, links and any url() or @import that is not the figure's own.

A ```chart block is a chart Flux draws itself, with the same marks, axes, colours and hover as a loop's Results charts, light or dark. The block is JSON:

{"type": "scatter", "title": "Area against fmax",
 "x": {"label": "MHz"}, "y": {"label": "um2", "log": false},
 "series": [{"name": "sweep", "points": [[800, 30], [1200, 18]]},
            {"loop": "bob/mul8", "x": "fmax_mhz", "y": "area_um2"}]}

type is line (the default), scatter or bar (whose x may be a category). An axis may say "better": "lower" (or "higher"): on a line's y the best so far is drawn as a step line through the points that count; on both axes of a scatter each series' front is drawn as a dashed staircase, and the axes say which way is better. "goal": 2 on an axis draws a dashed line there ("≤ 2"). A written point may carry tags after its x, as text: ["4 @failed", 2.3] is drawn hollow and never counts as the best or on the front, @decision is drawn orange with its ring, and a colour (@accent, @ok, @warn, @bad) rings the point (on a bar chart of one series, it colours that bar and greys the rest). A series is its own points, or a loop's metrics: loop is owner/loop, y a metric, x either design (the default: the designs in the order measured, as Results' Improvement by design) or a second metric, with an optional stage (else each design's deepest) and part (in a record from before one loop was one design, else the whole). A loop's series is read live, with your rights, from the same answer Results' graphs read, and drawn again when the loop's results change. It is drawn as Results draws it: a rejected design or one measured before a change to its stage is not drawn, a baseline is not a point, the decision has its orange ring and a design starred by hand is an orange point. Click one of its points to select it: the orange diamond, its numbers and Open in Results, which opens that design there. A loop you cannot read says "owner/loop: not available" under the chart and draws nothing of it, whoever wrote the block. At most 8 series, 500 points in a written series, and a loop's newest 5000 designs. Show the source, Copy and Fullscreen are on the chart's head, and on a line or scatter chart Zoom to an area: turned on, drag over the chart to zoom to that area (as on the Results graphs; a right-click goes back one zoom, a double-click shows it whole), turned off the whole chart again. A block that is not JSON, has a field not listed here, or a value of another kind stays as its code, with one muted line saying why ("Not a chart: colour is no field of a chart."); a block still being written stays as its code until its fence closes. Nothing of the block becomes markup: its names and labels are drawn as text.

An svg block is drawn in the page's colours too. currentColor and text with no colour of its own take the page's ink, and a few classes stand in for colours: box (the surface with its line), edge (a muted line), label (text), and the tones ink, muted, line, surface, accent, ok, warn, bad (box accent stresses one box, edge accent one path), and six soft tints box tint-1 to box tint-6 (pale in light, deep in dark) for steps of equal rank. They are drawn again when you switch between light and dark. A colour the agent wrote itself stays as written. Where the chat has a workbench you may write in, Save to the workbench on a drawn block writes it to plots/<name>.svg there and says the path. An svg block is saved with both themes' colours (the dark ones apply where the viewer prefers dark) and its classes as written, and so is a figure.

What you see of a drawing depends on your account. People with the Internals permission get the svg, figure and diagram blocks as described above. Anyone else, and anyone who opens a shared link, gets each one as a finished picture, drawn by the server in the page's theme and drawn again when you switch between light and dark. It has only Fullscreen and Save image: its source is not in the page, not under Copy, and not in what the server sends. Chart blocks are the same for everyone.

Flux no longer draws Mermaid. A ```mermaid block in an older answer shows as code to a server admin; anyone else sees a short note in its place. A new answer draws such a figure as a diagram block.

The page never runs what an agent wrote: pictures, drawings and diagrams are shown as images, which run no script and fetch nothing.

The message box stays at the bottom. Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line (Ctrl+Enter and ⌘+Enter send too). The agent is picked inside the box, from the agents offered for Ask, with your own agent settings (Models and agents). A small ! beside it means the agent is not ready (its connection untested, failed, or changed since its test); click it for Test and Set up.

Think, beside the agent, asks for a slower, more considered answer: FluxAgent reasons before it answers, its thinking shown live in Thinking & commands; a coding agent works at its effort for thinking, and off, at its effort for not (by default its own, and its kind's lowest). Think follows the agent picker: each agent starts as the admin set it (thinking by default) -- every agent on, FluxAgent off unless said -- and your browser remembers your own choice for each agent. A loop's Chat has the same switch.

While Think is on, Effort beside it picks how hard a coding agent reasons for this message: the levels its kind takes (Claude Code low to max, Codex and OpenCode minimal to their top), default its effort for thinking. It comes first -- before Think, the loop's box and the admin's default -- and your browser remembers it per agent.

FluxAgent has an Effort too, shown whether Think is on or not, from low to max: higher effort thinks, works longer and writes longer answers. default is its effort for Think as set in Admin › Runtime › Agents.

docs.title: Attached files
docs.text:
Attach files to a message with the paperclip beside the agent, by dropping them on the conversation, or by pasting (a screenshot too, named pasted--.png). Each is sent at once: a chip above the box shows its name and size (its progress while it goes), and Remove (its cross) takes it off. The files go with your next message and show as chips under it; click one to open it (a text highlighted, a picture shown) or download it. Any type is kept as it is. The admin sets the largest file and how many go with one message, 50 MB and 10 unless set otherwise (Admin › Runtime › Chat).

Where they are kept: with the chat's workbench on, in the workbench's uploads/ (kept across your chats, listed under Settings › Workbench); with it off, with the answer, in its folder's attached/. A name already taken gets a number, notes (2).md: nothing is overwritten.

A coding agent opens the files with its own tools, pictures too where it reads images. FluxAgent reads text files, PDFs, and Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files; it cannot see a picture or read another binary file, and says so when the answer depends on one.

In a loop's Chat (the loop's page, or a loop chat here) files attach the same way, for whoever may ask about the loop: for someone who may edit the loop, with the Workbench on (below), in the loop's Chat workbench's uploads/; otherwise in your own folder until the question is sent, then with its answer. Never in the loop's own folders. To put a file in the loop's library, use the loop's Files upload, or accept a chat's proposal.

A coding agent's answer has time and tool-call limits the admin sets (Admin › Runtime › Chat).

Your answers run in a sandbox of your own, kept between messages for a while (the admin sets how long, Admin › Runtime › Chat): the next answer starts sooner. When the admin changes what it runs with, or Flux is updated, an answer being written is written again on the new settings; its row says restarted: … and why, your message is not sent twice.

One answer is written at a time in a chat. Your message shows at once (Sending…). While the answer starts, the row says Starting…, then Starting OpenCode… (the agent's name). That takes a few seconds, more on a busy server, and is never an error. Once the agent works, the row shows what it is doing now (its latest command, or thinking…) with Stop. Only an answer that ended without answering shows a red notice. An answer stopped after the agent wrote it is kept, marked Stopped before it ended, with its question if it asked one. An answer that fails says why (a rate limit, say) with Retry (its circling arrow), which sends the same message again, to the same agent. When you open a chat, the box starts with the agent of its last answer.

docs.title: Loop chats
docs.text:
The rail's Loops tab has a card for each loop you can read (yours and those shared with you) that has conversations, the latest first: its name (and its owner's, for another's loop), how many chats, and under them the last conversation's title and how long ago it moved. A loop you may ask about but with no conversation yet has the same card, greyed, without a count, after the others: click it all the same to start one. Find a loop or a chat above the cards keeps the loops whose name has the words, or one of whose conversations has them in its title (the card then shows that conversation). A loop with a conversation being answered shows a spinner on its card; a running loop whose agent asks a question you may answer (you may edit the loop) shows the dot, as its Chat button does, and so does the Loops tab.

Click a loop to go into it: where the search was, the rail then shows ‹ (back to the loops) and a Search box, which keeps the loop's conversations whose title has the words (the dot at its end while the loop's agent asks you); then its conversations as Chats lists yours -- Pinned first, then Today, This week, Earlier --, each a one-line card titled by its first question with its age at the right, a spinner in place of the age on one being answered, the open one outlined; + starts a new chat on the loop (when you may ask about it). Nobody's conversations are grouped by person. A link to a loop's conversation opens Chat on the Loops tab inside its loop.

  • Click a conversation to open it in the middle, with the loop's name as a small tag in its head. It reads as a chat does: Thinking & commands under each answer, Stop while one is being written, and the loop agent's open question on its card while the loop runs. Write in the box to continue it -- also after an answer that ended without answering (stopped, interrupted, failed): the next answer reads the conversation so far, that turn said unanswered, and why. A stopped answer says Stopped and by whom; one whose process was interrupted from elsewhere says so. A message sent while an answer is still being written is refused with One answer at a time per loop, your text kept in the box. The loop's Chat panel keeps the conversation you had open when the page is reloaded. The answer comes from the loop's own Chat, so the same rules apply: one answer at a time per loop, an agent that reads the loop and changes nothing, and only people allowed to ask about the loop can ask there. Someone you shared the loop with without Ask can read its conversations but not ask, and a conversation asked privately (by someone who may not edit the loop) is shown only to them.
  • Settings shows what it uses: the loop, read-only, and, if you may edit the loop, its Chat workbench, with the tree and the file viewer of Settings › Workbench here.
  • Open in NAME opens the loop's page with its Chat panel on that conversation.
  • A conversation's more menu has Pin (Unpin), yours alone -- the conversation itself, and what others see, unchanged --, and Delete for someone who may edit the loop, and for the asker of a conversation only they see. Loop conversations have no Rename: each is titled by its first question.

docs.title: Project chats
docs.text:
A project keeps conversations too, read by its own members (see Groups: someone who sees the project only through its group finds neither its chats nor its card here) and asked by those of them who may edit, curate or manage it. The project's page has Chat in its head: it opens this page on the Projects tab inside the project, on a new conversation. The tab works as Loops does: a card per project you see (its title and its group, how many chats, the last one's title and age; greyed for one you may start one on), Find a project or a chat, a project clicked to go into it -- ‹ (back to the projects) and a Search box, a line under them with its accepted entries, those to review (for its curators) and its loops (12 entries · To review: 3 · 4 loops), its conversations Pinned and then by day --, + a new chat on it, Open (the project) in a conversation's head.

The answering agent reads the project, read-only, and changes nothing: its library (flux library), its accepted knowledge (flux library), its topics, and its loops you may ask about (flux loop summary, results and the rest, as a loop's chat reads its loop). What the project and those loops hide from their agents stays hidden here: what a project's chat proposes is what loops read. An answer runs on your own model and agent settings, with the sandbox's base network and no web tools, as a new chat starts (Settings); one answer at a time per project.

It may end with proposals, each a card under the answer, as Actions are: Knowledge an entry (its topic, its insight in a line, its analysis, the designs of the project's loops that prove it), which Accept sends to the project's To review for its curators -- never straight into the list, even yours; Topic a new topic; Library files of the project's Chat workbench copied into its library. Whoever may ask answers them, as themselves, each checked again then; a viewer sees them, not the buttons. The project's Chat workbench is that of a loop's Chat workbench, shared by its chats, for those who may ask (and the admin's Workbench). An archived project's chats stay readable; nobody asks in them.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Most answers ask nothing. An agent asks only when it cannot go on without your choice or a value only you know, never to offer more help or to ask permission. The question then ends the answer, shown as a card under it. An answer may ask up to four questions at once; each has a short header, and the headers are chips at the top of the card (✓ Type · Widths · Target, 2 of 3) that move between them. Each question shows

  • its options, one per line: a label, a line on what it means, and Recommended on the one the agent would pick (listed first); pick one, or any for a question that takes several;
  • named values it needs, such as a width or a library, as text, number or list fields;
  • Other, for anything else in your own words (for a free question, the only box).

1–8 pick an option and Enter goes on from anywhere in the card: to the next question, then Send. Next › and Back move too. Send stays off until something is answered; in a card of several, a question left blank is the agent's to decide. You decide lets the agent choose them all and say what it chose.

Your answer goes as one message, to the agent that asked (whichever agent is picked in the box), written plainly, a block per question:

Answer to: Which adder families should adder16's generator try?
- choice: carry-select
- choice: Kogge-Stone

Answer to: Which cell library?
- choice: sky130
keep it small

Your message then shows the answers as chips (Families carry-select, Library sky130), and the card shrinks to what was asked. A chat waiting on your answer is marked ? in the rail. Typing a message in the box instead also answers the question. After You decide, the next answer reads that you delegated the choice, and decides.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An agent never changes your loops itself. When you ask for a change, or one clearly helps, it proposes it, and each proposal is a card under the answer: what it does and in which loop, why, and a preview. Accept makes it, as you, with the same checks and the same audit trail as the page that does it by hand; Reject drops it. Each proposal is answered on its own; nothing is made without your click. The card then says Done (and what was done), Rejected, or Refused with why. The next answer reads what became of each proposal. A proposal that would copy a file the loop hides from its agents -- its text, or a workbench file to add, the same as that file -- is refused, saying which file.

Kind What it does Its preview Library copies files from your workbench into the loop's library/ (papers, notes its agents read) each file, its size and where it goes; replaces when it overwrites one Document writes a text file (.md, .txt, .rst) under the loop's library/, where its agents read it; a lesson (what a run taught) goes under library/lessons/ the text, or the change to the file it replaces Note sends a note to the running loop, as its Notes box does the note Hidden from AI hides paths from the loop's agents, or shows them again (Hidden from AI) the hidden paths before and after: each still hidden with its lock, one shown again struck through Idea adds an idea to the loop's notebook its title, hypothesis and test Queue queues an idea for testing, or takes it off the queue the idea and its place in line Merge merges ideas that say the same thing, as the notebook's cleanup does (it can be undone) the idea kept and those merged into it Design note pins a note on a design, shown in Results' design detail and in Live's inspector the design, its numbers, the note Reference marks a design as a reference for comparison the design and its numbers Settings changes settings of the loop's problem document -- its budget, who works a box, its model, anything the Configure page sets -- saved as the Configure page saves each setting now and proposed; when it takes effect Problem document replaces the text of the loop's problem document (its flow, checks, measurements), saved as Direct edit saves the change, line by line; when it takes effect Measure again measures a design again (a flaky timeout, a tool that failed), as Results' Reject with Measure again does the design, its numbers, the stages, and when it is measured

A note on a design and a reference are for reading only: the loop's decisions, its baseline and its search do not change. A loop reads its problem document when it starts: a Settings or Problem document change reaches a running loop at its next start (Restart starts it again after the pass it is on), and the card says so. Either is proposed only when the document would still load (as Check and flux task check load it); one that would not is refused with the loader's words, and one proposed on a document changed since is refused on Accept, nothing written. Saving settings drops the document's comments, as the Configure page's save does. Until a design is measured again its numbers count as rejected: shown, never chosen; a running loop measures it before its next pass, a loop at rest starts a run of its own. Files the agent brings (a paper it downloaded) go to your workbench first, and the proposal names them there.

The server checks every proposal, when the answer ends and again when you accept it: a loop you own or one shared with you with Edit, not archived. A loop you may only view or ask about gets no proposals at all. If Chat can't make changes for you at all, it says so instead. Then, the files in your workbench, never an overwrite unless the proposal says so, the problem document only as Settings or Problem document. An answer proposes at most 10 changes.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The panel's Uses says what this chat's answers may use:

Switch On Loops The agent may read your loops: your own, and those shared with you with Ask. The line says how many. Workbench The agent may read and write your workbench. Network The agent may reach the hosts the admin allows for chat, or any host when the admin opens it. Off, it has the sandbox's base allowlist only, which agents need to work. The line says which. On, FluxAgent also has its web tools.

The Workbench switch and the tree under it are shown to people with the Internals permission; for anyone else the workbench is on, unseen, and their answers still write it.

A new chat starts with the Workbench on, Loops and Network off and no loop in focus, even where the admin allows them: you turn them on here, for this chat. A switch the admin keeps off is greyed, and its line says why. Make these my defaults has your new chats start with the current switches instead (never a loop in focus); a chat keeps the switches it was made with. Each answer uses the switches as they were when you sent the message.

A loop's chat has no switches: it reads its loop, read-only, with the sandbox's base network and no web tools, and the loop's Chat workbench for one with Edit.

In focus (with Loops on) picks one loop from a list you can search, with your loops under Yours and the others under Shared with you: the answers look at that loop closely, and when an answer about another loop needs more, it suggests putting that loop in focus. With Network on, FluxAgent also fetches pages and papers and searches for them (On the web). A coding agent uses its own web tools, within the network the chat allows.

Under Uses is the workbench (see below). A PDF in it opens in your browser's own PDF viewer, as in Files.

The panel is closed until you open it with the button at the top right (the loop in focus · Settings), and it stays open or closed as you last left it in this browser. Opening a file an answer wrote opens it too. On a wide screen it sits beside the conversation; narrower than about 1360 px it opens over the conversation. On a phone the conversation fills the screen, the menu button opens the chats, and the panel takes the whole screen.

docs.title: On the web
docs.text:
With the chat's Network switched on, FluxAgent has web tools. Off, or not allowed, it has none.

Tool What it does fetch_url Gets a page or a document over HTTP or HTTPS and reads its text: HTML, PDF, EPUB, Office files, plain text. A PDF or other document is saved whole. search_papers Searches arXiv and OpenAlex. Each paper comes with its title, authors, year, venue, the start of its abstract, its DOI and an open-access PDF's address when known. web_search Searches the web, only when the admin set a search provider (Admin › Runtime › Chat).
  • It reaches the hosts the admin allows for chat, or any public host when the admin opened the network; never a private or intranet address. search_papers needs export.arxiv.org and api.openalex.org.
  • A saved file goes to the workbench's uploads/ when the answer has the workbench, otherwise with the answer. An existing file is never replaced: a second copy is paper-2.pdf. To add it to a loop's library, the agent proposes it, and you accept (Actions).
  • It cites the addresses it used, and never puts your data (files, designs, numbers, names) in an address or a query: only the search words go out.
  • Thinking & commands shows each fetch and each search. The audit records the hosts fetched.

docs.title: The workbench
docs.text:
The workbench is one folder for all your chats. Agents keep their tools in tools/, notes in notes/ and drafts in drafts/, so a later chat can use what an earlier one made. Chat does not create or run loops: a loop starts from New loop, and a draft for one (a document, a generator) waits in drafts/. FluxAgent writes here itself; the same way it writes a new loop's files when it is the author in New loop › Agent, there kept to the draft's folder (FluxAgent as the author).

The panel's Workbench shows it as a tree: a folder opens in place, and a file opens in place of the tree, read-only, with Download, Delete and Fullscreen. A text is highlighted as in Files, and a picture (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG) is shown. Workbench, above the file, goes back. Refresh reads it again; it is also read again when an answer ends. Each answer records the workbench files it wrote: those its agent's writing steps name, and any other file made or changed while it ran. When another of your chats was answering at the same time, a file no step of this answer names may be the other's: it is dimmed, changed meanwhile.

A workbench file the answer names is a link that opens it there too: a path in code, as a link's target, or written out as /workbench/... (/workbench/notes/speed.md, workbench/notes/speed.md or notes/speed.md). Only a file there when the answer ended is linked, never a hidden one, a link or a path outside the workbench, nor one in a code block; anything else stays as written. A path in your own message is plain text.

docs.title: A loop's Chat workbench
docs.text:
A loop's chats share a workbench of their own, the Chat workbench: one folder for every conversation on that loop, whoever asked. It is not the loop's own workbench/, which its agents use while it runs: the loop's runs never see the Chat workbench, and the chats never write the loop's. The answering agent keeps tools in tools/, notes in notes/, drafts in drafts/ and attached files in uploads/, as here. The files an answer wrote are listed under it, dimmed when another answer ran meanwhile, and open here, in the loop conversation's Settings: Workbench, the same tree as Settings › Workbench; so do the Chat workbench's files an answer names. In the loop's own Chat panel they open this page on that conversation, the file shown.

It is for those who may edit the loop: its owner, someone it is shared with with Edit, an admin. They read it, their answers write it, and they can delete a file. Someone who may only view or ask about the loop has none of it: their answers get no workbench, the files they attach stay with their answer, and the files other answers wrote are neither listed nor linked for them. Losing Edit takes it away at once. The admin's Workbench (Admin › Runtime › Chat, per group and user) governs it too: a person without it neither sees it nor has their answers write it. A person without the Internals permission (Admin › People › Users) has no workbench to browse, here or in Chat: no tree, no list of the files an answer wrote. Their answers still use it, and a file an answer links or a file they attached opens from that link. It is made on first use, and moves, is renamed and is deleted with the loop; deleting a conversation, or resetting the loop, leaves it. A project's Chat workbench is kept apart from the library and knowledge its loops read: it moves, is renamed and is deleted with the project.

docs.title: Share
docs.text:
Share, the first tool of a conversation's head (a chat's, a loop's in Chat and in the loop's Chat drawer), makes a read-only link to it. The dialog asks:

  • What it shows: the whole conversation, or one answer (its question and answer alone).
  • Who can open it: people signed in to this Flux, or anyone with the link.
  • Expires: in 1, 7 (the default), 30 or 90 days; never only for a link for the signed-in. A link for anyone lasts as long as the admin allows at most (90 days unless Admin › Runtime › Chat › Sharing says less).

Make link shows the link with Copy; under it, this conversation's links, each with Copy (any time later) and Revoke (the next open fails). Account › Shared links lists every link you made.

The link opens a page of its own, with no app around it: Flux's mark, read-only, who shared it, then the conversation. It is live: the page is made from the conversation each time the link is opened, so an answer written after the link was made shows too, and nothing is copied when you make it. An answer reads as in Chat (its code, tables, its diagrams drawn from its own text); a picture of the workbench it shows (![…](/workbench/plots/x.png)) is shown, served through the link (only that picture). Any other workbench file it names, and the files attached to a message, are their names alone, marked not shared. Never in a link: the workbench, attached files, Thinking & commands, proposals, the loop, the library, settings.

  • A loop's conversation needs the Share right on the loop (its owner has it); without it there is no Share tool. The link shows your own questions and their answers alone: another person's question is left out and counted ("1 question of another person is not shared"); a private question of someone else is not even counted. Losing the Share right stops the link (it opens again if the right comes back).
  • Hidden files (Hidden from AI): a conversation that quotes a file its loop hides from its agents is not shared; when you share with anyone a conversation that reads such a loop, the dialog says so.
  • A link that does not open -- revoked, expired, its chat or loop deleted, its sharer disabled, the right lost, links for anyone turned off -- shows one page, This link does not open, the same for every reason. A link for the signed-in, opened without a session, leads to the sign-in page and back.

The page asks search engines not to index it, and nothing of the app is served with it.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: A loop's Files tab shows its folder four ways, each a view in the row under the tabs with its count: Workbench, Library, Inputs and All files. Every file of the loop is in one of the first three, or in what they leave out: out/ and runs/ (what runs write), the document (its place is Settings › Problem) and what All files hides unless asked. On a phone each view lists first; a file opens on its own, with ‹ Back to the list.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text:
This view is for people with the Internals permission (Admin › People › Users); for anyone else the workbench is not listed or opened, and a Full export leaves it out.

The agents' own folder, workbench/: a search over names and first lines, then Overview (the setup's workbench/README.md, opened first when there is one), Tools (five shown, then "+N" and a chevron, its title "N more"; Less folds them back), the notes by age (*Today**, Yesterday, This week, and Earlier folded with its count and a clock turning back; a row one line: the name, its first line cut short, its age), Numbered notes -- notes named one name and a number (draft1297-…, orch-pass12-…), three or more of a name, folded into one row with their count and the newest's age -- and Other for the rest. Each row is a file's name, its age and its first line; it opens in the same viewer as All files (edit, save, download, Actions).

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
What the agents can read: the loop's own library/, one row a document (its kind -- PDF, MD, SRC for a folder of source code -- its title, its pages, lines or files), ✓ digested once it has been summarised, not relevant when its digest says it does not bear on the problem. N of M digested sums it up; a search filters the list; ↻ reads it again and {} shows the digests. + Add a document opens the uploader: files and folders dropped or chosen go into library/ (a paper as library/paper.pdf, a folder as library/<folder>/, a single .zip unpacked there). Each project library the loop reads (library/<project>@<group>/) follows as its own group, read-only (a lock), the open icon opening the project's Library tab. Digests of files outside the library (the loop's notes, its knowledge files) are listed under Also digested, and so are the digests of files no longer there: a paper deleted or moved, or one of a project library the loop no longer reads.

A digest stays until you delete it: open its document (or its row under Also digested) and use Delete digest (the bin) on its head; the group's head deletes those whose files are gone (Delete N digests, Delete all N when the whole group is). Each asks first. A digest whose file is still there is made again the next time the loop reads its library, and the confirm says so. A running loop need not be stopped. Deleting needs Edit on the loop, and is in the audit log.

Open a document and it shows beside the list: what it is, Download and Raw, Actions on your own, then its Digest (who made it) and its Outline -- its sections with their pages or lines, as flux library outline reads them. A folder shows its files.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Everything else the loop was given: In the problem -- the files and folders the document names beside it (its golden model, the files of its commands, the files its knowledge library lists), as the loop's own check reads them -- then Skills (a skills/ folder, or the one the document's skills names) and Other. A folder whose files all belong to one group is one row; a lock marks what is hidden from AI. Its foot names the document and links Settings › Problem.

docs.title: Large folders
docs.text:
The views stay quick on a loop of hundreds of thousands of files. A big workbench folder is one row, data/ with 12345 files and its newest change; it opens as a folder. A list shows the newest first in the workbench and counts the rest -- "102 more · All files". The counts in the sub-row are of every file. Links, other file systems mounted in the loop, dot folders, __pycache__ and what .gitignore ignores are not walked. In All files, a folder opened shows the files that fill the viewer at once and the rest as you scroll to its end ("100 of 12345 entries" while more are left).

The configurator's Files (under Prompt) and its Library's list fold big folders the same way: click one and its files are listed in its place. library/, skills/ and each skill's own folder are never folded, so every paper and each SKILL.md stays listed. The loop's problems (problem.yaml and every NAME.problem.yaml at its top) are not inputs, and are not listed.

docs.title: All files
docs.text:
The folder as it is: the document, your scripts, library/, the workbench and what Flux writes (out/, runs/). Open a file to view, edit, save or download it; Raw and Fullscreen show the whole of it. Drop files or folders onto the list, or use Files (the upload arrow) and Folder (a folder with a plus).

  • Actions on a file or folder: Rename, Move, Delete, and Hide from AI (or Show to AI), which adds the path to knowledge.hidden (Knowledge, skills, hidden paths). A hidden file or folder has a lock before its name, in the list and in the open item's head, and no pill or word beside it. Its tooltip says hidden from AI, or which folder or pattern hides it.
  • A name with @ at the top of library/ is refused (when adding, renaming or moving): that is where a project's library appears, library/<project>@<group>/.
  • Under library/, after the loop's own folders, each project the loop is linked into shows its library, in the loop's project order, marked project · read-only (a link to the project's Library tab): browse and download it here, change it on the project's page (see Reading the library). You see the projects whose link you see (a global project's only to its owner, admins and the project's keepers), and open those whose library you view.
  • The loop's .gitignore files hide what they ignore; .gitignore'd and dot files lists them greyed.
  • A picture (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) is shown; an SVG stays text, to edit. A PDF opens in your browser's own PDF viewer, filling the viewer, with Download, Open in a new tab and Fullscreen on its head. The same goes for the Workbench, Library and Inputs views, a project's Library and a Chat workbench. The PDF is shown isolated from the app. Firefox draws it in place; in Chrome and Edge, and in any browser without a PDF viewer (a phone's Chrome), the viewer shows Open (the PDF in a tab of its own) and Download instead. On a phone a large Open stands above the preview.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: A loop's Settings has two parts, Preferences and Problem. Each card of Preferences is drawn as soon as what it shows is read, the others a few grey lines under their title meanwhile.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• Measurements: per metric, whether it is shown, whether it is a main one (in lists and summaries), and whether it shows as change from the baseline. Charts and the decision always use every measurement.
  • Environment variables: the loop's own, over its projects' (its first project's first, each "from project <group> / <title>", Groups › Variables), your account's and the server's; a change reaches it at its next start.
  • Sharing: the member grid of groups and projects (the words): the Owner row fixed on top, then a row a user or a group shared with, a Level (Viewer, Asker, Contributor, Maintainer; Custom a mix) and a box per word: view (runs, log, results, files; always on), ask (ask an agent about it in its Chat; a chat's agent reads it), edit (its files, the document, its settings, notes; accept Chat's proposals for it), run (start, stop, restart, measure again) and share (this list); there is no Member column on a loop, view is what being shared gives. People (with a plus) under the grid searches the users and groups and adds the one picked as a Viewer; its level menu or boxes give the rest. Ticking a box saves the row; one with share who is not the owner gives at most what they hold (hover a word's column for its meaning). Edit without Run changes the loop but cannot start or stop it; Ask without Edit chats about it and changes nothing. Under the shares, a read-only row per project the loop is linked into (a folder, its title, its address as a link), its level via project: its words are the most any of its people gets on the loop, a quiet tick for a word given and a short dash for one not (a global project "no rights (global)", an archived one "archived: none", one with no members "no one yet"). ▸ unrolls its people: each member (the words their level gives), a member of its group who gets more through their membership ("via group"), and one row for what its group access gives everyone in the group ("Everyone in hw · open (Asker+)"); Change on the project › opens its page, where they are set. Your rights on a loop are your row, your groups' rows and what its projects give you, together; being in a group with its owner gives nothing. A run started by someone else runs as the owner's, on the owner's model settings and limits.
  • Projects: the projects the loop is linked into, in its order: a grip to drag a row, or its up and down chevrons (the order its projects' libraries come in, each read-only at library/<project>@<group>/ after the loop's own files; an exact copy of a paper in a later one is read once). Each row has the project and its address, Learns (whether the project may learn from its runs) and ✕ to take it out. Add to a project… searches the projects you may link it into: those where you hold the link role, and the global ones that take loops. Linking it is your consent: each of the project's members gets their loop words on it (view, ask, edit, run; never share), and the group's members what its access gives. A global project gives no rights; its learning is off until an admin or one of its managers turns it on, and you may turn it off. Others see the card read-only.
  • Name & ownership: rename the loop (1 to 60 letters, digits, _ and -), or transfer it to another user. The loop must be stopped, with no agent and no chat answer reading it at work. Everything that names the loop moves with it -- its record, results, runs and settings, chats that focus on it or proposed changes to it, scheduled changes, waiting notices' links, its usage (counted once). There are no redirects: the old address stops working. A transfer leaves the admin's overrides, the shares and the agents' tests behind (they were the old owner's); the log, transcripts and the audit keep the old name where it was written.
  • Advanced (admins): whether the loop runs in the sandbox, its memory, CPU, process and scratch limits (under each, the server's default and maximum; an ask above the maximum is clamped to it, see Sandbox limits), parallel work (how much, the configurator's Extra › Running, which says whether it is allowed), extra hosts it may reach, raw TCP/UDP, host folders mounted inside, and extra Nixpkgs or Nixchip packages. Everyone else sees what they are, in a line under Name & ownership.
  • Maintenance (folded): the clean-ups on this loop now -- Clean disk (its scratch, old pass folders, its sandbox cache), Condense history (its log, journal and transcript) and Compact and check (its records, its document loaded); each asks first.
  • Record (folded; open while something waits for the next start): what edits this loop's record -- Prune stale records, Prune empty starts, Prune failed designs (asks at which stage), Invalidate all, which sets every design aside without measuring anything, on this loop at rest only (it is no admin task, so this is the one place it runs, after its confirmation), and Re-Evaluate, which asks the next start to measure again the designs of the Results tabs ticked -- Accepted, Rejected, Failed, Pending (by default), each with its count; all four is every design -- and pass 0 with Rerun baseline (see Results). What waits for the next start is said on its row and on the Overview, with Cancel; it can be asked while the loop runs. The tasks that change what the record counts are red and ask first. While an invalidation's designs wait to be measured again, its row says how many are done (Results).
  • Archive, reset or delete: Archive keeps a finished loop read-only and frees its disk (see Archive). Reset clears what the runs generated (you choose what to keep: the workbench, results and history, caches); the document, your files and the settings stay. Delete removes the whole loop. All need the loop stopped and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
Archive (the loop's owner, or an admin) asks for the loop's name and lists, with their sizes, what goes and what stays.

Kept Deleted The results, out/: designs, measurements, decisions (Results and its exports) The passes' working files The document, your files and the library The tools' whole outputs (Live keeps each one's end) The workbench's notes and tools The sandbox's tool caches and scratch The last start's log, the answer, notes and Chat Work in progress and build folders What Live shows of the past starts The log of the starts before the last

An archived loop is read-only: Overview, Live, Results, Files and Chat (an agent answers from the record) still read it; the document, files, settings, ideas queue, starts and resets are refused until Unarchive (a plain confirm). A start then rebuilds the deleted scratch. The loop lists hide archived loops; their Archived chip shows them, each with its date, and a search or a link still finds them. Run clean-ups leave them alone.

docs.title: Export and import
docs.text:
Export (the loop's owner, its editors, an admin) writes the loop as one .zip, to keep or to open on this or another Flux. Its dialog offers two kinds, each with its size as the server last measured the loop's folders, and says that hidden files go too (the checks need them):

Loop only Full The problem document, your files, lib/, skills/, the library yes yes Hidden files (listed in the file's manifest) yes yes The results, out/: designs, measurements, decisions, ideas yes The workbench's notes and tools (no build folders), the answer, the notes yes

Never in either: variables and secrets, credentials, agent instructions, shares and their links, rights, a project's library read through the loop, Chat's conversations, Live's history, agents' working files, tool outputs, caches, logs, links, a repository. The file starts with a manifest: its kind, who made it on which server and when, its documents, hidden paths, how many commands its documents run, and its sizes. The audit says "loop exported" with the kind and the size.

Import replaces this loop's contents with a file's (either kind); the loop must be stopped. The file is sent, its manifest read alone and shown (kind, made by, when, format, sizes, hidden paths, commands), with what will be replaced: "This replaces x's document, files and library, and its results: 12 designs are replaced by 40 designs." Replace then puts the file's document, files and library in place -- and with a Full file its record, workbench, answer and notes (the record renamed after this loop when it was named after the old one), Results and Overview reading it at once. A Loop only file into a loop with results clears them by default (they belong to the old document); Keep the current results keeps them. The loop keeps its name and id, owner, shares, project links, variables, settings, Chat's conversations and its run history; the Overview says "Replaced from x.full.zip, made by ada@host, date, Full". The audit says "loop replaced". Someone who may edit the loop clears that notice with its ×: it goes for everyone who looks at the loop, and this card keeps one line, "Imported from x.full.zip on date: made by ada@host, date, Full". The next import shows its own notice again.

Nothing of the file runs on import: no agent, no step, no digest -- its commands run in the sandbox when the loop starts. The whole file is checked before anything is replaced; a file of a form before Nov 12, 2026 -- its documents, or a Full file's record -- is refused, naming the Flux that still brings it up (open it there, import it, let the loop start once, and export it again), and so is one made by a newer Flux ("update this server first"). Any refusal leaves the loop as it was. An admin's server settings loop_import_max (the largest file, 2 GB) and loop_import_unpacked_max (the most it unpacks to, 16 GB) bound it.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Someone who may view the loop but not edit it reads the problem here: the configurator's steps beside the document as written, the chosen step's lines lit. Nothing can be saved or checked.

  • Configurator: the document in six steps, as the Loop crafter shows it. A save shows its diff first; what the form cannot express is kept as written, greyed at the end of the document beside each step (Copy and Download give it whole) and listed on Save. A check or measurement the loader refuses is outlined on its row, with why. Save counts the document as checked once Check passed on its files as they are, or a start on those files got going. Every step but Graph and Save is a few light cards of rows, as the Graph's panel below: a label, then its box or menu, a greyed value its default, a unit (s, MHz, %, a number's own) inside its box, and no hint under a field -- the line at the step's foot says what the setting pointed at or in focus does. Prompt is the name, language, what to make and the rules, then Files; Check & Measure a Checks card (the list, a row opened to set it) and a Measurements card (the list); Objective how designs are compared, then the numbers, a goal's unit in its box. Extra's sections (Parameters, Running, Resources) are cards that fold, each saying what is set while folded; one set away from its default, or at fault, opens. On the Graph, left of the loop, the Setup group holds Plan and Baseline (a pass 0 measured first: off, first or only it, from the project, a file, a command, or numbers given; off, its box says so and stays quiet), and under it the Knowledge group a bubble per part of what the agents and prompts get: Skills, Library, Workbench, Insights, Ideas, Notes and Hidden, each saying its state on the right (off dashed, an AI pill when FluxAgent or an agent does it). All of them are drawn in one grey; Choose's arrow points into Knowledge, as what is measured and decided is what the loop knows next. A box clicked opens its panel: the box's name and what it does, then a few light cards. Worker says who works it, the same rows wherever a worker is chosen (a box, its Critic, Choose's Tie-break, a Knowledge section, an AI search): the kinds -- off first where it may be off (the workbench digest too), then agent, then the box's own (rules, mined, script, files, goals) -- then with agent an Agent menu, FluxAgent first, then the agents the server offers (their program found, as in the chat), then its Thinking and effort (not drawn where they would do nothing, as for an agent with a command of its own) -- an agent the document names that is not offered here (written by hand, or its program gone since) stays picked, greyed and marked (not available), never offered for another box, the Graph's error saying the loop won't start until it is fixed; Search's How it picks (FluxAgent only) follows, and right under them, folded, a coding agent's options, titled <agent> · options, their values beside the title while folded: Questions and at most, Wait, Time limit and last turn, May time out, Session -- the same rows in the same order in every place, a row that does nothing there not drawn. Questions is for an agent that can stop and ask (Design and Knowledge's papers, workbench and ideas), at most once someone answers, Wait once that someone is you; May time out and the last turn are Design's; under trunk Design has its Time limit alone. FluxAgent has no options. A value the document says in a row not drawn stays: a save keeps it and the document beside the steps shows it. Session is one per pass, the default, or one per loop (Design's: one per design, warm start, the default -- each design's session starts from a shared one that read the loop's files and tools first, with a Study time row under it in minutes, 60 unsaid (seed_timeout_s, in seconds, 5 minutes to 3 hours) -- one per design, cold start, session: fresh, or one per loop), then with its turns beside it and Until stopped after them (8 unsaid: session: keep, turns:; Until stopped turns: forever, never renewed, the turns greyed); the papers' digest, the workbench and the ideas have none: each of their turns stands alone. A box with a worker and a critic reads as two such blocks. Design's Probe is a card of its own while a coding agent works Design: on or off, the gate's checks it may run, and while on its gate runs and measure runs. Under trunk each agent past the first has the same block, with its model and a remove. Switching to another kind or agent and back brings back what it had (an agent's own settings, FluxAgent's thinking). The box's own card follows (Design's Per pass, Search's Policy card: the Policy, the Search once there are settings (an algorithm, or AI -- who proposes the points, FluxAgent with its Thinking and effort, or an agent with its card, picked under it) and the settings it searches), and Limits, folded (Design's prototype limits and FluxAgent's tool turns, which are the whole loop's: always in Design's panel, elsewhere where FluxAgent works). Under a search over parameters Design is off, a script or files; with a script or files making each point, all its kinds. Check, Measure, Choose are one block saying who works them, linked to where their commands or goals are set. Each Knowledge bubble opens its own panel: Skills its list and switch, Library what is read and who sums up the papers, Workbench and Insights who sums up or draws conclusions (Insights also says the record they read is always on), Ideas who cleans up and when, Hidden the paths no agent reads. A card folds, its values said beside its title while folded; a dot marks a value the document sets, a greyed one is the default, and the line at the panel's foot says what the setting pointed at or in focus does. The document's issues (what Check and Direct edit list: an error stops the loop, a warning is a key it ignores) are shown where they are set. A step's line in the rail says them with their mark -- a round "!" for an error, a triangle for a warning: "▲ 1 warning", "● 1 error · 1 warning" -- and Save's line counts them all ("1 to fix · 2 warnings"). On the Graph, the box the setting belongs to wears the mark in its top-right corner, its look otherwise unchanged (flow.plan on Plan, flow.design on Design, flow.search on Search, flow.check on Check, flow.measure on Measure, flow.notes on Notes, flow.knowledge on Knowledge, ...); with an error, the box shows the value as written (codx), not the default it would fall back to. Its panel outlines the setting at fault and says each issue in a note: the plain words, "Did you mean X?", its fix (Use codex, Remove) and Open line N to Direct edit there. A check's or a measurement's setting is said at the top of Check & Measure, an objective's on Objective. A fix is written to the file (refused if the file changed meanwhile), then the form and its issues are read again; changes not saved are asked about first. The banner of a document that does not load says the error in the same plain words. A save from the configurator keeps the keys the loader ignores as written, under the setting the form wrote (a stage's misspelled timout_s, notes: human), so they stay for you to fix.
  • Direct edit: the YAML as written, saved with its diff. A document that does not load is said before it is saved.
  • Several problems. A loop's problems are its problem.yaml and each NAME.problem.yaml in its folder (not in a subfolder, not another name: foo.yaml is an input file, not a problem). With more than one, a menu beside the ways picks the one the configurator, Direct edit and Check show ("problem.yaml · selected" is the one the next start runs by default); one that does not load is listed as such, in red, and opens in Direct edit to be fixed (the configurator says what it could read of it). Edits not saved are asked about before another one opens. The address keeps the one open (settings/problem/edit?doc=fast.problem.yaml). Opening or saving a problem here does not select it: the problem a run takes is picked in the Start dialog, as before.
  • Agent: say what should change; an agent revises a copy of the loop's files and shows its diff (not while the loop runs).
  • Check runs flux task check on the document as it stands: whether it is ready to run, what it refused or found missing, then its checks, stages, objectives, tools and model. The whole output is under Details.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: Groups, in the top bar between Loops and Admin, is every user's page for the teams they are in: who is in each group, what their membership gives them, whose settings their runs use, and the group's projects. Admins set groups up under Admin › People › Groups (Server and admin); this page is where everyone else sees them.

docs.title: A tab per group
docs.text:
The page has a tab for each of your groups and one for Global (with its number of projects), with no title above them (the bar says Groups). The tab you chose is in the address (#/groups/<id>, #/groups/global) and remembered in this browser; a project opens under its group's tab (A project's page).

Under a group's tab:

Part What it shows Projects The group's projects: title and about, address (<group>/<name>), invite only or open · level beside the title, and your level on it -- what the project gives you (Viewer, Asker, Contributor, Maintainer, Lead; Custom only for a mix of boxes), with your group's curate or manage said beside it ("Asker + curate"); its words on hover; "—" when you only see it. An invite-only project you are not added to is not listed. The address is one line, cut with an ellipsis when it is long (the whole on hover). Members who may create, and admins, get the New project form under the list You in group A few facts: your Level (its words on hover, the words), what it Gives in plain words (curate or manage every project of the group, create projects; loops only through the projects you are in or that open to the group), Open projects (the level they give, for its managers and admins to choose) and Credentials in one line (the server's settings through it, through another group, or your own) Members · N Who is in it: names and levels for everyone; the member grid (a box per word) for whoever manages the group

On a phone You in comes first, then the projects and the members.

docs.title: Members
docs.text: A membership's level is Member, Maintainer (curate, create) or Lead (curate, manage, create): a group membership has no loop word. Being in a group gives nothing on any loop: a loop is reached when its owner shares it, or links it into a project you are in (or that opens to the group). A member who manages the group (a Lead) sees the members in the member grid, adds people with People (they join as Member), removes anyone but themselves with ×, and gives levels and words up to their own; admins any. A member who may not manage the group sees the other members, their names and levels, read-only (never the words' table), and is told whom to ask. Nobody leaves a group from here.

docs.title: New project
docs.text: New project asks for a Title (free) and a Name, made from the title until you type one. The name is checked as you type: letters, digits, - and _, at most 60, and not one the group already has whatever its case. Create project makes <group>/<name>, blank and invite only, and you are its Lead (every word). Nothing is said under the form but an error, when there is one. A project's title opens its page.

docs.title: A project's page
docs.text:
Think of a group as an organisation and a project as one of its repositories, with members of its own; loops are linked into it. Its page opens on the Groups page, in its group (a global project in Global): #/groups/<group id>/<name>, #/groups/global/<name>. Every link Flux makes to it is this one. An old address, #/projects/<group>/<name>, still opens it (a link in an older notification, a bookmark) and is replaced by the new one.

The group tabs are not drawn over it: its head is one row, then its tabs.

  • Its head: its group ▾ / its title ▾ -- the group's name goes back to the group's projects, its ▾ lists your other groups (and Global) and opens the one you pick on its projects; the title's ▾ lists the group's other projects you see, with their loops, and + New project for whoever may make one -- a pick opens the other project on the same tab when it has it; the title's address (<group>/<name>) on hover. Then what the group's members get (Invite only, with a lock, Group views, Open; a global project Public or Private, with a lock; its sentence on hover), and at the row's end Chat, which opens its conversations in Chat's page, on a new one (see Chat › Project chats: read by its members, asked by edit, curate or manage -- shown to its members alone), You: your level (its words on hover) and Leave, a quiet button, for its own members. Its about, when it has one, under the row. On a phone the row wraps: the group, the title and its access first, the buttons under them.
  • Its tabs: Overview, Files, Knowledge, Variables and Settings (only for whoever may change something there -- a Contributor's holds the topics alone; a plain member or a Viewer has none) -- Files, Knowledge, Variables and Chat for its own members (and admins) alone (Its contents are its members'), each its own address: …/<name>/library, …/<name>/knowledge, …/<name>/variables, …/<name>/settings. Files, as a loop's, has sub-tabs for the project's folders, Library and Skills (…/<name>/library, …/<name>/skills; …/<name>/files opens the first), each the same file browser. The tabs are drawn as a loop's page draws its own: underlined, and the sub-tabs on their own row under them, each with its count -- the library's files, the skills found ("Library 12 · Skills 3"). An empty folder says so inside the file list's card ("Nothing in the library yet.", "No skill yet."). At the sub-tabs' row's end, no row of its own: the library's use of its limit ("1.2 GB of 5 GB", Library shown) and, to whoever may change nothing in the folder shown, that it is read-only and why.
Overview What it shows Loops · N Each loop linked into it that you may see: owner / name, its state and its design agent (as the Loops list says them, following them as they change), when last active, and for your own its place in the loop's order of projects ("1st of its 3"). + Link one of my loops if you hold the link role (anyone on a global project that takes loops); the cross takes one of yours out (the loop stays). A global project lists only your own loops, every one to admins and its managers, with whether each learns from its runs.
