What linking gives is on the ⓘ People · N Its members, names and levels (their words on hover); Manage › opens Settings for whoever keeps them Library How many files it holds and their size; Open › Your access Your words, and how you have them in a line: as a member, through the group, everyone on a public global project (what they give on its loops on hover)

On a phone the Overview is one column, Loops first.

Words: view, ask, edit, run -- what a member may do with every loop linked into it -- then link (link one's own loops in), curate (review what is learnt, keep the library) and manage (title, members, access; rename, archive, delete). Each implies view. A global project's members hold only curate or manage (Member, Maintainer, Lead): its visibility gives view. Sharing a linked loop stays its owner's. Words only add up: a project never takes one away.

Who manages it: its managers, the group's managers (manage on the group) and admins, each giving words up to their own. They also set what the group's members get -- Invite only (private: hidden until you're added -- only its members, the group's curators and managers and admins see it; a new project's default), Group views (they view it and its loops) or Open to the group (every member gets its Level for open: the group's default, or one of its own -- Viewer, Asker, Contributor or Maintainer -- that level, nothing more). There is no joining; anyone may leave a project. Others see its people, names and levels, in the Overview.

docs.title: Its contents are its members'
docs.text: A project's files (Library, Skills), its knowledge (topics, entries, proposals, the collector's runs), its variables and its chats are read by its own members alone -- what their level there says -- and admins. Its group gives none of them: a member of the group who is not on the project's member list -- through Group views, Open to the group at any level, or a membership's curate or manage -- sees the project, its people and the loops its access gives, and no Files, Knowledge or Chat: a link to them shows the project's head and "You see that this project exists. Ask its managers to add people.", and Chat's Projects tab does not list it. The group's managers still keep its members, so they may add themselves. A loop linked into the project reads its library, skills and knowledge only while its owner is a member who views it; its Chat, asked by someone who is not, answers without them; the collector proposes nothing from a loop whose owner is not. A global project's view is as its visibility says (public: everyone).

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
Files › Library, a project's library, is a folder of papers, specs and notes for its loops, browsed exactly as a loop's Files tab: the tree, the viewer (text in the editor, anything else to download), Files and Folder (or a drop; a single .zip is unpacked) into the folder open in the viewer (the library's top when none is), and Rename, Move, Delete on the selected item. Its use is shown beside its limit -- "1.2 GB of 5 GB" at the end of the sub-tabs' row, its files the Library sub-tab's count (whose limit on hover): the project's own, else the server's for every project, both set by admins in Admin › People › Projects, else a loop's room, 8 GB, and 100,000 files. An upload, a part or an edit that would take it past its limit is refused, saying what it holds, may hold and what it adds. A library over its limit (an admin lowered it) keeps its files and says so in warn: it cannot grow, while a delete, a move or a smaller file in a file's place still go. Every loop linked into the project reads it, read-only, at library/<name>@<group>/ of its own library (library/<name>@_/ for a global project), whoever runs it -- a loop's Files tab shows it there; the Library tab no longer lists the loops that read it. An archived project's library is read by no loop, nor by a loop whose owner no longer views the project -- is not its member with a word --, nor by a loop's agent answering someone who may not read it.

Who May Its members who view it (any word; everyone for a public global project) and admins -- never through its group browse and download edit, curate or manage on it as its member (a global project's members with curate or manage) upload, rename, move, delete, edit a text file manage as its member (its managers, admins) Hide from AI / Show to AI: the paths the agents of its loops will not see (under its place, library/<name>@<group>/drafts/)

An archived project's library is read-only. Uploads, renames, moves, edits, deletes and hidden paths are on the audit trail.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Files › Skills is the project's skills/ folder, beside its library: a folder per skill, each with a SKILL.md -- front matter with name and description (when it applies), then the instructions -- and the files it uses (Skills). It is browsed and changed with the library's file browser, by the same people (upload, rename, move, delete, a text file edited in place), and lists the skills found, a folder that is no skill said with why. Every loop linked into the project gets them, read-only, at skills/<name>@<group>/, listed on its configurator's Skills card beside its own.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
A project's Knowledge is what its loops have taught: short entries, each one insight, filed under the project's topics and proven by designs -- results of loops, never a number typed in. The accepted entries reach the project's loops at their next start: their agents query them with flux library (the list, flux library "<words>", flux library entry <id>; see Knowledge). Proposals, rejected and retired entries never reach a loop; a run reads the entries as its start saw them. People add entries by hand, the collector proposes them from the loops' best designs (below), and the project's chat proposes them too (Chat › Project chats): accepted there, an entry comes to To review ("from bob's chat"), never straight into the list.

Under the list a quiet line says whether the loops use it: "Read by 2 of 3 linked loops this week, 14 times" -- how many of the loops it reaches ran flux library in the last 7 days, and how often. Archived loops count among the linked and are said apart ("Read by 2 of 4 linked loops (1 archived) this week"): they never run, so they never read it.

The tab is a row of chips and one list. All and a chip per topic (with its count; the topic's question on hover) filter the list; To review, for its curators, holds the proposals; + Add is at the row's end. A row is an entry's headline with two muted lines of its analysis, its topic and how many designs back it at the right -- "✓ maria · 2 designs" when a curator ticked it, "+1" when it was reinforced today. A click opens it: the analysis at a reading width (a design named #142 in it is a link), its Designs (each a link to that design in its loop's Results, with its rank then -- "top 1 of 61" --, the day, how it came: "added by cy", "collected from nlu-gelu", later "from bob's chat in nlu-gelu"; one added later marked "+ … reinforced"), its Ideas -- "in 3 loops' ideas · tried 2 · won 1": each linked loop gets an accepted entry as one idea in its ideas notebook, scored and queued like its own (tried: a design of that loop followed it; won: one measured a win; see Knowledge) --, who accepted it, and its tools for whoever may, one toolbar of icons (each named on hover): Reinforce (a shield), Pin (a pin, pressed while the entry is pinned), Merge (two paths joining), Edit (the pencil) and Retire (an archive box: put away, still asking first).

Who May Its members who view it (and admins; never through its group) read the list; their own proposals, marked in review edit, curate or manage + Add an entry -- a topic, the insight in one line, the analysis (why it works, what the top designs did differently, citing them as #142, the cost, where it does not hold, what is open) and at least one design of a loop of the project they view; Reinforce an entry in the list with another design, at once, no review; write the Topics curate as its member (its curators; a group's curators and managers only once they are its members) To review: open a proposal to change its headline and analysis, ✓ accepts it, ✕ rejects it, Merge into an entry in the list; Edit, Retire, Pin and Merge an entry in the list

An entry's proof is enough with designs from 2 different loops: every row says backed by N loops, however many designs each gave, and opened it lists those designs loop by loop. The list leads with the pinned entries, then the best backed. A proposal always waits for a curator; a curator's ✓ on one with less proof accepts it and ticks it ("✓ maria"), and the list says so. A curator's own entry goes straight in (ticked when its proof is short) -- on a global project another curator accepts it. A proposal may be marked contradicts: an entry's headline. Accepted, rejected and retired entries stay on the record; the author is told when a curator decides. An archived project's knowledge is read-only. Every change (topics, add, accept, reject, edit, retire, reinforce, merge, pin, a collector's run) is on the audit trail.

Merge joins entries of one topic that say the same thing: in the dialog you choose the entry to Keep, tick the others to merge into it, and edit its headline and analysis. The others' designs back the kept entry, each with its source; the merged entries leave the list and review and stay as its history -- opened, Merged lists them ("#12 headline · in review · merged by maria") with Unmerge, which puts them back as they were (the kept entry's text too, unless someone changed it since). A proposal that says the same as an entry in the list is merged into it from To review (Merge into); an entry in the list merges only into another in the list. Pin puts an entry first in the list, tagged pinned, and first in its topic in flux library and first among the entries a flux library "<words>" matches, the best backed after them -- an order only: loops still read knowledge by asking for it.

Stale. Flux marks an entry in the list stale for its curators when the evidence no longer backs it: it has gone a long while without reinforcement or use, or its ideas were tried in several loops and won in none. The row says stale, a Stale chip lists them, and the mark says why with ✓, which retires the entry, and ✕, which keeps it. Nothing is retired by itself, and a mark whose reason no longer holds goes by itself.

docs.title: The collector
docs.text:
With the link's learning on (on by default in a group's project; in a global one only its managers or an admin turn it on, and the loop's owner may turn it off), Flux reads the best designs of the loops linked into a project with topics, once they have changed, and writes what they teach as proposals, outside the loop: nothing in the loop changes. A look is billed to the loop owner's FluxAgent settings for that loop, as knowledge collector in Admin › Activity › Usage.

What it can find:

It finds What happens The new designs work by an accepted entry's mechanism They reinforce it at once, no review: "+ … collected from nlu-gelu, reinforced" They work by the mechanism of a proposal in review They join its designs: the proposal stays in To review, now backed by that loop too A new insight A proposal in To review, "collected from nlu-gelu" They contradict an entry A proposal marked contradicts: its headline, and on the entry a mark like 1 of 4 loops disagrees until a curator rejects that proposal; opened, the entry lists those designs under Against An entry is superseded or shown wrong A proposal retire: its headline, with the reason: ✓ retires the entry, ✕ keeps it. Nothing is retired by itself

Collect now, beside Runs on the line under the list, is for the project's managers (and admins). It opens a dialog listing the linked loops, each with its state: how many top designs are unread, nothing new, or why no look can run (learning off, no measured designs, not linked, its owner's model missing...). Untick the loops to leave out. An archived loop is listed too, marked archived and unticked: tick it to read its top designs. Its record is only read -- the loop is never started, unarchived or changed. Flux also reads an archived loop by itself when any of its top designs is unread -- once it is archived, and again when the project's topics change -- rather than waiting for more than 3, which an archived loop will never have; after that it says nothing new. Without Read designs again, even those already read, a look reads only what is unread; with it, a look reads the loop's top 5 designs whatever was read before. Either way a look is one model call per loop, billed to the loop's owner, and what the project holds already is reinforced or left out, not proposed twice. Looks run one at a time in the background; the button says how far it is (Collecting 2 of 7…) and the press is on the audit trail, with its loops.

A loop whose owner is not a member of the project (they left it, or linked the loop without joining) is still collected, but never on its owner's model: a look sends the project's topics and entries to the model, and those are for the project's members only. So such a loop is listed its owner is not a member: on your model and read only when you press Collect now, on your own model and billed to you -- if you can view the loop (it is shared with you, your level in the project gives it, or you are an admin). If you cannot, it says so and stays unticked: its owner joins the project or shares the loop with you. Flux never looks at such a loop by itself.

Compare loops in the same dialog looks for what several of the ticked loops share, after the looks: one model call per topic, roughly 10-20k tokens each, on your own model and billed to you, as knowledge compare in usage; the dialog says the rough total first. It needs two ticked loops you view and a model of your own, and it never runs by itself. Its findings are proposals "compared by" you, backed by the loops they cite.

Curators see the last run in a quiet line under the list: Last collected: nlu-gelu · Oct 23 · 2 proposed, 1 reinforced; Runs at its end opens Collector runs, every run newest first: its loop, when, what it proposed, reinforced or would retire, what was dropped and why, or why it failed. A line under the chips counts what became of the entries (7 accepted · 0 to review · 1 merged · 1 dropped): a proposal is one entry only once a curator accepts it.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: Off until a curator turns them on in Settings › Suggestions. Then each proposal in To review has Suggest (opened): a model reads it against the entries in the list and suggests one thing -- accept, reject (for a retire proposal: retire or keep the entry), merge into an entry of its topic, or a better headline -- with a paragraph of why. The suggestion sits on the proposal's card, with the model and whose model it ran on; Apply does it as you could by hand (✓, ✕, the merge, or the headline changed with the proposal still in review), or you ignore it. Nothing is ever applied by itself. It runs on the FluxAgent settings of the curator who presses Suggest. Also as each proposal arrives, on my model asks for one as each proposal comes in (by hand or from the collector), on the model of the curator who ticked it, named under the setting. A suggestion reads the project's knowledge only, never a loop's or a library's files. Each call is on the audit ("knowledge suggest") and in Admin › Activity › Usage as that curator's, knowledge suggestions in its Agent table.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables holds the project's environment variables, in the editor a loop's and your account's use: a row a variable -- its name, its value (a secret's shown as secret · set: its value is stored encrypted and never shown or answered again; set it anew to change it) -- the bin to remove one, and Name, Value, secret, Add under them. Names are checked as everywhere: letters, digits and _; the sandbox's and Flux's own (FLUX_SANDBOX…, PATH, HOME, the model settings, ...) are refused.

Every loop linked into the project reads them at its next start, in each of its processes (a run, a check, its Chat's and its agents' turns), in this order, each over the one before:

  1. the server's (Admin › Runtime › Agents › All agents),
  2. the loop owner's (Account),
  3. each project the loop is linked into, in the loop's order -- its first project wins over the later ones,
  4. the loop's own (Settings › Variables), which always win.

A project counts as its library does: unarchived, and while the loop's owner is its member who views it; a loop's agent answering someone else (its Chat) reads only the projects they may read too. A loop in no project reads what it always did. A change -- set, removed, a loop linked or unlinked, the order changed -- reaches a loop at its next start, never a run already going. The loop's Settings › Variables lists them under its own, *from project

/ *, a plain value shown to whoever may read the project's variables (else the name alone), one that something above sets marked **overridden**. A secret reaches every linked loop's processes, so whoever runs one can use it -- as the server's secrets. | Who | May | |---|---| | Its members who **view** it (any word; everyone for a public global project) and admins -- never through its group | the names and the plain values | | **edit** or **manage** on it as its member (a global project's managers), admins | add, change and remove them -- not while it is archived | A rename keeps them (they are kept by the project's id); a delete takes them. Each set and removal is on the audit trail by its name alone, never its value. ### Settings For its managers (and admins): **Members & access** first -- its members in the same grid as a group's: a level ([the words](admin.md#the-words)), the Member mark, a box per word, **×**; **All members** gives or takes a word from everyone; **People** (they join as Member); and what the group's members get, with the **Level for open**. Then **About** (title and about), **Name** with **Rename** -- the new name is checked as typed, the old address stops working (no redirect) and its members, its group's and the owners of the loops linked into it are told the new one once (a notice with its link); the page opens at the new address. A rename is refused while a loop linked into it runs (or an agent writes it, or answers in it); their next start reads its library at the new place, `library/<new name>@<group>/` -- **Archive** / **Unarchive** and **Delete** (type its name; its loops stay, taken out of it). On a global project admins also choose its **Visibility** -- **Public** (everyone sees it, its library and knowledge) or **Private** (only its members and admins) -- and who links loops into it (everyone, or admins only; a private one's members only). **Topics**, for whoever may edit the project (a Contributor too, who sees only this card): a row a topic -- its id (lower-case letters, digits, `-` and `_`) and the question its entries answer -- edited in place, **+ Topic**, **✕**, **Save**; the raw tool (**{ }**, pressed while on) shows the project's `knowledge.yaml` as written (`pipelining: Where do pipeline stages pay off, and what do they cost?`, a line a topic, comments kept). A topic renamed takes its entries with it; one that still holds an entry is not removed. A member who may change nothing there (a plain member) sees no Settings tab. ## Global **Global** lists the global projects you see: the **public** ones (everyone sees them, their library and knowledge) and the **private** ones you are a member of (nobody else but admins finds them). Their members curate or manage them; there is no curator group. Only admins make them: **New global project** under the list (admins only), **Admin › People › Projects**, or `flux project create _/<name>` (public; `--visibility private`). Anyone may link a loop into a public one, a private one's members into it (admins only when its join rule says so); it gives nobody any right on the loop, shows you only your own loops in it (admins and its managers see every one; in a private one its members do not see each other either), and learns from a loop's runs only once an admin or one of its managers turns that on. ## In no group A user in no group sees what a group is, that an admin adds them to one, and the **Global** tab. Their own loops and those shared with them are under **Loops** as always. ## Admins An admin sees their own groups; **Every group (admin)**, at the end of the tabs, adds the others, marked "not a member". In every group an admin sets any member's level in the grid, the group's **Credentials** (Server settings or Own settings) and its open level, adds and removes members, and makes projects. **Every group in Admin › People › Groups** opens **Admin › People › Groups**.

docs.title: Live
docs.text: A loop's Live tab shows what its run does, task by task, as it happens, and what earlier starts did. It has two views, Graph and Timeline, and always shows every pass of the start: the Graph picks the pass it draws from its chain of passes, the Timeline draws them all side by side. It opens on the Graph; live/timeline opens the Timeline. An address of the Tree or the Log, views Live had before (live/tree, live/log), opens the Graph; the start's log is the Overview's Log when a run stopped on an error, and Files.

docs.title: The toolbar
docs.text:
• Start picks the start to show: the one running, or an older one, which replays its passes, tools and conversations. It lists the latest 50 starts; Earlier at its end brings the ones before them.
  • Follow keeps the latest work in view as the run goes on, in the Graph and the Timeline alike: the Timeline at its end (now), at any zoom, the latest task's bar in sight. Pressed while it follows (its tooltip says which); scrolling the view, zooming or selecting a task stops it and leaves the view where you put it; Follow again resumes, back at the latest work at once.

The head over the view is one line: All passes, then its counts -- its tasks (grey), done, failed, retried -- each count's word in its tooltip. When pipelining is off and the loop's record holds three passes or more, a quiet line under it may say turning it on is worth it: "Pipelining could make passes about 24% shorter: Settings › Problem › Extra › Pipelining." -- worked out from the record with nothing run (the time from each pass's design passing Check to its decision, against the whole pass), and said only when it is 10% or more. With pipelining on, nothing is said. flux loop passes ends with the same advice (budget.pipeline: true).

docs.title: Graph
docs.text:
The pass as the loop's drawing: Search, Design, Check, Measure, Choose, and a critic where one is set. Each box says what it is set to (Search what it picked), whether it passed (✓ or ✗), and ×N when it ran again; a design of several tries has a bar per try, ✓, ! (not built) or ✗. Boxes the loop skipped are dashed. A pass that tests an idea queued in Results › Ideas runs no search: the queued idea is its direction. Its Search box says queued idea (the queue's icon) instead of skipped, as do the tree and the pass's flow; its Design carries the same tag, the idea it follows in its tooltip, and the Search's inspector names the idea with a link to Results › Ideas. With nothing queued, a pass may suggest the best-scored idea not measured yet; when the design takes it, the Design box says suggested idea, the idea in its tooltip. Above the flow is the chain of passes, one bubble a pass in the colour of how it came out, and which pass is drawn (Pass 4 shown); a bubble draws its pass and opens it in the inspector. The chain shows the start's Setup, the pass before the one drawn, it, the one after and the latest; a … between them opens every pass of the chain, Less folds it again. A pass that is over is read, not followed; Follow comes back to the work at hand. A step bar fills once its step is done; one at work pulses, light. A Check or Measure box has a bar per step, not per run: five checks run three times are five bars, one stage measured ten times is one; a bar's tooltip sums its runs (check unit: 9 of 11 passed, 1 failed, 1 running), amber when it failed on the way, and a click opens its latest run. Measure has a bar for each stage the document sets, in its order (area, perf): a stage no run has reached yet is a grey bar while the box is at work (measurement perf: waiting), hollow once it is over (not reached), as Check's checks to come. A box of one task opens it; a Design of one try opens its draft, the agent's conversation, while it drafts, while its check runs and once it is over; one of several tries opens its list. A design agent's draft, and the Design box, show the rundown it gave of the design it handed in (Rationale, a few points: its key points, what it changed and why), once its short follow-up has answered.

A pass that checks and measures each design apart -- the re-check measuring designs again, several at once -- lists them a design at a time. Check and Measure count designs (×246, its tooltip 246 designs measured), not stretches of work. Check has a row per design with a dot per check (✓ #214 ●●●●) and Measure a row per design with a dot per stage (✓ #246 ●● 24m 07s, the design's measuring time). A dot is green when done, red when failed, blue at work, grey while waiting and hollow when never reached; its tooltip names the step, its state and its time. A stage whose command exited non-zero is a failed measurement: its dot is red, its design's row and its task are ✗, and a box whose last run it was is ✗ too (a journal from before Flux read it so is shown the same way). The latest five show, the earlier ones folded on top ("34 earlier designs"). A design's check opens its checks, a design's Measure row its stages (Measure · #246), and each check or stage opens its own detail: its command, exit and output, with ‹ Check · #210 or ‹ Measure · #246 to go back.

After a pass's design is measured, the loop has the standing design's numbers on the same stage, so the two compare under one setup. When the standing design had to be measured again, Measure lists it as a row of its own (✓ #68 ● and ✓ #42 ●) with an amber tag naming why: tools changed, inputs changed, command changed, readout changed (how the stage reads its numbers), params changed, last try failed or not cached. Its tooltip and its panel say it in full (standing design, measured again: its stage's tools changed since 2 Nov), with what changed (yosys rebuilt, bench.py edited); its numbers from before are kept, these added beside them.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
The start's time in three rows, each named once: Setup, Design and Tool. It takes the page's width, the inspector under it; a long start scrolls sideways, the row names kept in view, and only the part in sight (and a view's width either side) is drawn.

  • Setup: the start's own steps -- opening the record, a baseline reused, the papers, the workbench -- each in its box's colour, on as few lines as steps at work at once need; the decisions that are over many designs: the baseline's, the re-check's, the closing decision; and a design's Choose that ran without a tool slot (below).
  • Design: a line per design at work at once, budget.designs_at_once lines. A pass is one design's work, in one box on its line: its Search (yellow) first, then each try its own bar (blue), and at the hand-in the design's tag (#42). The time between two tries draws nothing.
  • Tool: budget.tools_at_once lines, whether pipeline is on or off. A design's tool work is one box: its Check, a bar per Measure stage, then its Choose, in the boxes' colours, the design's tag (#42) at the end of its Measure part where there is room. While it runs the box is dashed to now. A pass whose earlier pass has not decided yet waits for its turn before its Choose, its tool slot given back meanwhile: its box ends at its last Measure stage, and its Choose, run without a slot, is an orange bar on the Setup row, its tooltip naming the design. So the Tool row never needs more lines than slots. A search pass's checks and measurements are bars of their own (its designs are checked and measured together). A check or measurement an agent ran itself in its try (a probe) takes a Tool line too, hatched in its kind's colour and outlined in the agent's pink; a try's check that sent the design back is a short outlined bar there.

Hovering a design -- its box on the Design line, its tag, its box on the Tool line or its Choose on Setup -- lights them all, so you can follow a design from its Search to its decision. One pass at a time, each pass is a column behind the rows, white and light grey by turns, its number at the top; passes at work at once have no columns, the Design lines say them.

A bar is a step's work, not its wait. A step waiting for a tool slot (or for room on the machine) draws nothing until its tool starts, so the Tool row never draws more boxes at once than there are slots (tools_at_once: 8: eight tools at once, a design's check, measurements and decision holding one). How long it waited is said in its task ("waited 3m for a tool slot"), and in the box's tooltip when a step waited inside it (a journal of an older version, when checks and measurements had slots of their own). Lines are filled by time: a line a design freed is the next design's, and a bar never moves to another line as the run goes on.

A row draws at most six lines; the work on the lines past them is not drawn (the row's name says "+3": the lines hidden). The unroll tool (two bars, arrows spreading), in the header when a row is that wide, draws every line instead; pressed again, it folds back. Clicking a row's "+3" does the same. This browser remembers the choice. A task picked elsewhere (the Graph, a link, the arrow keys) whose bar is on a hidden line unrolls the rows; while Following, the row's "+3" is marked instead.

Every bar is its own: a click selects that one step and opens it in the inspector, and Tab and Enter reach the bars in time order. A bar too short to see is still clicked a few pixels either side of it. Beside the unroll tool, Zoom out, Zoom in and Fit to the window widen the time axis (twice as wide each click) and bring it back to the page's width; the chart then scrolls sideways inside its box (by touch on a phone), the time axis's ticks spaced to round steps. Zooming keeps the moment in the middle of the view where it is, or the end of a running start when it was in view, so the chart keeps showing what runs now. Ctrl and the mouse wheel (a trackpad's pinch) zoom around the pointer; double-clicking a bar zooms in until it fills half the view. The zoom is kept for each loop until the browser tab is closed, apart from the unroll tool's choice. Where an agent or FluxAgent works a step (a try's draft, a Setup step, a Search), a pink strip along the foot of its bar says when; the strip is always inside its own bar, at any zoom. The Setup row holds what the start reads and writes before its work: opening the record (from the moment its file is opened: on a first start its tables are made then), a baseline reused (baseline: its decisions read back), and before a re-check's first Check its row on the record (re-check on record) and its queue (re-check queue: the designs to measure again and the measured ones read back); and at a pass's end its connection to the record closing (close record: the record's log written back into it, slow on a slow disk). Each Setup step is a bar when it takes half a second or more, its tooltip saying which part took the time, and a note in its box otherwise. Per box: how many calls, the average, the longest, the total, and its share of the wall clock.

docs.title: A trunk-mode loop
docs.text:
A loop run as a trunk has a Live that shows its trunks and its branches instead of passes.

The Graph starts with the trunk: a Design box per agent (Design · claude · t1), at work for the whole run. Its line says what it does now -- writing, queue full (its share of the queue is waiting), waiting (between turns) or stopped -- then its turn, how long it has worked and how many designs it handed in; a bar for each of them, in the box's colour when measured, red when it failed its Check, amber on an error, faint while it waits or runs, and one more pulsing while the agent writes. Only the 10 latest are drawn: after a long run +137 starts the row, the earlier hand-ins counted (1k past a thousand; its tooltip says 137 earlier hand-ins). Pressing the box opens the agent's latest turn. Under it, 3 running · 2 waiting of 6, then the chain: the start's Setup (S) and a chip per design (#42), the running ones with a blue dot, a failed one red, those waiting dashed at the end. Picking a chip draws that design's branch as a pass's boxes -- Check, Measure, Choose -- under a line saying the design, what it came from, its agent and why; pressing a box opens its task. Live opens on the latest running branch. A Setup run again during the trunk is a chip of its own (S3) where it began among the designs.

However many designs there are, the chain is one line, as the pass chain: the first chip, …, the chip before the one picked, it, the one after, …, the last (a waiting design while some wait). Picking a chip moves that window onto it; a … opens the chips it hides, in its place (the line scrolls sideways when they do not fit), and Less folds them again.

Run setup, beside Stop in the head of a running trunk loop's Live, runs the Setup again (when the library changed, say), the document unchanged. It is greyed out while one runs or is asked; who pressed it is in the audit log.

The Timeline is the one passes have -- the same zoom, unroll tool, selection and rows: Setup, Design and Tool. Setup: the start's own steps in their boxes' colours -- the re-check's and the closing decision's choice among them -- then a bar for each Setup run again (a setup or Search bud). Every step is in its box's colour as in a flow: a Search bud's own Setup steps (tools ready, the record opened) are grey bars before its Search bar, and that bar opens the bud's Search turn; hovering it names who answered (FluxAgent and its model, or the agent) and the tools it read the record with. No words are written on these bars: hovering one names it (Decision, S3, Q2). Design: a line per trunk, named at the left (t1, t2), a bar per turn -- a turn is one design -- from when the trunk began readying the turn (its brief) to its end, a pink strip on it where its agent works, and at its end the tag of the design it handed in (#47). Each turn has its own transcript in the inspector, titled with the design it handed in (*Design · t3 · turn 4 ·

docs.title: 47*); a turn that handed none in says how many in a row. Tool: budget.tools_at_once lines; each design's Check, a
docs.text:
bar per Measure stage and its decision in one box, its tag at the end of its Measure part where there is room; a failed Check ends its box with a red mark. Hovering a design -- its turn, a tag or its box -- lights its turn, its tags and its box; each bar -- a turn, a step, a stage -- opens its own task. The re-check at the start has no turn: its designs' boxes sit under a grey band, R · re-check, each with its tag. The checks an agent ran itself in its turn (flux loop gate, flux loop measure) take Tool lines too, hatched in their kind's colour and outlined in pink: probes, counted with the tasks, never the loop's measurements. Past six lines the rest are hidden (+N: the lines hidden); the unroll tool or the +N draws every line.

Every count on a trunk's Live is the start picked in Start: a trunk box's handed in, running, waiting, the chain and the Timeline count what that start did, not what earlier starts left on the record (a design still waiting from before is in the queue this start takes from).

docs.title: The inspector
docs.text:
Selecting a task opens it beside the list. A tool's task shows its command, folder, exit and time, and its output as it runs. An agent's task shows its reply, then its conversation: text, thinking and tool calls, each input and output. A model's try reads the same way: the tools it called, then its reply in parts (why, the idea, the design as code, each edit as a diff) and its tokens. Raw and Fullscreen open the whole of it.

Only people with the Internals permission (Admin › People › Users) see the prompts the loop's agents and models were given, their thinking, and each of their actions: every tool call, command, file read or written, search and result. Everyone else, the loop's owner included, sees the turn's status, its final reply, a pass's search direction without its reason, and its actions as counts and time: 14 tool calls · 3 probes · 12m 30s, one line where the calls would be. This holds for every agent: the loop's own, Chat's and the New-loop author. The commands of your own stages and checks are your configuration, not an agent's actions, so they stay visible.

An agent's or a model's turn starts with its facts as one row of small pills, each with its icon: the agent (in the agent's pink), the model, its status, exit 0, 37 turns, its tokens in and out, its cost, thinking on, Tool calls (12). Hover a pill (or read it with a screen reader) for its label: tokens: 2.0M in · 19.0k out. An exit other than 0 and an error take their colour; the turn's state stays in the pill beside its title. The Agents tab and Chat's Thinking & commands show a turn's facts the same way.

Under its title a task says where it is, the whole path: Pass 2 › Design › try 8, a tool call … › try 8 › call 6. An improve says the stage it starts from (from the esl stage), and its steps are rows that open them (its draft). A try that failed or was not built says why in a line under that. A box shows its runs with their state and time, its total time in its head; a box still to come says what the document sets it to, in a few words, with the YAML folded under them. A pass shows what it measured last and whether that was kept, where its time went (in the bar's order) and its six boxes, each with how many times it worked ("Design · 3 tries · 2 not built"); once it is over, a box it never reached says "not run", and a failed pass says why. A check's failures read "14 of 18 fail".

Choose's panel names its pick and its pool. A design a critic rejected is struck through in its table with a critic tag, and the critic's reason is said under the table; the tag, the reason's Open and the step Choose · critique · #N -- rejected all open the critic's turn. Only this Choose's critiques strike its rows, not another pass's. A dictionary metric is one number there, as the loop ranks it: its objective's aggregate, else the dictionary's own _a, else the mean; hover a cell for its entries. The rows sort by it, and "same numbers as" compares it.

The table also lists the designs measured by then that were not in the pool, muted, each with why in a few words: "screen only" (its pass ended, or the run stopped, before it climbed to the stage the choice is made on), "cut on screen" (a cutoff), "stale" (measured before a change to how its stage is measured), "same design as #137", "rejected by the critic", "the baseline", a stage the document no longer has. Hover a row for the whole reason; when nothing recorded says why, the row says why not recorded rather than guess. When such a design beats the pick on the first column's objective, a notice over the table names each one with its value and why it was not compared: "3 designs have a smaller jx_time than #131 and were not in the pool: #140 (377 ns) was measured on screen only: its pass ended before it climbed to full. ..."

docs.title: Older runs
docs.text: A start recorded by a much older Flux is shown as written, under a notice saying so.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text: A loop can measure some of its steps on another machine: one with an FPGA board, a licensed tool, more cores or more memory than the server has. You add the machine once with one line; from then on, a check or a stage whose needs names one of its labels runs there, and its numbers come back to the loop as if it had run on the server (Resource hints).

docs.title: Whose machine it is
docs.text:
A server machine Your own machine Added by an admin any user Used by the loops of users whose group's Credentials is Server settings (as the server's agents) only the loops you own: never a loop shared with you, never anyone else's Code made with Admin › Runtime › Machines, or flux machines join-code on the server Account › Machines, or flux machines join-code --mine --user NAME on the server

A loop always uses its owner's machines, whoever starts it.

docs.title: What the machine needs
docs.text:
• Linux with systemd and Podman 4.9 or later from the distribution (cgroup v2): Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora, RHEL 9.4 and later have it. The line lets Podman limit the flux account's jobs itself. When the account's user manager does not have the cpu, memory and pids controllers yet, it writes /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/delegate.conf, runs systemctl daemon-reload and restarts that manager. It restarts only flux's manager, and only when nothing of flux's runs under it; otherwise it asks you to restart it later or reboot. A drop-in of yours that already delegates them is left alone. A host still on cgroup v1 stops the line (details).
  • Nix, multi-user (the official installer). The line sets it up for the flux account itself: it adds flux to allowed-users when Nix does not let it in yet, and adds Flux's binary caches and their keys (cache.nixos.org and nixchip0.cachix.org) when they are missing, then restarts nix-daemon. It writes them to /etc/nix/nix.custom.conf when your nix.conf includes that file (the Determinate installer's), else to the end of /etc/nix/nix.conf, in a block marked # Flux, keeping your own settings and a copy of the file as it was (nix.conf.before-flux). It never makes flux a trusted user. On NixOS it prints the nix.settings to add instead. FLUX_INSTALL_BUILD=1 leaves the caches alone (the tools then build on the machine, for hours).
  • The network to the Flux server and to the public Nix caches. Nothing else: no Git, no access to any repository, no credentials.

Run the line with sudo. The runner is a system service, flux-worker, running as the account flux (the line makes it when it is missing; on the server's own machine it is the server's account). When something is missing, the line says exactly what to install and stops; run it again afterwards.

docs.title: The Machines page
docs.text:
Admin › Runtime › Machines shows every machine, the server's and every user's (a user's carries its owner's name); Account › Machines shows your own and, below them, the server machines your loops may use (when your group's Credentials is Server settings): each one's name, labels, size and health, read-only, so you know which labels a step's needs can ask for. Both show:

  • At the top: how many cores, how much memory and how many of each device (a label with a number, such as fpga=1) the machines have, and how many are in use (on the admin's page, this server's own machine included). A device in use on every machine is simply busy, not a fault; "1 unhealthy" beside a total says a machine with it takes no step now.
  • A row per machine: its labels (× takes one away, + adds one: lab, fpga=1, board=zcu104), its use (2/16 cores and 8/56 GB: what its steps count of its size, each with a bar), its health (healthy, unhealthy with the reason, setting up or updating with what it is doing and for how long -- fetching its code, building its environment (with the paths fetched so far), checking itself --, draining or drained, away when it has not been heard from for five minutes, even while it was setting up), its running steps, its Flux version (old while it is behind the server's) and when it was last heard from. Point at a row for Rename, Drain/Resume, Rotate keys and Revoke (asked first).
  • This server is the first row on Admin › Runtime › Machines, tagged this server: the machine the server runs on, where every step without a label runs. Its use is what the steps running on it count. An admin gives it labels in its row (× and +, as any server machine's); nothing to drain or revoke, and Rename (its name is its host name until an admin renames it). On Account › Machines it is the first of the server machines, for everyone, its labels read-only.
  • Waiting: the steps no machine has taken yet, whose they are, what they need and why they wait.
  • Codes not used yet: each join code still good, with Cancel.

+ Add machine (an admin's: a server machine, or one of a user's own, chosen under Role) or + Add my machine asks for a name and labels, then shows the line to run on the new machine once, with Copy and, folded under it, the checked form for plain HTTP.

Labels set on the page replace the ones the machine was given before (on the code, on the line or in its capabilities.yaml): a label taken away here stays away. A user's own machine's labels are set by that user alone, on Account › Machines; on Admin › Runtime › Machines they show read-only, and an admin can still Drain, Resume or Revoke the machine.

docs.title: Add a machine from the server's console
docs.text:
On the server, make a join code (an admin's makes a server machine; --mine makes one of a user's own):

flux machines join-code --machine fpga-1 --label fpga=1 --label board=zcu104 --url http://flux.example.org:8765

It prints the code and the line to run on the new machine:

curl -fsSL http://flux.example.org:8765/worker/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- 'fx1-…@…'
  • The code works once and for one hour (--minutes for less). A second run of the same line, or a run after the hour, joins nothing: make a new code.
  • The line checks Podman and Nix, makes the flux account and its folders, joins the server, gets Flux from the server itself, prepares its tools from the public Nix caches (about 2 GB the first time), checks that a container starts, and starts the runner as the system service flux-worker (systemctl status flux-worker, journalctl -u flux-worker -f). It says each step as it goes.
  • The runner keeps its files in /var/lib/flux-worker and its cache in /var/cache/flux-worker.
  • Run the same line again (no code needed once the machine has joined) to repair the machine or change its options: it does only what is missing, keeps the machine's identity and restarts the runner.
  • Over plain HTTP, the server also prints a second form of the line that checks the installer's hash before running it; prefer it when the network between you and the server is not trusted.

Options after the code: --label KEY=VALUE (repeat) and --jobs N (steps at once, default 2; a run again keeps the number it had).

docs.title: A machine added before the system service
docs.text:
A machine added with an earlier form of the line (its runner a user service of your account) is no longer moved over by the line, and takes no step: the Machines page says it runs code older than the server's. Stop and remove its user service, then add it again with a new code:

systemctl --user disable --now flux-worker.service
rm -rf ~/.config/systemd/user/flux-worker.service ~/.local/share/flux-worker
systemctl --user daemon-reload

docs.title: Labels and needs
docs.text:
A machine's labels are what a step can ask for:

flow:
  measure:
    board:
      run: "{python} {home}/on_board.py {artifact}"
      metrics: [latency]
      needs: {fpga: true, board: zcu104}
  • key: true: the machine has the label; a number (fpga: 2) counts boards, GPUs or seats.
  • key: "2025.2": exactly that value; key: ">=2025.1": that version or newer.
  • cores, memory, disk, arch and os are what the machine measures itself; a label cannot set them.

A command that writes designs can ask for a machine the same way: Design's run, the baseline's, a search's run and the scope's commands take needs too (Resource hints). An agent's work always runs on the server.

Give labels on the code (--label), on the line (--label after the code), or in capabilities.yaml in the runner's folder (/var/lib/flux-worker). A label only your machine has (alice-board: true) sends your steps there and nobody else's.

This server's own machine takes labels too: in its row on Admin › Runtime › Machines, or on the server with flux machines label NAME --label fpga=1 --label board=zcu104 (all of its labels at once; none clears them; the same command sets a joined server machine's). A step whose labels it has runs on it like any other step, for users who may use the server machines.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Each step runs in its own Podman sandbox with the loop's sandbox settings (CPUs, memory, processes, /tmp), never above the machine's own size, and the server's network policy. A step whose needs says no memory sets none aside on the machine: it goes to any machine with its labels, and the sandbox's memory is its only limit.

docs.title: Which machine a step goes to
docs.text:
When several machines have a step's labels, a free one that already holds most of what the step needs gets it: the design's earlier stages (a runner keeps a design's intermediate files between its steps) and its input files. A step never waits for "its" machine: if that one is busy, another free machine with the labels runs it at once, with the same numbers. When several users' steps wait, the user who has waited longest since their last step started goes first. When this server has a step's labels too, the step runs here as soon as this server has room for it, and on a joined machine as soon as that one does: whichever is free first.

What a runner keeps counts toward its cache limit (FLUX_WORKER_CACHE_GB on the machine, default a quarter of its disk, at most 50 GB); the least recently used goes first.

docs.title: Proxies
docs.text: The line and the runner honour HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY. Set them in your shell before the line (it reads them even though sudo does not pass them on); the runner keeps the ones set then. Nix fetches through its own daemon: give the daemon the proxy too (its service's environment) when the caches are only reachable through it.

docs.title: When a machine cannot run a step
docs.text:
A full disk, a sandbox that does not start, or tools that are no longer there are the machine's problem, never the design's: the step goes back to the queue and runs on another machine that has its labels (or waits for one), and the machine is marked unhealthy until it checks itself again. flux machines list on the server shows each machine, its labels, its jobs and its health.

A step killed because the machine ran out of memory runs once more, on another machine when one has its labels.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
A machine added with the line updates itself when the server's Flux changes: it takes no new step, gets the new Flux from the server, prepares its tools again (only what changed, from the public Nix caches) and checks itself while its running steps go on, then restarts on the new Flux with the same identity in a few seconds. The steps it was running carry on through the restart and their results come back as usual; one that cannot (its container stopped meanwhile) is measured again, on this machine or another. Nothing to do on the machine, and no new join code. The machine shows "updating" only while it prepares and restarts; its steps stay in its jobs.

If an update fails (its tools do not build, its check fails), the machine stays on the Flux it had and takes no step until an update succeeds: flux machines list shows it as unhealthy with the reason, and it tries again after ten minutes or at the server's next update. A runner started by hand from a Flux checkout cannot update itself: run the install line on it once more (it keeps its identity). A machine added before the system service cannot either: add it again (above).

docs.title: Drain a machine
docs.text:
To take a machine out of use for a while (maintenance, a board to swap), drain it on the server:

flux machines drain fpga-1

It finishes the steps it is running and takes no new one; other machines with the same labels take them meanwhile. flux machines resume fpga-1 puts it back. Its owner can drain their own machine too.

docs.title: A storage machine
docs.text:
With many runners, each one fetching a loop's files from the server adds up. A storage machine holds those files for them: each file comes from the server once, and the runners fetch it from the storage machine. It runs no step itself.

Add one as an admin: + Add machine, Role Storage, or on the server flux machines join-code --role storage --machine store-1. Run the line it gives on the storage machine; it ends in --role storage:

curl -fsSL http://flux.example.org:8765/worker/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- 'fx1-…@…' --role storage
  • It needs Nix and the network to the server, but no Podman.
  • The runners must reach it on its port, 8766 by default. Options after --role storage: --listen HOST:PORT (where it listens, default 0.0.0.0:8766) and --url URL (the address the runners use, default http://<its name>:8766).
  • It keeps files unused for a week at most, and at most half of its disk (FLUX_STORAGE_GB on the machine for another limit); a file it no longer has is fetched from the server again.
  • While it is down, drained or unreachable, the runners fetch from the server as before. Nothing else changes.

It shows on the Machines page with a Storage tag.

docs.title: Rotate a machine's keys
docs.text:
Each machine has its own keys, made when it joined. To replace them (a machine that changed hands, a disk that was copied), choose Rotate keys in its row's menu (an admin for any machine, you for your own), or on the server:

flux machines rotate fpga-1

The machine makes new keys at its next heartbeat, within seconds, and carries on as the same machine with no new join code; its old keys stop working. Steps it is running finish as usual. The row says "new keys asked" until it has done so.

docs.title: Rename a machine
docs.text:
Point at its row and choose Rename (an admin for any machine, this server's own included; you for your own), or on the server:

flux machines rename fpga-1 lab-east

A name is lower-case letters, digits, ., _ and -, and no two machines share one: a name another machine has (a revoked one's too, or one a join code not used yet gives) is refused, and the refusal says whose it is. It is the same machine under a new name: no new join code, its keys, labels and steps stay its own, a step it is running finishes there and shows the new name at once, and the machine keeps its new name from its next heartbeat. Results measured before keep the name the machine had then.

docs.title: Remove a machine
docs.text: flux machines revoke NAME on the server (or, for your own machine, its Revoke): the machine is refused from then on. On the machine, sudo systemctl disable --now flux-worker, then remove /etc/systemd/system/flux-worker.service, /var/lib/flux-worker and /var/cache/flux-worker.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A loop's Results tab holds every design measured across all its starts. The decision is said in a line above three views: Designs, Graphs and Ideas. The library's digests are under Files › Library (an old link to Results › Library leads there).

docs.title: Designs
docs.text:
One card of the designs, in five tabs, each with its count -- each status led by the mark its STATUS column draws, in its tone (a check, the reject mark, a cross, a ring; All only its word):

  • All: the designs with numbers that count -- the accepted and the rejected, the decision first. The Graphs draw these only.
  • Accepted: checked and measured, every limit met at the stage that judges it.
  • Rejected: checked and measured, but a number misses a limit or a stage's cutoff; or rejected by a person or a critic (a pill under its name: "rejected by bob", "rejected by the critic"; a select critic's says what it rejected: "rejected by the critic (final)" for the design itself, "rejected by the critic (this pick)" for a pick that counts again once its numbers change). A rejected design keeps its row (Restore undoes it), and no graph draws it, not even faint: its numbers may be wrong. A design that went no further than an early stage -- a cutoff cut it, an estimate skipped the next stage, or its pass ended (or the run stopped) before it climbed -- is here too, with a pill stopped at screen: its numbers are that stage's, drawn muted and italic, early, not final.
  • Failed: a check refused it, or a measurement gave nothing (refused, failed, no numbers), or it was measured again and refused. No measurement columns: its checks (one pill, below: where it failed, ✗ gate, what failed heading its tooltip -- "check failed · gate: ..."), the failure reason (its words alone), when. A draft that Stop now or a kill cut before it was handed in ends the list, muted: its number, "stopped before handed in", when. It is no design: no text, nothing checked or measured, not counted in any tab, nothing to open. Its number stays spent and is never given to another design.
  • Pending: designs still to be measured: checked and not measured yet ("its pass ended before a stage measured it", "not measured yet: its pass is still running", "the run stopped before a stage measured it"), measured while their pass goes on and a later stage judges them (their numbers so far), and those asked to be measured again (re-measure pending, their old numbers muted: any standing rejection that asks for it -- yours, a critic's, Invalidate all's, the stale card's Re-measure -- as the loop itself sets the design aside). Once measured through, a design leaves Pending for Accepted or Rejected -- a refusal of an earlier re-measure no longer holds it.

A design measured before a change to how its stage is measured (its command, how its numbers are read, the params it takes, the files it reads or its tools: When a measurement still counts) stays in its tab with its numbers, muted, a small "measured before a change" mark after its name. The loop does not count those numbers, so no graph, ranking, pool or best draws them, and its detail says Not counted today. The Overview's card offers Accept as current, Leave as stale and Re-measure.

Checks (Failed and Pending) is one pill, one line high: the deepest stage the design went through, in the flow's order (build, quick check, gate, admit, then the measuring stages), with its latest outcome -- ✓ gate for a design waiting for its measurement, ✗ esl for one whose esl measurement failed. Hover it for every stage's latest outcome. Each stage's latest attempt is the design's state there: a gate that passed after it failed is passed; a stage measured through after it gave nothing is passed; a build that failed and was built later is passed (the gate that passed after it ran on what built). Which tab a design is in, Re-Evaluate's boxes (a box per tab) and the Overview's counts read the same.

A design's standing is its latest attempt, in the flow's order. When a newer attempt fails at a stage -- the gate refusing it after you changed the tests and re-evaluated, a stage that measured it before giving nothing now -- every stage after it from the older attempts is superseded: its old numbers are not the design's any more. It shows ✗ gate, not the old ✓ area; it is in Failed, with no numbers in the table, the Graphs, the ranking, the Pareto, the Overview or the Loops list's counts, and the loop itself no longer reads them (its frontier, who climbs, its decision). A design checked again and still being measured (a re-evaluation under way) is Pending with only what this attempt measured so far. The old attempts stay in the design's detail, folded under their stage, marked superseded ("the gate failed after it").

Only an attempt of the design supersedes. A pass that tries to improve a design and makes no new one (its agent wrote the same design again, failed, ran out of time) is no attempt of the design it started from: the refusal is on the record as "no design", in Live and the log, and the design keeps its numbers -- and stays the decision if it was one. A record from before this rule keeps such a refusal under the design's own name, as a failed gate; it is passed over the same way.

The measurements listed are the current ones. The table's columns, Settings › Preferences' Measurements, the Graphs' pickers, the Overview and Compare list what the designs' current attempts measured, and what the document names (its objectives, cutoffs and stages' metrics:). Change your scripts' metrics (or rename a stage) and re-evaluate: a metric only the old attempts carry -- superseded, set aside for a re-measure that has not measured them yet, or at a stage the document no longer has -- leaves the lists, as soon as anything is measured again. A design still waiting for its re-measure shows its old numbers under the columns that are still current; its detail keeps every number it had. A hidden or main measurement saved for a metric that left counts for nothing and comes back if the metric does. With every design set aside and none measured since, the lists are what the record holds.

Results opens on Accepted; the browser remembers the tab you choose; the address names it (…/results?tab=failed), and a link to a design opens it in its tab.

A page at a time. The table reads the rows it shows: scrolling to its end reads the next page (a spinner and "32 of 300" in the last row meanwhile). Choosing another tab or header reads the first page again in that order. Rows do not reshuffle while you scroll a running loop's results: the rows loaded are read again in place, the scroll where it was. A design opened from a graph or a link is brought into sight. The tab counts, the decision line and Compare work with every design, loaded or not.

Sorting. A header click sorts the table; the arrow turns at once, and the rows shown stay, dimmed under a small spinner, until the new order comes.

The table's own buttons are icons at the end of the tabs' row, each saying what it does on hover: the eye (hidden columns, how many beside it), the braces { } (inspect one dictionary), % (relative values), the star (the loop's ranking) and the two columns (compare, 1/2 once a design is ticked). A pressed one is tinted.

  • Order: the table opens in the loop's ranking (the star pressed and filled), as the Overview's Best 3: the decision, then the loop's rank, then the objective, best first. Click a header to sort by that column's values, the objective's and the limits' best first (a minimized one smallest first), designs with equal values in the ranking; click again for the other way, a third time (or the star) for the ranking. A design with no value in that column ("—", or a value that is not a number) is listed last whichever way.

  • Relative (%): numbers as they are, or, pressed, as percent change from the latest baseline (without one, from the accepted designs' 90th percentile, the 10th for a minimized objective, the median for a metric no objective ranks). Hover a cell for the value and its reference.

  • Numbers from an earlier stage: when stages measure different things (one timing, one area), a design's row shows each metric's deepest measurement; a number carried from an earlier stage is muted, and hovering it says which ("· from timing"). The design's detail writes that stage under the number.
  • Hidden columns (the eye): the columns hidden in Settings › Preferences shown again, dimmed, while it is pressed.
  • Dictionary metrics: a dictionary's column is its own name, its aggregate (its own _a, else the mean, when no objective says another: one no objective names is folded like any other). Its entries are no columns of their own: untick the dictionary's row in Settings › Preferences and it leaves the table whole -- no entry takes its place; tick one of its entries there (open the row with ▸) and that entry is a column after the dictionary's, read for it. To look into one, press { } among the table's icons ("Inspect one dictionary"; there only when the loop has dictionaries) and pick it in its menu (each with its entries' count): the table then shows that dictionary's entries alone as its columns -- cases, or the measurements under that metric -- under its name, every other measurement out of the way, sortable like any column. The icon stays pressed and a chip beside the icons names the dictionary ({ } timings ✕); ✕, or None at the end of the menu, brings the table back. The columns change at once, a spinner in each row while the entries are read; a dictionary hovered in the menu is read before you pick it, and one read already is drawn again without a read until the results change. A table of many rows and columns draws the rows in sight as you scroll. One dictionary at a time; your browser keeps the pick for the loop. A missing or empty entry stays unmeasured, never zero. Graphs charts a dictionary as its aggregate or per entry. {} raw has every number.
  • Compare (the two columns): tick two designs to see every number at every stage, the change (green where better, red where worse; a metric no objective ranks is not coloured), and their sources' difference.
  • A design opens with what it does not meet, its numbers at each stage, its idea and rationale, the rundown its design agent gave of it (Rationale: its key points, what it changed from the design it started from and why, "in its design agent's own words"; none for a model step's design or an agent that cannot resume), its checks -- one row per stage, in the flow's order: its latest attempt (outcome, time, output); the attempts it superseded folded under it (2 earlier attempts, a chevron before it, muted: the record keeps every one); a build said passed by the gate after it ("the gate passed after it, on what built": a build that passes is not recorded on its own); a stage that only ever measured it is in the numbers, not a row; a stage a newer attempt superseded is a muted superseded row ("the gate failed after it: not the design's now"), its attempts folded under it; its pass opens in Live with each check's log -- and its source; notes pinned on it from Chat, and Reference for comparison when it is marked so (for reading only: not the baseline the numbers compare with). The address names the open design (…/results?design=NAME): a link or a reload opens it.

docs.title: Checked, not measured
docs.text: A design only its checks judged opens the same detail as a measured one, with Not measured and why at its top: the check that refused it, a measurement tried that gave nothing ("its screen measurement was refused: estimated to fail"), or what it waits for. Check and measure again (its owner, with a reason) has it checked and measured at every stage: by the running loop before its next pass, or at rest by a run of its own; it waits in Pending until then. flux loop show NAME says the same reason ("not measured: …").

docs.title: Probed by agents
docs.text: A draft a design agent probed in its turn and did not hand in is listed, unverified -- never in the graphs, the decision or the standings. The Rejected and Failed tables end with them, under a quiet divider, probed by agents (3), folded until you open it. Each is a row of the table: its name says the pass it was probed in and its try there (#p4.2: pass 4, the second draft saved there; #pt1.1 under a trunk's branch t1), its agent's numbers sit in the table's columns, muted, and a column its agent did not measure is empty. Its state is an unverified pill; hover it for the reason ("not verified by the loop — probed by the agent only", or "failed the agent's own gate probe" with the check that failed) and why its numbers are not the loop's. Evaluate (the owner or an editor; audited) has the loop check, measure and choose it as a design of its own; it then has a number and the loop's verdict, and leaves the group. A draft also leaves the group once a design with exactly its text passed the loop's Check; flux loop show on that design says it was probed earlier.

docs.title: Reject a design
docs.text:
Reject on a design (its owner, with a reason) marks it: it stays shown but is never chosen. Tick its numbers to have them measured again or cleared. A rejection is the one way to set a design aside: it stays listed in the rejected tab with why and by whom. A design someone hid by hand before Nov 2026 (Also hide the design, Invalidated by hand) reads as such a rejection: "rejected by you: why", restored or measured again as any. A critic's rejection reads the same way; its detail names the critic (its agent), what it rejected (the design itself, final; or this pick, which lapses when its numbers change) and links Show the critic's reasoning: its critique in Live. Restore on a rejected design undoes every rejection standing on it at one press (a person's, a critic's, a refused re-measure); the loop, running, counts it again at its next decision. A design whose re-measure was refused offers Check and measure again beside Restore. The detail says when a re-measure happens: before the next pass (the loop running), by a run of its own (at rest: Live shows it), at the next start (Re-Evaluate's), or when a re-evaluation runs (Invalidate's).

A press (Restore, Reject, Check and measure again) reads the results again in place: the same table, its tab, order and scroll, the design open kept, the row and the tabs' counts drawn anew.

docs.title: Who made a design
docs.text: In a loop whose designs come from more than one maker -- a trunk: loop with several trunks, or several coding agents taking turns -- each design carries a small tag after its number: the trunk's id (t2), or the agent alone. Each maker keeps one colour throughout the table. Hover over the tag to see the whole of it ("made by trunk t1 (claude, opus)"); the design's head says who made it too ("made by trunk t2 (codex)"). A loop with one maker shows no tags.

docs.title: Star your key designs
docs.text:
Star, the first tool of a design's head (before Reject), marks it as one of your key designs: a bookmark for the loop, several at once. The loop's owner and its editors star and unstar, while it runs or at rest; everyone who may read the loop sees the stars. Each press is kept on the loop's record with who and when (Admin › Activity › Audit lists it too). The tool is an outline star; starred, it is filled in Flux's orange, its tooltip says who starred it.

The decision and a hand star are drawn apart: the decision is the loop's pick, a filled orange trophy after its name; a design you starred has a plain open orange star -- the same orange, a person's mark -- after its name in the table and in the design's head (a design both decided and starred has the trophy, then the star). Both sit on the text line at the same size. The table lists every design, starred or not: the star in a row is how you find it. The Graphs draw a starred design's point itself in Flux's orange (the legend says Starred); the decision's ring and the selected design's diamond stay as they are. The Overview's charts do not: there a starred design is a point like any other.

A star changes nothing the loop does: its decision, critics, pool and passes never read it. flux loop starred lists each starred design with who starred it, when, and its numbers.

docs.title: Share a design
docs.text:
Share, after the Star in a design's head, makes a read-only link to that one design, for people signed in to this Flux or for anyone with the link, for 1 to 90 days (never expires: signed-in only). It needs the Share right on the loop (its owner has it); without it there is no tool. The dialog lists the design's links, each with Copy and Revoke; Account › Shared links lists them all.

The link's page is live (an update to the design shows): the design's short name and the loop's, its standing (accepted, pending, failed, rejected) and the decision's trophy, its Measurements at each stage, its point Among the designs -- the objective's two numbers, this design in Flux's orange and every other design an unnamed grey dot -- its idea, its rationale (its design agent's rundown) and its Checks' outcomes. Never in a link: its code, a check's output, notes, people's rejection reasons, other designs' names, the loop, the library, and nothing the loop hides from its agents. Revoked, expired, the right lost or the design gone, the link shows This link does not open (Share says the rest).

docs.title: Invalidate, re-evaluate
docs.text:
After a check or a measurement script changed, the loop's Settings › Record has three tasks for the record:

  • Invalidate all (this loop only, at rest, after a confirmation; never from Admin › Server › Maintenance) sets every design on record aside: each stays listed in Pending with its old numbers, marked re-measure pending and never chosen. Nothing is measured again yet: above the table (and on the Overview's designs tile) it reads "40 of 40 set aside since …: re-measure pending until a re-evaluation runs". Running it again adds only designs recorded since.

  • Re-Evaluate asks the loop's next start: after its baseline, that start checks and measures again the designs of the Results tabs you tick, then its passes go on. Its dialog has a box per tab, each with its count as the tabs say it ("Rejected · 143"), and Rerun baseline; above them it says what the choice does, counted ("Re-checks and re-measures 12 accepted and 143 rejected designs at the next start, after its baseline"). One box at least:

    • Accepted, Rejected, Failed, Pending: the designs in that tab now, and no other. Pending is ticked by default -- those waiting for a stage (checked, not measured) and those set aside (re-measure pending): what Invalidate all set aside is measured only with Pending ticked. A design rejected by hand is in Rejected; measured again, its rejection stands. All four ticked is every design on record, invalidated first.
    • Rerun baseline: pass 0, first (a baseline on record otherwise stands).

A design already re-measure pending (a rejection asked for it) is measured at the start whatever is ticked, as at any start. Until that start the task's row and the Overview say what was asked ("the baseline measured again, then the failed and pending designs re-evaluated") with Cancel; it can be asked while the loop runs. Each design's new numbers replace the old as it is measured: "re-measured 12 of 40 since the invalidation at …". A stop keeps every design measured so far: "paused: 12 of 40 done; continues at the next start" -- the next start measures only the designs still pending, the one a stop cut short included. Stop now keeps every design measured so far too, those measured at once beside a slower one included; only the designs still being measured are measured again. A design today's checks refuse goes to Failed with why (check failed), until a later re-measure measures it through. - A design a check or a stage refused (it failed, did not build, crashed, timed out, or measured nothing) is refused there again from the record when it comes back with the same text, its check or tool not run: its row says "refused here before as #N, not run again", then what the check or stage said the first time. A check that passed a design is passed again the same way when the design comes back (a stage refused it, or it is written again): its row says "passed here before as #N, not run again". An edit to the loop's document or to a file the check reads, or Re-Evaluate, runs it again; the latest run's verdict, passed or refused, is the one kept.

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text:
• Pareto front: any two metrics, by default at the stage the loop decides on: the designs it decides among (its pool) drawn, every other design faint at the numbers it has, its point saying why it is not in the pool in Live's Choose words ("measured on screen only: its pass ended before it climbed to full", "cut on screen: …", "the same design as …", a stage the document no longer has); picking a stage draws that stage's numbers instead. The legend calls them excluded (left out of the pool). Accepted and failed coloured, the decision ringed, the front joined (its line has no legend key). Focus fits the axes to the feasible front and fades every point not on it (still there, still hoverable).
  • Improvement by design: the best so far for each metric chosen, design after design, each chart titled by its best and its change from the baseline ("best cycles (-12.9%)"; its value with no baseline). The best so far counts the designs the loop decides among (its pool), as the loop decides; every other design is drawn faint, its point saying why it is not in the pool. Baselines are gray reference lines. Focus keeps the metric's front -- the designs that set a new best, the corners of the best-so-far line -- as they are and fades every other point; the axes stay as they were. It is offered while a metric with a direction is charted (an extra number has no best); with Accepted only on as well, the accepted designs alone, those that set no new best faded.
  • The selected design is one for the page: a point clicked in any graph, a row opened in the table, or the design the address names. Every graph that plots it marks it the same way at once -- a diamond in Flux's orange (the logo's), larger than a point, over every other mark; on the Pareto front faint orange lines from it to both axes -- and its row in the table has an orange edge. A graph without it draws nothing more. Clicking it again, or Escape, clears it. In the Overview, a point clicked in a Best chart is marked in its other charts and on the Pareto front the same way (a Pareto point there still opens Graphs). The selection is the page's alone: nothing of the loop or its results changes.
  • Fullscreen (⛶) in each graph's card (here and the Overview's Best and Pareto front): the card's controls and graph in the fullscreen viewer, the graph drawn again at the larger size; Escape or ✕ closes it.
  • Zoom to an area (a dashed box, the last of each graph's controls, after Focus): turned on, drag over a graph to zoom both axes to that rectangle -- a nearly flat drag zooms x alone, a nearly upright one y alone; drag again to zoom further, a right-click goes back one zoom (up to 20), Escape drops a drag under way, a double-click shows the graph whole. Each graph keeps its own zoom while it is on; turning it off shows every graph whole again. A click still selects a point. Off, a drag does nothing.

Which way is better is an objective's alone: its direction, or its goal (>= 300, <= 0.5). A measurement no objective names (an extra number, a dictionary's mean) has none -- it is never guessed from its name: its graph draws its designs with no best so far and no best line ("not an objective"); a Pareto front with it on an axis draws the points and no front; its change in Compare is not coloured. Sorting its column works both ways.

Both graphs draw the designs of All (accepted and rejected; a failed or pending design has no numbers that count). A point says its design's standing in the table's words, from the same tab: a design is pending on a graph only when Pending lists it. One that went no further than an early stage is drawn hollow and its tooltip says stopped at screen and why ("went no further than screen: its pass ended without it climbing"), as its row does -- never "pending" or what it waited for.
